articles.title_zh: 2 of the best resorts in the world are in New England, according to Conde Nast Traveler readers
articles.content_orig:
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
Two seaside resorts in New England are among the best on the planet, according to Conde Nast Traveler readers.
The travel publication released a list of the 50 best resorts in the world on Tuesday, part of its 39th Annual Readers’ Choice Awards , and Chatham Bars Inn in Chatham ranked No. 18. Weekapaug Inn in Westerly, R.I. ranked No. 28.
Chatham Bars Inn , which was also named the No. 1 resort in New England , is “a benchmark of luxury on the Cape,” Conde Nast Traveler wrote.
“If you’re looking for a full-service resort with all the bells and whistles and then some, this is it, including an eight-acre private farm to stock the resort’s numerous dining and drinking outlets; one of the better spas on the Cape; an expansive pool deck with F&B service; a private quarter-mile beachfront; tennis courts with lessons available; and a 24-hour gym,” wrote the publication.
Resort officials celebrated on social media , writing, “Thank you to our incredible team and to our guests and supporters who voted for us. We’re grateful to be recognized alongside so many remarkable destinations.”
Weekapaug Inn, also named the No. 2 resort in New England , is a historic getaway in Rhode Island.
“A recently renovated legendary seaside inn on the National Register of Historic Places, the 27-room, six-suite Weekapaug Inn is a three-hour drive from New York and less than two from Boston—ideal for a quick weekend jaunt,” wrote Conde Nast Traveler .
Visitors enjoy guided nature walks, golf, tennis, and boating expeditions in historic vessels, noted the publication.
Officials at Weekapaug Inn also shared their excitement on social media , writing, “Thank you to the Condé Nast Traveler readers who voted, and to our incredible teams for truly delivering the best of service, cuisine, and luxury, year after year. We hope to share our award-winning experiences with you soon.”
The No. 1 resort in the world is Cheval Blanc Seychelles, according to Conde Nast Traveler readers.
This year, Conde Nast Traveler readers cast 798,867 votes for the annual awards, determining the very best in hotels, resorts, spas, airlines, and more worldwide. The results will be featured in the magazine’s November issue.
Kristi Palma is the travel writer for Boston.com, focusing on the six New England states. She covers airlines, hotels, and things to do across Boston and New England. She is the author of the award-winning Scenic Six , a weekly travel newsletter.

articles.title_orig: Why China’s export engine may hit a ceiling as trading partners face limits
articles.title_zh: Why China’s export engine may hit a ceiling as trading partners face limits
articles.content_orig:
Exports likely to keep growing in near term but could face pressure in the years ahead, analysts say
While China’s export engine still has room to grow, many of its trading partners may be approaching the limit of how much more they can absorb, which could place a ceiling on further growth over the coming years, according to a Goldman Sachs report.
“At least over the next few years, there is still room for Chinese exports to maintain their strong momentum,” analysts said in the report led by the American investment bank’s chief China economist Hui Shan on Wednesday. “Over the longer term, however, stronger economic growth in importing economies will be required for continued Chinese export gains.”
Even under the bank’s most conservative projection, China’s real exports could grow by 8 per cent annually in the near term, despite the country posting a record US$1.2 trillion trade surplus last year.
Much of that momentum was driven by supply-side factors in China, according to the report, with export volumes rising since 2021 even as profitability across industries declined. In the automotive sector, for example, export value nearly doubled between 2021 and 2025, while profit margins fell from 6.4 per cent to 4.8 per cent.

articles.title_orig: FO Live: German Economy Now Faces the China Challenge: What Lies Ahead?
articles.title_zh: FO Live: German Economy Now Faces the China Challenge: What Lies Ahead?
articles.content_orig:
In this episode of FO Talks, Atul Singh and Stefan and Mauritz Halusa discuss China’s transformation from a major market for German exports into a powerful industrial competitor. Germany’s former economic model is buckling as Chinese competition exposes its dependence on exports, energy imports and traditional manufacturing. However, Germany could recover by accelerating innovation, strengthening European cooperation and building a more resilient economy.
This article saved into your bookmarks. Click here to view your bookmarks.
Editor-in-Chief Atul Singh speaks with Stefan Halusa, founder and managing director of Halusa Advisors, and Mauritz Halusa, its co-founder, about the mounting Chinese challenge to German industry. The father-son duo explains how China evolved from a lucrative market for German machinery and automobiles into a formidable competitor in many of the same industries. Atul, Stefan and Mauritz examine Germany’s growing trade deficit, the crisis facing its carmakers, the German struggle to innovate, rising energy costs and whether Europe’s largest economy can adapt.
Stefan began visiting China in 1997, four years before the country joined the World Trade Organization (WTO). China’s subsequent industrial expansion initially brought enormous benefits to Germany. In the years after Beijing joined the WTO, Chinese companies bought German machinery, Chinese consumers purchased German cars and German businesses became major investors in the country.
Trade between Germany and China was nearly balanced in 2001 and 2002, with China recording an annual surplus of only about €3 billion. Even in 2019, immediately before the Covid-19 pandemic, Germany’s bilateral trade deficit stood at approximately €13 billion. By 2025, however, it had approached €90 billion. Chinese exports to Europe continued growing in 2026 while German exports to China declined.
Several factors drove this reversal. The collapse of China’s property market damaged household wealth because many Chinese families had placed much of their savings in real estate. Falling property values weakened consumer confidence and reduced domestic consumption. Beijing responded to slowing growth by emphasizing industrial production and exports, particularly in electric vehicles (EVs), robotics, industrial automation, advanced materials, medical devices and biotechnology.
These are also sectors in which German manufacturers traditionally excel. China and Germany are therefore no longer competing only for Chinese consumers. Their companies increasingly confront one another across international markets.
Stefan points to Chinese state subsidies and what he considers a significantly undervalued renminbi as additional advantages for Chinese exporters. Meanwhile, US tariffs have restricted access to the American market, redirecting more Chinese products toward Europe, Germany’s most important trading region.
For decades, Germany pursued Wandel durch Handel , or change through trade. This policy rested on the liberal expectation that deeper commercial ties would encourage political openness in China. Mauritz calls that assumption a “drastic miscalculation.” Trade enriched both countries, but it did not produce the political transformation Germany anticipated.
Mauritz argues that China’s dependence on exports is not simply a temporary response to economic weakness. In his view, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) has consistently prioritized manufacturing and exports over household consumption. The CCP’s Five-Year Plans devote far greater attention to production and trade than to stimulating domestic demand.
Low consumption enables China to direct resources toward industrial expansion, but it also creates excess production that must be sold abroad. This pressure has intensified as the property crisis has reduced household spending and increased dependence on exports. Falling prices, factory closures and job losses could depress consumption further, creating a damaging economic cycle.
Atul adds that Chinese society has endured the Taiping Rebellion, foreign occupation, civil war, the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution. Such upheavals can produce habits of caution and saving that outlast a political system. Germany also saves more and consumes less than many English-speaking economies, partly because of its own history of hyperinflation, war and economic destruction.
Atul therefore doubts that Chinese consumption would rise dramatically even if the country became a liberal democracy. Mauritz accepts the importance of culture but maintains that China’s political economy reinforces these tendencies through deliberate planning.
Whatever combination of history, culture and state policy explains Chinese behavior, Stefan believes German companies must accept the result. China’s export orientation is “not just a phase of two or three years,” he says. Germany cannot wait for the old commercial relationship to return. Its industries must prepare for sustained competition from Chinese companies in China, Europe and the wider world.
The automotive industry exposes Germany’s predicament particularly clearly. Mercedes-Benz, BMW, Porsche and Volkswagen built their reputations on engineering excellence, reliability and carefully controlled development. Yet EVs have changed the basis of competition. Software, batteries, digital features and rapid product updates now matter as much as traditional mechanical engineering.
Stefan divides the challenge into two related contests: cost and technology. German carmakers typically take 30 to 36 months to develop a vehicle. This method produces a refined and high-quality product, but Chinese manufacturers can release a model and update it two or three times before a German competitor completes one development cycle. Their initial product may be less polished, but they improve it rapidly in response to consumer demand.
German companies must consequently learn how to shorten development cycles and integrate software more effectively. Stefan says this helps explain why several manufacturers are transferring research and development capacity to China. They want to operate closer to the world’s largest automotive market and absorb the speed and customer focus of their Chinese competitors.
China also offers a substantial cost advantage. German manufacturers pay higher wages and energy prices while carrying a heavier administrative burden. Major German manufacturers and suppliers still make between 20% and 40% of their products in Europe, with Porsche producing an even larger share there. Stefan does not regard high wages as a problem in themselves, since prosperous societies should compensate workers well. He instead emphasizes automation, industrial artificial intelligence and reduced bureaucracy as ways to improve productivity.
Germany can learn from countries besides China. South Korean companies adapt products quickly to local markets, while India combines engineering talent with unconventional and economical approaches to innovation. German companies are already establishing research and competence centers in India to incorporate industrial AI into their production processes and products.
Volkswagen’s expanding innovation center in the Chinese city of Hefei illustrates the difficult choices facing German industry. The facility contains over a hundred laboratories for software, hardware, batteries and electric powertrains. In November 2025, Volkswagen said it could manufacture an EV entirely in China for half the cost of producing one elsewhere.
Stefan describes the logic as “if you can’t beat them, join them.” Volkswagen has invested heavily in China and earned substantial profits there; it cannot easily abandon the world’s largest automotive market. China’s rapid adoption of electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles also gives German companies access to valuable battery expertise and an enormous base of consumers.

articles.title_orig: A UMass study has revealed two of the world’s loudest birds. Here’s what they sound like.
articles.title_zh: A UMass study has revealed two of the world’s loudest birds. Here’s what they sound like.
articles.content_orig:
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
University of Massachusetts Amherst biologists have discovered two contenders for the world’s loudest birds, both from Brazil.
The bare-throated bellbird and the red-legged seriema are louder than jackhammers and may just be the loudest birds in the world, according to a study published in Evolution by UMass professor Jeff Podos and his former graduate student João Menezes.
This isn’t the first groundbreaking discovery for Podos. In fact, his research established a Guinness World Record in 2019 when he discovered that the Amazon’s white bellbird had the world’s loudest bird call, louder than a revving chainsaw.
The latest discovery is the result of Podos and Menezes’s years of ongoing research to understand the role evolutionary biology plays in how birds communicate with each other. Their research aims to solve the mystery of why some birds are so much louder than others, and whether there are certain physical traits that can predict their volume.
Menezes said it’s difficult to measure how loud a bird call is in the field, and there’s little data available. But using cutting-edge tools, Podos and Menezes have gathered reliable amplitude data on 123 species throughout Massachusetts and Brazil, 113 of which had never before had their volume catalogued.
“We’ve been able to vastly increase the number of species for which there is amplitude data,” Podos said. “This is basic, foundational research that no one else has managed to do on this scale, and it points to all sorts of other questions that would be fun to follow up.”
Podos and Menezes discovered there’s a 58-decibel range in the volume of bird calls, from the hummingbird, whose calls are 64 decibels and about the volume of a normal conversation, to bare-throated bellbirds and red-legged seriemas, who register at over 120 decibels.
They found that the loudest birds are typically bigger, with wider beak openings and bulky muscles that may allow greater air compression for explosive volume. But Podos and Menezes said there’s still a lot unknown about how birds communicate.
“We now know some of the hows,” Menezes said. “Bigger bodies and wider beaks. But we’ve yet to discover the whys, and we probably need much more data from many more species to be able to tease out what’s going on on the ecological and evolutionary front.”

articles.title_orig: Dow falls 500 points as 10-year yield rises to highest level in 24 years: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow falls 500 points as 10-year yield rises to highest level in 24 years: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stocks fell on Wednesday as pressure continued to build in the bond market, pushing Treasury yields to levels not seen in more than two decades .
The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 503 points, or 1%, while the S&P 500 shed 0.6%. The Nasdaq Composite slipped 0.7%.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield climbed more than 8 basis points to trade at 5.356%. The yield reached its highest level since April 2002 . The 30-year bond yield gained more than 8 basis points to 5.725%. It had hit its highest level since May 2002.
The moves come ahead of a planned auction by the Treasury Wednesday, in which it's planning to sell $39 billion of 10-year notes.
Bank stocks dropped as investors feared higher interest rates would hinder lending activity. Shares of Goldman Sachs moved down nearly 3%, while Citigroup pulled back more than 2%. Others such as Bank of America , Wells Fargo and JPMorgan shed more than 1%.
Technology stocks also came under pressure amid worries that higher borrowing costs would limit the artificial intelligence buildout. CrowdStrike shares were lower by 3%, while Palo Alto Networks and Meta Platforms each lost more than 2%.
Meanwhile, U.S. crude prices also crept back toward $90 per barrel. International Brent crude futures , meanwhile, traded nearly 1% higher at around $101 per barrel. Those moves led yields, which took a breather in the previous session, to resume the recent surge that drove them to multiyear highs.
The S&P 500 closed above 7,800 for the first time on Tuesday, led by gains in chipmakers. Bond yields also eased, giving equities a boost.
"Stocks have gotten cheaper since January which is ironic, since we're hitting all-time highs," said Nancy Tengler, CEO and CIO of Laffer Tengler. "I don't mind multiple compression because it tells me that this bull market is sustainable and it elongates it. I like where we sit for this bull market, and earnings growth does ultimately drive stock price performance."
Investors are awaiting the minutes of the Federal Reserve's last meeting in September, at which the U.S. central bank raised interest rates for the first time since 2023. Minutes are set to shed light on how monetary policymakers are thinking about economic conditions.
Gold hit a low of 4,091.2 on Wednesday, reaching the lowest level since Aug. 3, when it traded as low as 4,074.
The move lower is helped in part by a strong dollar which make dollar-denominated metals more expensive to foreign buyers.
Gold has not traded below 4,000 since July 20 when gold hit a low of 3,986.
Gold Miners (GDX) are down 3.85% on pace for worst day since Sep. 28 when the GDX fell -5.36%
Silver also hit a low of $59.23, the lowest level since Aug. 4 when silver traded as low as $58.18.
— Gina Francolla and Paulina Likos
The three major averages began Wednesday's session in the red.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 340 points, or 0.7%, just after 9:30 a.m. ET, while the S&P 500 dropped 0.4%. The Nasdaq Composite declined 0.5%.
Morgan Stanley upgraded Gold Fields to Overweight, saying the stock's underperformance has created an attractive risk-reward setup.
Gold Fields has lagged global gold peers by about 16% this year. But according to Morgan Stanley's analyst Christopher Nicholson much of the uncertainty around its Tarkwa mining lease is already priced in.
"We think Tarkwa lease risk is largely priced; in addition, a potential Northern Star deal looks accretive on a pro forma basis. We update earnings estimates and price targets on the back of our latest price deck – the risk-reward for gold skews upwards," said Nicholson.
Overall, the analyst remains bullish on the gold , naming the yellow metal as its top commodity pick and forecasting an average price of $5,050 an ounce in 2027. Nicholson said gold could benefit from concerns around government debt, potential intervention to cap bond yields, swings in oil prices and continued central-bank buying.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury note rose nearly 8 basis points to hit a high of 5.350% on Wednesday, officially topping its high from Monday.
The marks the highest level since April 3, 2002, when it reached 5.379%.
— Nick Wells and Sean Conlon
Check out the companies making headlines before the bell:
Constellation Brands shares fell 5% even after the company reported better-than-expected results for its fiscal second quarter.
The beer distributor earned an $3.74 per share on revenue of $2.63 billion. Analysts expected a profit of $3.56 per share on revenue of $2.54 billion.
That said, beer operating margins decreased by 160 basis points year on year. Depletions, a key demand metric for the company, fell slightly from the year-earlier period as well.
The chief executive of U.S. oil giant Chevron on Wednesday warned it would be "unwise" for the Trump administration to move forward with a diesel export ban , saying the policy runs the risk of making the supply situation worse.
"The U.S. has been a reliable supplier to the world at a time when it needs it," Chevron CEO Mike Wirth told CNBC's " Squawk Box Europe " in an exclusive interview on Wednesday.
"And I think it would be unwise for the U.S. to create questions in the minds of our allies and our partners as to whether or not we will be there with reliable supply when times are difficult — and so, there are other options," he added.
Average house prices in the U.K. were flat in September, according to data from lender Lloyds , after falling 0.3% the previous month.
The average property price in the country is now £298,441 ($395,005), compared to £298,395 in August. The index was also flat on an annual basis.
"While the market overall has been fairly subdued, property prices have so far proved resilient during a period of higher mortgage rates, which has been driven by changing expectations around the future path of Base Rate," Andrew Asaam, mortgages director at Lloyds, said in the data release. "That's mirrored in wider economic data, with household spending holding up better than many expected despite energy and other cost pressures arising from the Middle East conflict."
Japan's Nikkei 225 closed 0.92% lower at 70,035.71, and the broader Topix fell 0.70% to 4,154.11.
South Korea's Kospi declined nearly 2% to 6,803.90, while the small-cap Kosdaq lost 2.34% to 898.43.
Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 ended flat at 8,727.70.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was down 0.50% as of its last hour of trade on Wednesday. Mainland China market remained closed for the Golden Week holiday.
Shares listed in Europe opened broadly lower on Wednesday, with the regional Stoxx 600 index down 0.4% shortly after the bell.
Mining and tech stocks led losses, while Germany's DAX — down 0.9% — notched the biggest decline among major regional bourses.
Yields on bonds issued by various governments moved higher on Wednesday morning, amid lingering economic concerns.
The yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury was up 4 basis points to 5.309% as of 2:30 a.m. ET. Yields on the longer-maturity 30-year Treasury note added almost 5 basis points to 5.688%.
Bond yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Yields on U.K. government bonds, known as gilts, also rose across the curve, with 10- and 20-year bond yields rising by 5 basis points.
Meanwhile, French and Italian 10-year government bond yields rose by 8 basis points. Japanese bonds bucked the trend, with yields trading marginally lower.
NLFI, a non-profit organization that manages shares of nationalized or bailed-out financial institutions owned by the Dutch state, said Wednesday that it would sell part of its stake in lender ABN Amro.
The sale would be carried out through a pre-arranged trading plan, executed by BofA Securities Europe, it said. Once completed, it would reduce NLFI's holding of ABN Amro to a 10.5% stake, down from 20.7%.

articles.title_orig: Reports of sexual violence are up. Data from Cornell and other colleges in 8 charts.
articles.title_zh: Reports of sexual violence are up. Data from Cornell and other colleges in 8 charts.
articles.content_orig:
Professors and staff at Cornell University grilled administration officials Tuesday as outrage builds over the alleged gang rape of a former student at a fraternity house in 2024, with questions raised about how the school and law enforcement responded.
University officials confirmed two students named in a civil lawsuit filed last month by the woman are still enrolled and attending classes, according to a recording of a virtual webinar obtained by CNN.
Some faculty members said they are struggling to teach classes the accused students are in and raised questions about how to accommodate them and other students. They also pressed for answers about transparency and a perceived lack of communication over the case, and how to address cultural issues with Greek life on campus.
“This is certainly and most intimately a Cornell community cultural challenge that we’re facing,” Ryan Lombardi, vice president for student and campus life, said at the meeting. “But we know that the world is watching, and we know that we’re all feeling that.”
A spokesperson for Cornell University did not respond to CNN’s request for comment.
The meeting comes a day after faculty members submitted a resolution for a vote of no confidence against the school’s administrators.
Since the lawsuit was filed, frustrations on campus have grown with students and community members rallying in support of Jane Doe and calling for more accountability by university administrators.
A seven-hour sit-in is planned on campus Wednesday. The mayor of Ithaca, where Cornell is located, is also expected to hold a council meeting over his proposal to pause Greek life and student gatherings .
University President Michael Kotlikoff released a video over the weekend saying the school would take a “serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities on campus,” but cautioned Tuesday against targeting only Greek organizations.
“This is obviously an absolutely horrendous and inexcusable situation that occurred in a fraternity,” Kotlikoff said Tuesday. “But I have to make the point that this doesn’t only occur in fraternities, I worry about pushing this into the shadows, into houses which we don’t own, which are private houses, which have parties, and which things can occur beyond our purview.”

CNN’s Hanna Park, Kara Scannell, Taylor Galgano, Holly Yan and Isa Mudannayake contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Russia says plague institute worker's death does not risk an epidemic
articles.title_zh: Russia says plague institute worker's death does not risk an epidemic
articles.content_orig:
The victim was working at the anti-plague institute in the Siberia city of Irkutsk
US President Donald Trump has said he will speak with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin soon about the death of a lab worker at a plague research centre in Siberia.
"So far we are in very deep discussions," Trump said, adding that he would be able to report on his talks with Putin "probably" on Thursday. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said no phone call had been scheduled.
Russian officials say they are investigating the cause of the 28-year-old's death and have not confirmed that the suspected disease is pneumonic plague - a serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague.
They insist "there are no epidemic risks for the population".
The US, however, has issued a formal diplomatic message to Russia requesting additional information. Peskov told reporters he was not aware of such a request.
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for transparency from Russia.
"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks," Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, President Vladimir Putin's spokesman said Russia's reporting of the death to the WHO was in line with standard practice. He accused the media of reporting "false information".
Reports first emerged on Friday of almost 200 people being placed under observation in Siberia's Irkutsk region following the death.
The lab worker, named in Russian media as Darya Shipilova, had reportedly fallen ill a couple of days earlier.
Unconfirmed reports suggested that she had become ill after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen at the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East where she worked - or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents.
As the US and the WHO sought more information, the country's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, issued a statement saying "there are no epidemic risks for the population of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk region".
It said more than 90% of the people who had been in contact with the victim had "completed medical observation" and "no health disorders associated with infectious pathology were detected".
In the immediate wake of the laboratory worker's death, Rospotrebnadzor had issued a statement saying the woman had died of "pneumonia of an undetermined etiology" and that testing found "no microorganisms related to her professional activities".
However, after this announcement, a pro-government federal news outlet deleted five posts mentioning a possible plague case, and authorities in the town of Baikalsk deleted a message advising against travel to Shelekhov because of a possible plague infection.
Ongoing speculation into the lab worker's death has sparked a back and forth between Russia and the US, with questions about a possible spread outside of Russia.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US had "measures" available to help Russia if the situation turned out to be more serious than claimed.
According to the WHO, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours - and can be fatal, if not diagnosed and treated early.
People can be infected through:
contact with bodily fluids or contaminated materials
the inhalation of respiratory particles
Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often with blood-tainted phlegm.
The bacterium that causes the plague, Yersinia pestis, found among rodents such as marmots in the area.
It killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death .
It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, was founded just over 100 years ago.

articles.title_orig: The School Near Paris That Shows Why French Students Are Protesting
articles.title_zh: The School Near Paris That Shows Why French Students Are Protesting
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz condemns violence in Paris, says open-border and migration policies helped fuel frustration now boiling over across France.
FIRST ON FOX: President Donald Trump warned Tuesday that France’s escalating riots were being driven by "out of control mass migration," as U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz echoed those concerns and blamed unchecked immigration and broader European policy failures for helping fuel the unrest.
Asked by Fox News Digital about Trump’s comments and the scenes emerging from France, Waltz condemned the violence while also linking the unrest to European immigration and economic policies.
"I think we would always condemn lawlessness, condemn the violence that we're seeing in Paris," Waltz told Fox News Digital. "But I think we also have to recognize that when you have open borders, when you [have] this pro-migration, unchecked immigration kind of policy, coupled with policies over the years that deny people basic energy, that overspend on all kinds of other government programs, that you see a level of frustration boiling to the surface."
FRANCE EXPLODES AGAIN AS STUDENTS RIOT OVER EDUCATION
Protesters hold a Palestinian flag during demonstrations in Strasbourg, France, on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. (Kai Pfaffenbach/Reuters)
Trump weighed in as the unrest intensified, arguing that what was unfolding went beyond the students’ complaints about France’s education system. "What’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration. This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!" Trump wrote on Truth Social Tuesday.
"Unfortunately, I think you're seeing the results of some of that, and President Trump has brought that to light," Waltz added.
The comments came as France faced its biggest day of school unrest since the protests began in September. On Tuesday, police fired tear gas in Paris and other major cities, protesters lit fires and hurled projectiles, and France’s Interior Ministry said 6,100 people had been arrested, the overwhelming majority of them minors, according to Reuters. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu described the clashes as producing the school system’s "heaviest toll in decades".
FRANCE’S VIOLENT STUDENT PROTESTS RAISE WARNING FOR AMERICA: ‘A CAUTIONARY TALE’
A protester feeds a burnt barrier during a blockading action outside the secondary school Le Corbusier, in Aubervilliers, northern Paris on Oct. 1, 2026. (Lou Benoist/AFP via Getty Images)
France’s Interior Ministry said 6,100 people have been arrested so far, the overwhelming majority of them minors. Lecornu told lawmakers Tuesday that at least 215 teenagers and 85 school staff members have been injured, while his office said more than 700 police officers have also been hurt, according to Reuters .
The latest demonstrations brought clashes in Paris , Lyon, Strasbourg and Rennes, where police fired tear gas as protesters lit fires and hurled projectiles. More than half of France’s roughly 3,700 high schools were blockaded or expected to close Tuesday, according to the High School Students Union. The ⁠Paris police said the clashes there had come about when some 300 people attempted to face off against security forces, adding that the protest was generally unfolding well elsewhere.
Theo Wold, a former assistant attorney general and former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy under Trump, also argued that immigration was contributing to the unrest .
FRANCE ROCKED BY STUDENT RIOTS AS HUNDREDS ARRESTED, VIOLENCE SPREADS NATIONWIDE
Masked protesters install a barricade amid clashes with police during a protest near the Lycee Berthelot high school in Aubervilliers, near Paris, Oct. 2, 2026. (Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters)
"The French are notorious for strikes, labor stoppages and street demonstrations. It’s a core part of the Fifth Republic’s civic culture," Wold told Fox News Digital. "What’s new is the violence, lawlessness and rioting. This is a consequence of mass immigration."
While Trump, Waltz and Wold linked the violence to immigration, Reuters and AP have reported that the protest movement began over school conditions , including teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms , deteriorating buildings and education funding. Students have cited overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and deteriorating school buildings — including water leaks and rat infestations — among their grievances.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Rioters clash with police in Lyon, central eastern France, on Oct. 1, 2026. (Alex Martin AFP via Getty Images)
The unrest has increasingly become part of a broader political fight ahead of France’s presidential election in April and May 2027. Reuters reported last week that French authorities and political opponents have accused lawmakers and mayors from the hard-left France Unbowed party , or LFI, of stoking the demonstrations. LFI has denied the accusations.
Fox News Digital's Greg Norman-Diamond and Reuters contributed to this story.
Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict , global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.
Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

articles.title_zh: TKACHOVA AND GARNIER WIN GOLD AS LEIPZIG CLOSES THE EUROPEAN SEASON
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine’s Daria Tkachova and France’s Marceau Garnier took the Speed titles at the final World Climbing Europe Series event of 2026
The World Climbing Europe Series 2026 concluded in Leipzig, Germany, with closely contested Speed finals. Spain and Ukraine each claimed two medals.
Ukraine’s Daria Tkachova won gold in 7.88 seconds, finishing ahead of Poland’s Magdalena Blachnicka, who stopped the clock at 8.58. The victory adds to Tkachova’s bronze medal from St. Pölten, Austria, earlier this year.
Blachnicka improved on her previous podium result, stepping up from bronze in Žilina, Slovakia, to silver in Leipzig.
Ukraine’s Mariia Shymkova, who won silver in Žilina, returned to the podium in third place. She clocked 7.58 to narrowly beat teammate Sofiia Tulchynska’s 7.63.
For the women’s Speed event complete results click here .
France’s Marceau Garnier won the men’s Speed event in 4.99 seconds, beating Spain’s Miguel Gómez Barrios by five hundredths of a second in the gold-medal race.
Gómez Barrios had earlier set a personal best of 4.96 in his semi-final against France’s Jérôme Morel, becoming the second Spanish climber to break the five-second barrier after Erik Noya.
Spain secured another medal through Alberto García Rodríguez de Sepúlveda, whose 5.49 edged Morel’s 5.50 in the bronze-medal race.
For the men’s Speed event complete results click here .
Following the release of next year's international competition calendar, the 2027 European events calendar will also be presented in the coming days.
All European events have been live streamed on the World Climbing Europe YouTube channel and are available on demand. News and updates about all World Climbing events will be available on the World Climbing website , and on the Federation’s digital channels: Facebook , Instagram , LinkedIn , Threads , TikTok , X , YouTube , and exclusively for the Chinese audience, Douyin, Weibo , and Xiaohongshu.

articles.title_orig: Germany: Ex-spy chief sent to pretrial detention on treason charges
articles.title_zh: Germany: Ex-spy chief sent to pretrial detention on treason charges
articles.content_orig:
Former German foreign intelligence agency boss August Hanning appeared before a federal judge in the western city of Karlsruhe on Wednesday following his arrest on espionage and treason charges Tuesday.
He has been ordered to remain in detention ahead of his trial, according to federal prosecutors.
Manfred D., Hanning's former chief of staff at the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) , was also detained.
Manfred D. is accused of having stolen secret documents and turned these over to Hanning, who, as a private-sector security adviser, in turn reportedly sold the secret documents to an as yet unnamed foreign spy agency or agencies.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Investigators estimate the two stole and potentially passed on more than 2,000 secret documents between 2010 and 2023. Federal investigators say it is unclear how much information was stolen and to whom it was sold.
Hanning ran the BND, Germany's foreign intelligence service, from 1998 until 2005 before becoming state secretary at the Federal Interior Ministry and then entering private business as a security adviser.
The issue has raised serious questions about the trustworthiness of Germany's intelligence agencies and shocked politicians into action as they claim not enough is being done to ensure high-ranking officials do not abuse their experience when transitioning to jobs in the private sector.
Although it is currently not known who Hanning's potential customers were, Germany's weekly Der Spiegel magazine on Wednesday named Azerbaijan as one. The Azerbaijan Media and Broadcasting Council vehemently denied the accusation, calling it "unfounded" and adding, "The malicious intent of the ‌forces behind this disinformation operation is ‌to ​damage Azerbaijan-Germany relations."

articles.title_orig: 11 Places to See the World's Most Magnificent Wildlife Migrations
articles.title_zh: 11 Places to See the World's Most Magnificent Wildlife Migrations
articles.content_orig:
Seeing an immense number  of creatures assembled in one place is a phenomenon worth travelling for. Here’s when, where and how to experience some of nature’s wildest gatherings.
Seeing any animal in the wild is a privilege — but seeing huge numbers is something else. For a start, it’s both humbling and heartening to encounter any species in abundance. It’s also genuinely exciting. When big groups of creatures seasonally cluster in one place, there’s always something to watch — from courting and mating to fighting or family-raising. It may be a sensory assault, too: noise, tumult, pungent smells, crashing waters, mad flurries of dust. And where masses gather to move together, hungry predators may lurk, adding a macabre but fascinating dimension. Here, we’ve picked the most dramatic migrations through the year and around the globe.
When to go: December to March
How does an insect the weight of a paperclip make a journey of 3,000 miles? That’s the feat of the extraordinary monarch butterfly, which somehow flutters from its summer breeding grounds — spread across Canada and the American northeast — to a patch of oyamel fir forest in the highlands west of Mexico City. Most only survive for a month or so but, in autumn, a generation emerges that lives eight times as long, capable of making this perilous trip. How they know where to go is a mystery — the butterflies that migrate are the great-great-grandchildren of those that left Mexico the previous spring. No matter, the results are spectacular: millions upon millions of orange-black wings blanketing trees, raining like tickertape. The Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve, in the mountains of Michoacán state, is home to more than half of the overwintering colonies of the monarch butterfly’s eastern population. The sanctuary of El Rosario is easiest to reach; lesser-visited Sierra Chincua can be explored on horseback. The colourful, cobblestoned Mineral de Angangueo makes a good base.
The Indigenous Sámi of Europe’s far north work to their own calendar. Their year has eight seasons, and giđđa (spring) means melting snows, fast-increasing daylight and reindeer on the move: around April, the animals start migrating from their inland pastures towards the coast for summer grazing. Norway has around 275,000 reindeer, some wild, but mostly semi-domesticated herds that are ushered across the country’s Arctic plateaus by Sámi families whose livelihoods have depended on the practice for generations. Finnmarksvidda, an empty vastness of low hills, glacial lakes, pine barrens, birch woods and bogs in northernmost Norway, is a Sámi stronghold, where a few operators offer the chance to join the herders on the move. Days are shaped by the reindeer and the weather, perhaps involving sledding, snowmobiling or feeding the animals, followed by sharing stories around the fire, feasting on Arctic fish and sleeping in lavvus (traditional tents). Seeing swathes of animals trot across the tundra is a treat; being immersed in Sámi culture is an even greater privilege.
A strange thing happens off the South African coast each winter in the Southern Hemisphere: sardines in their millions, maybe billions, swarm north from Cape Agulhas, following a cold current towards the Indian Ocean. Strange, because it doesn’t benefit the sardines at all. But it’s a bumper buffet for other creatures: dolphins, tuna, seals, sharks, orcas and whales, plus dive-bombing cormorants, gannets and gulls. The result is marine mayhem. The sardines become silvery shape-shifting bait balls, chased down by great gangs of hungry predators and pierced by an avian invasion from above. Fish numbers have plunged in recent decades and the Sardine Run has become less predictable, but it’s still known as one of Earth’s greatest shoals. Activity peaks off Eastern Cape province, with boat trips leaving from towns such as Port St Johns and Gqeberha (formerly Port Elizabeth, handy for Addo Elephant National Park, too). Diving amid this chaos is thrilling, if challenging; snorkellers can launch into the action more quickly. Or, stay on board to watch the feasting frenzy from above.
With their massive bills and bodies, capacious pouches and wide, powerful wings, pelicans look both immensely impressive and distinctly prehistoric. Come spring, around 32,000 of them — mostly great whites, plus a significant scoop of dalmatians, the biggest species — leave their winter hangouts and make for Europe’s largest natural wetland, the Danube Delta. This splurge of rivers, lakes, marshes, forest, sandbars and reedbeds spreads mostly across eastern Romania. It’s a paradise for the pelicans, as well as other birds such as herons, storks and white-tailed eagles. The pelicans begin arriving in March, but May is an ideal time to visit, when colonies are a-bustle, large pods gather for herd-fishing and adults are in full breeding splendour, their great gular pouches beaming bright-orange. June, on the other hand, is good for spying chicks, and July the time to go for sheer numbers. Navigate the delta on boat trips with licensed guides (mandatory for exploring core areas) or stay on a floating hotel for 24/7 avian action.
When to go: July to October
No migration is easy, but the journey of the Pacific Northwest salmon reads like a Greek tragedy. Born in fresh water, they head out to sea, mature for a few years, then navigate back to their natal streams using the earth’s magnetic fields and their own sense of smell. They battle against the flow, leaping rapids, dodging grizzlies and eagles, only to spawn — and then die. It’s a privilege to witness this fatal journey, either from the riverbank, as the fish fling themselves from the froth, or in the water amid the shoals. The town of Campbell River, on Vancouver Island’s east coast, is the self-proclaimed ‘salmon capital of the world’, and the top spot for snorkelling with the chinook, coho, chum, pink and sockeye fighting to return home. Floating in the swift current, you might see hundreds, even thousands, of salmon swim past — and possibly some bears hanging about. From the banks, you can watch salmon leaping two metres into the air, perhaps only to be snatched by those waiting bears. From mid-August to late October, the Homalco First Nation run bear-watching trips to Bute Inlet.
When to go: October to December

From the banks, you can watch salmon leaping two metres into the air, perhaps only to be snatched by those waiting bears.
When to go: June to October
Sea turtles: so cumbersome on land, so graceful underwater. These reptiles swim vast distances across oceans but must return to shore — back to the beach where they were born — to nest. There are seven species worldwide, five have nesting grounds in Costa Rica. Unsurprisingly, given its name is derived from ‘ tortuga ’ — the Spanish word for ‘turtle’ — Tortuguero is a hotspot. This national park on the country’s Caribbean coast is home to the western hemisphere’s largest green turtle rookery, as well as significant populations of leatherbacks and hawksbills.

articles.title_orig: New Real-World Data for Miach Orthopaedics’ BEAR® Implant Demonstrate Low Retear Rates and Clinically Meaningful Improvements Following ACL Restoration
articles.title_zh: New Real-World Data for Miach Orthopaedics’ BEAR® Implant Demonstrate Low Retear Rates and Clinically Meaningful Improvements Following ACL Restoration
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
BEAR Implant Surpasses 10,000 Patients Treated Commercially
WESTBOROUGH, Mass., October 07, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )-- Miach Orthopaedics, Inc. , developer of the BEAR® Implant for anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) restoration, today announced publication of new two-year results from the post-commercialization Bridge Registry, published in Knee Surgery, Sports Traumatology, Arthroscopy ( KSSTA ) 1, demonstrating low ACL retear rates and excellent patient-reported outcomes in real-world clinical practice. Publication coincides with the milestone of more than 10,000 patients treated with the BEAR Implant in the U.S. since commercial launch.
In the first 100 Bridge Registry patients followed for two years, the overall ACL retear rate was 5.6%, with no retears during the first postoperative year. Among patients treated using a modified surgical technique, the retear rate was 2.5%, compared to 8.0% with the original technique. Patient-reported outcomes demonstrated substantial and continued improvement in knee function: At two years, mean IKDC was 87.4, while KOOS scores were 94.7 for pain, 97.6 for activities of daily living, and 88.2 for sports and recreational function. The study authors reported that these improvements were clinically significant and meaningful, with postoperative scores exceeding established patient-acceptable symptom-state thresholds.
"These two-year outcomes reflect real-world use of the BEAR Implant after its commercial release, and they show low retear rates across a broader range of patients than the original trials studied," said Jocelyn Wittstein, MD, lead author of the Bridge Registry two-year analysis. "The registry includes younger patients at high risk and older patients at lower risk. Seeing low rates of retear and continued improvement in patient-reported outcomes through two years gives surgeons greater confidence as they counsel patients and select candidates for ACL restoration."
Clinical Experience Improves Outcomes
While the BEAR Implant itself has remained unchanged since commercial launch, the study documents how the BEAR Implant procedure has evolved through commercial experience. Surgeons have increasingly adopted modified approaches involving different fixation methods, stronger sutures and alternative suture patterns.
The BEAR Implant rehabilitation protocol has also evolved based on surgeon and physical therapist experience, with refinements designed to support healing while helping patients safely progress toward their functional goals. A central focus of the refined protocol is guiding each patient's progression toward return to activity at a pace that supports the healing ligament. Most patients in the Bridge Registry who played sports before their injury returned to play, with 87.2% back in sport by two years, underscoring why a measured return matters.
"The Bridge Registry results are outstanding and provide real-world validation of the BEAR Implant procedure after commercial launch," said Jamal Rushdy, president and chief executive officer of Miach Orthopaedics. "Combined with the experience of more than 10,000 patients, these data demonstrate the momentum we see with surgeon adoption. Miach is on a path to define the standard of care for joint preservation through ACL restoration."
The Bridge Registry ( NCT05398341 ) was initiated in May 2023 to assess real-world outcomes for the BEAR Implant. Primary outcomes being tracked include knee function and feeling measured by the International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) Subjective Knee Evaluation at two years and knee laxity measured with Lachman scoring at one year; Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) domains were also measured at two years. A total of 300 patients were enrolled at nine sites: AdventHealth, Boston Children's Hospital, Duke University, Hospital for Special Surgery, Oregon Health and Science University, Stanford University School of Medicine, Steamboat Orthopaedic & Spine Institute, Victory in Motion/Auburn Community Hospital and Virtua Health.
The BEAR (Bridge-Enhanced ACL Restoration) Implant was first granted De Novo Approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 2020. In 2025, the FDA expanded the indication to include children as young as age 2, with no upper age limit, as well as partial ACL tears. In 2026, the FDA updated BEAR Implant labeling to reflect a reduced risk of post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA) compared with ACL reconstruction using hamstring tendon autograft.
The BEAR Implant is a proprietary collagen-based implant used to facilitate healing of the torn ACL. The BEAR Implant is the first medical technology to demonstrate, with Level 1 clinical evidence, that it enables the body to heal its own torn ACL. Unlike ACL reconstruction (ACLR), which is the current standard of care, the BEAR Implant does not require a second surgical wound site to remove a healthy tendon from another part of the leg or the use of a donor tendon. The BEAR Implant acts as a bridge to help ends of the torn ACL heal together. The surgeon injects a small amount of the patient's own blood into the implant and attaches it between the torn ends of the ACL in a minimally invasive procedure. The combination of the BEAR Implant and the patient's blood enables the body to heal the torn ends of the ACL back together while maintaining the ACL's original attachments to the femur and tibia. As the ACL heals, the BEAR Implant is resorbed by the body.
In patients 14 years and older who have an ACL injury with concomitant knee injuries, ACL restoration with the BEAR Implant reduces the risk of developing PTOA (Kellgren-Lawrence grade 2 or higher), at 6-years post-surgery, compared to ACLR surgery using hamstring tendon autograft.
The BEAR Implant is indicated for adults, adolescents and children with a complete or partial rupture of the ACL, as confirmed by MRI. Patients must have an ACL stump attached to the tibia to construct the repair. Children with open physes must have sufficient bone in the femoral and tibial epiphyses on either side of the intended tunnel locations to avoid disruption of the growth plates. Visit www.miachortho.com for complete product information, including Instructions for Use.
About Miach Orthopaedics, Inc.
Miach Orthopaedics, Inc. , is a privately held company located in Westborough, Massachusetts, dedicated to developing surgical implants to facilitate connective tissue restoration. The company's initial focus is the BEAR® Implant, which represents a paradigm shift in the treatment of ACL tears. For more information on Miach Orthopaedics and its products, visit www.miachortho.com and follow the company on LinkedIn .
BEAR® Implant is a registered trademark of Miach Orthopaedics.

articles.title_orig: Jaguar unveils electric car in gamble on US tech millionaires
articles.title_zh: Jaguar unveils electric car in gamble on US tech millionaires
articles.content_orig:
Luxury carmaker Jaguar has launched its new all-electric vehicle, two years after the famed British company's controversial rebrand prompted a social media backlash.
The automotive manufacturer, which is owned by India's Tata Motors , unveiled the Type 01 model on Tuesday at an event in New York City, describing it as the "most technically advanced" and "most powerful and aerodynamic" Jaguar ever.
It marks a radical new direction for the company, which was criticized in November 2024 when it revealed a series of changes ahead of becoming a fully electric brand.
Jaguar posted a 30-second clip on X at the time which featured several models in brightly colored clothing and marketing slogans such as "live vivid", "delete ordinary" and "copy nothing."
Notably, the ad did not feature a car or the company's traditional cat logo. Among those to criticize the ad was Elon Musk , with the owner of the X social media platform asking : "Do you sell cars?"
Jaguar sought to defend the ad campaign, telling Sky News at the time that the company wanted "to be bold and disruptive."
Italy's Ferrari and Britain's Bentley have also launched their first EV models this year, seeking to test wealthy buyers' appetite for going electric as luxury carmakers seek to compete with cheaper Chinese car brands.
Jaguar's Type 01 has a starting price of £130,000 (roughly $172,000) in the U.K. and around $130,500 in the U.S., according to multiple media reports , which is significantly higher than previous comparable models.
Jaguar later confirmed to CNBC on Wednesday morning that the Type 01 model has a minimum price tag of $130,000 in North America.
The four-door "Grand Tourer" has an ultra-long bonnet, low roofline, frameless doors and a camera instead of a rear window. It has a range of up to 450 miles and can accelerate from 0-62 miles per hour in 3.2 seconds.
The launch of the model comes as Jaguar Land Rover continues its recovery from a cyberattack that forced the company to halt production last year, and one month after JLR announced it would cut 4,000 jobs as part of a major cost-cutting drive.
JLR CEO PB Balaji described the unveiling of Type 01 as the start of "an exciting new era" for Jaguar.
"Combining British heritage, bold creativity, advanced technology and groundbreaking engineering, it reflects our ambition to create objects of desire that will help us invite a new generation of clients into Jaguar's loyal and passionate customer base," Balaji said in a statement.

articles.title_orig: How is the horse infected with New World Screwworm in Grant County and more
articles.title_zh: How is the horse infected with New World Screwworm in Grant County and more
articles.content_orig:
Nick Seibel, editor and publisher of the Silver City Daily Press, covers top stories each week in the Silver City Report. This week, he updates us on the horse that was infected with New World Screwworm, talks about a recent candidate forum, and more.
Susan Morée: You have an update for us on that poor horse that was infected with New World screw worm. How's the horse doing?
Nick Seibel: Yeah, well, I mean, the horse is recovering. You know, it was according to the veterinarians that treated the horse. The wound on the horse when they discovered it really didn't have the strong odor that's usually associated with that infestation. until they started to clean up the wound and found larvae deeper in the horse's tissue.
Yeah, it was unpleasant, but so far, no new cases reported in the area. Of course, there's an infestation zone, which is a 20 kilometer radius around where the horse was in Mimbres. There's a lot of sort of mystery around that particular infestation, because a lot of folks say, well, did the horse come from somewhere? But as it turns out, the horse had not left that property. Other animals that were on the property hadn't recently traveled on or off of the property. So a lot of mystery around how the fly got there to infect said horse. Generally, the experts say the flies travel at most about a mile or a mile and a half, but they can travel up to 10 miles per day. But not having had any other cases, we don't really know how that came to pass. So whether there's undetected infections that are out there, whether there's infestations in wild animals in the area. At the public meeting, the person from the state said that as far as they knew, the fly could have traveled in the cabin of a truck from somewhere else. You just don't know how that went down. But they are continuing with monitoring. They've got that infestation zone where you're supposed to have permission to transport animals in or out of there. They're also releasing sterile flies throughout the area to try to address the potential for flies out there in the wild and make sure that this doesn't spread any further.
Susan Morée: So if you're driving around in your vehicle and you've got a fly in the vehicle, maybe you want to kill it?
Nick Seibel: I mean, I usually want to do that anyway. One of the things they said is you can't really tell, and it doesn't really look any different from any other fly, to the naked eye.
Susan Morée: I don't think I'm going to get too close to a fly anyway to examine it.
Nick Seibel: This is where having a newspaper subscription really comes in handy because that rolled up newspaper is excellent.
Nick Seibel: That's right.
Susan Morée: I love that you got a little plug in there. And let's talk about the candidate forums for District 39. The election is in November. What was your forum like?
Nick Seibel: Yeah, well, early voting got started, well, got started yesterday, in fact, across New Mexico. Not a lot of contested races on the local level here in Grant County. Most of it was decided in the primary. But there is of course a contested race for Grant County Sheriff, but the Republican candidate there declined to participate, so we won't be able to have one there, which left us with New Mexico House District 39, which is currently held by Republican Luis Terrazas. He's being opposed by Democrat Raul Turrieta, and they squared off in a forum last Friday night sponsored by the Daily Press. That was just one night after they met in a similar forum sponsored by the Grant County Beat, which is an online publication here. In the Thursday night forum, the Beat forum, was confrontational, a little testy at times. And things started out that way in the Friday forum, too. They definitely, you know, the candidates took some hot shots at each other. But it definitely ended on an odd note. I mean, having done a lot of these candidate forums, I can't ever recall anything quite like that. The last audience question that we asked was about, asking each one of them to say something positive about the other's service to the community. And it really got emotional. In fact, the candidates at the conclusion of the question stood up and hugged it out, which was the main photo on our front page on Tuesday at the Daily Press.
Susan Morée: Let's move on to Gila Regional Medical Center. You've got some news for us about that.
Nick Seibel: Yeah, and that's pretty positive news there. Gila Regional, of course, is the county-owned hospital here in Silver City. And they've been named a regional hub in the new state health initiative known as the Healthy Horizons Initiative. They're gonna be coordinating the expenditure of about a little more than $15 million to improve rural healthcare in this part of the state. So Gila Regional is right at the center of that.
Susan Morée: Okay, and where can readers find these stories, Nick?

articles.title_orig: Nobel chemistry prize goes to pair who solved mystery of 'mirror image' molecules
articles.title_zh: Nobel chemistry prize goes to pair who solved mystery of 'mirror image' molecules
articles.content_orig:
Henri B Kagan and Kensō Soai awarded prize for discovery that has aided understanding of how medicines work in the body
The Nobel prize in chemistry 2026 has been awarded to two scientists for discoveries that showed how chemical reactions can produce an overwhelming excess of one of two mirror image forms of a molecule.
Henri B Kagan at Paris-Sud University in France and Kensō Soai at Tokyo University of Science in Japan have been awarded the prize “for the discovery of nonlinear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis”.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, Sweden, on Wednesday. They will each receive an equal share of a prize of 12m Swedish kronor (about £900,000).
Many molecules, including amino acids that form the building blocks of proteins, can exist in two forms that contain the same atoms, but are mirror images of one another, much like a person’s left and right hands. This property is known as chirality.
However, the chemistry underpinning life is surprisingly “homochiral”, or same-handed. Proteins are built almost exclusively from L-amino acids, while the sugars that form the backbone of DNA and RNA have the opposite D- configuration.
How this homochirality could have emerged when chemical reactions in the laboratory typically produce equal quantities of both forms had long puzzled scientists. The question also had practical consequences: “Although these molecules look very similar, they can behave very differently when they interact with other molecules,” said Prof Andre Cobb, an organic chemist at King’s College London.
“This matters enormously for medicines because many of the molecules in our bodies, including proteins that drugs target, are themselves chiral. So the ‘left-handed’ and ‘right-handed’ versions of a drug can interact with the body in different ways which can lead to different or weakened drug effects.”
The drug thalidomide provides a potent example. During the early 1960s, thousands of children were affected by birth defects after their mothers were prescribed it to combat morning sickness during pregnancy. Researchers subsequently found differences in the biological effects of the drug’s two mirror image forms.
Manufacturers wanted a way of steering reactions towards particular forms of the molecules that they produced, and Kagan and Soai eventually provided a solution.
It began in 1986, when Kagan discovered that a relatively small imbalance between left- and right-handed forms of a catalyst could create a greater excess of one of the mirror image products than the other.
Soai took the idea further, developing a reaction in which the molecules produced themselves acted as catalysts for making more of themselves, a process known as autocatalysis. “You have to be aware, this is probably the coolest experiment in organic chemistry ever,” said Prof Peter Somfai, an organic chemist at Lund University and a member of the Nobel committee for chemistry.
In 2003, Soai demonstrated a reaction that produced almost exclusively one mirror-image form, reproducing the kind of molecular one-handedness found in living organisms for the first time.
Speaking by telephone at Wednesday’s announcement, Soai, 76, said he was “very proud” of the experiment as it offered a potential explanation for how the molecular one-handedness of life could have arisen. He described hearing the news about the prize as “one of the most exciting days of my life”.
Taken together, Kagan and Soai’s discoveries had “reshaped our understanding of molecular chirality, how it is created, amplified and transmitted”, Somfai said.
These insights have since become embedded in the development of catalysts that steer chemical reactions towards producing a particular mirror image form across different industries. “It is in the backsides of our heads all the time,” said Somfai.
“It might be difficult to say that this drug or that drug was developed using this. I would say all of them because we use this as a tool. We use this as an understanding of how to develop catalysts and how they function.”

articles.title_zh: US 30-year mortgage rate hits highest in nearly three years
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Oct 7 (Reuters) - The interest rate on the most common US home loan jumped last week to its highest in almost three ‌years, worsening affordability for buyers four weeks before elections that will decide ‌if President Donald Trump's Republicans keep control of Congress.
The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage surged 19 basis points ​to 7.49% in the week ended October 2, the Mortgage Bankers Association said on Wednesday. It was last higher in November 2023.
Mortgage rates are tied closely to the yield on US 10-year Treasury notes, which earlier this week hit a 24-year high, driven ‌by worries over inflationary pressures ⁠from soaring oil prices and data showing stronger US economic growth.
The cost of living is the top issue on Americans' minds ⁠as they decide how they will vote on November 3, a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday showed, and is one reason why Trump's approval rating is at a record low ​of ​32%.
Home borrowing rates are up about 1.4 percentage ​points since joint US-Israeli strikes ‌against Iran began in late February, tracking a similar rise in the 10-year Treasury yield, which topped 5.3% on Monday.
Inflation is also on the rise, registering 3.4% in August by a measure that the Federal Reserve targets at 2%.
Fed policymakers have signaled they expect to follow their September interest-rate increase with another rate hike by year's ‌end, though markets are for now betting they ​will not move at their upcoming policy meeting ​at the end of October.
Mortgage loan ​applications fell 4.2% last week from the previous week, the ‌MBA said on Wednesday, with refinancing applications ​dropping sharply. Overall application ​volumes are the lowest since February 2025 and have fallen nearly 50% since January.
"Very few homeowners have an incentive to refinance at these rates, and ​the jump in borrowing ‌costs has caused many potential borrowers to step back from the purchase ​market," said Joel Kan, the MBA's deputy chief economist.
(Reporting by Ann Saphir; ​Editing by Jamie Freed and Nick Zieminski)

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 7, 2026
Built on the world's largest live video map, Atlas turns authentic video into real-world intelligence for AI, search and commerce.
SAN FRANCISCO , Oct. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Atmosfy today announced Atlas, a platform that gives AI a live view of the physical world. Atlas is built on Atmosfy , the world's largest live video map, with more than 500 million experiences spanning 100 million places across 20,000 cities in 150 countries.
The video map is powered by Atmosfy's global community, capturing moments at restaurants, bars, hotels, stadiums and other places around the world. Each video connects a real place to a moment in time.
Spectra, Atlas's latest intelligence model, turns those videos into time capsules, connecting them into a single, living picture of the world.
Building on existing partnerships with Capital One, Expedia, SeatGeek, GetYourGuide, Virgin Hotels, Resy, Funko and others, Atmosfy is expanding through Atlas into video and data licensing for frontier AI models.
"As AI takes on more decisions for people, it needs to understand what's happening in the real world," said Michael Ebel, Founder and CEO of Atmosfy. "Where to go, what to book, what to recommend: those decisions depend on how places and experiences are changing. Atlas gives AI a continuously updated view of that world."
Atmosfy is the "what's happening" app for millennials and Gen Z. Its global community maps what's happening across 20,000 cities through real-world video, creating city-based feeds that show where people are going and what they're doing right now.
Atmosfy is backed by Redpoint Ventures, Capital One Ventures, Canaan Partners, Industry Ventures, Streamlined Ventures, DNX Ventures, Suntory Ventures, Plug and Play, and others. See Atlas in action at atmosfy.io .

articles.title_orig: World Athletics referee and race walking judge Costin's steps to success
articles.title_zh: World Athletics referee and race walking judge Costin's steps to success
articles.content_orig:
Zuzana Costin at the World Athletics U20 Championships Oregon 26 ( © World Athletics Media Academy Lenny Patram Jr. )
Zuzana Costin is a former athlete turned official, currently the only active female technical official in the world to hold both World Athletics Gold Level Referee and Gold Level Race Walking Judge qualifications.
The two-time Olympian, who competed in the 20km race walk at the Athens 2004 and Beijing 2008 Games, most recently served as a race walking judge and referee during the World Athletics U20 Championships Oregon 26. While there, she reflected on her journey in athletics.
You hold both World Athletics Gold Level Referee and Gold Level Race Walking Judge qualifications – currently the only active female technical official in the world to do so. What does this achievement mean to you?
"There are three of us who hold both qualifications but, yes, I am the only female official. It’s quite amazing to have achieved this. I always try to do the best that I can, therefore it’s nice to see that the work I have put in was recognised, and it paid off."
When you first began your journey as a technical official, did you ever imagine you would reach this level?
"No, I didn’t. I got involved in athletics at a very young age. My dad (Jozef Malik) was the Vice President of the federation (Slovak Athletic Federation) for several years and was active as an administrator, coach and also as an official, so I grew up in the world of athletics. Any time he organised any competitions, I was helping out. So it has always been a part of my life and I never thought about it too much at that stage. Achieving this level in officiating in athletics after finishing my racing career gives me a strong sense of accomplishment and satisfaction."
Throughout your career, have there been mentors who helped shape your journey?
"Undeniably, my dad played a big role at the beginning of my journey and he has kept supporting me since.
"After retiring from being an athlete, I started to officiate in Ireland on a regular basis (I had moved there a few years beforehand). I met with support and encouragement to pursue this to an international level. I was very lucky that I was immersed in an environment where people knew what they were doing, not just on a local level but on an international one, too. So, whenever I came across any problems, I had people I could rely on.
"After passing the Silver level exam, I started getting appointments at European competitions and there were always senior technical officials who were happy to share their knowledge and experience with ‘newbies’.
"That was also the case during one of my first big international appointments as a member of the Jury of Appeal at the European Championships in Berlin where Anna Riccardi was our chief. She took me under her wing, gave me confidence and guided me through this new experience.
"During the Covid-19 pandemic, European Athletics began organising online webinars for technical officials, focusing heavily on the practical aspects of officiating. Those webinars were primary led by Chris Cohen and Niels van der Aar and they helped me to become a more knowledgeable and effective official.
"Later, I was selected for the European Athletics mentoring programme for technical delegates and was appointed as a mentee technical delegate for the European Championships in Rome. I was fortunate to have Chris and Niels as my mentors; their guidance provided invaluable insights and allowed me to expand my knowledge even further."
What practical support is most beneficial for upcoming female officials during the early stages of their careers?
"Having someone you can turn to, talk to and learn from is major. Mentorship is something you can’t replace, especially when you are trying to excel.
"After World Athletics changed its educational programme for officials to the current one, it really opened the door for younger people. Originally, the educational programme and exams to become an international official were only in English, which could be a bit of a barrier for people who don’t have a good standard of English. That is still the case for the Gold level. And this could be something that a mentor could help with – dismantling the language barrier. However, for the lower levels, World Athletics has gradually introduced more languages in which its certification courses and exams can be taken. This shift definitely benefits new candidates who don’t have a sufficient command of English."
Since you started your career, have you seen an increase in more female judges, applicants or volunteers for athletics?
"Absolutely. I don’t remember seeing many female officials in the leading positions when I started, and that has definitely changed now. Also, World Athletics’ encouragement to member federations to enter an equal number of female and male candidates for exams has started to pay off. Panels of international officials are now nearly gender balanced.
"I have also seen a growth in the numbers of younger officials, with more opportunities and positions available for them. It’s more achievable and something that one can work towards now."
What kind of advice would you give someone, especially a younger woman, who is interested in following your footsteps or becoming a judge in athletics?
"Now is the right time. Ask your federation about upcoming courses and exams. If you get opportunities to take part in them or you get any appointments, don’t turn them down because you can always learn something. You might not succeed all the time, but you learn from the experience.
"It is also important to believe in yourself and to have someone, or a group of people, that you can get support from.
"It is nice to see new candidates growing in confidence. When they first get started, it’s all very nerve-racking and there’s so much going on all at once – it creates a lot of feelings of fear. But that’s a normal thing to experience. Sometimes all they need is someone in their corner telling them that this is normal, to believe in themselves, and that someone else has confidence in them."
What kind of legacy do you hope to leave – not only through the competitions you’ve officiated, but through the people you’ve inspired?
"I just hope that all the younger officials coming in see that they can do this. That this, as well as whatever else they want to strive for, is achievable regardless of whether they are coming from a country with a strong tradition of international officiating or not. And that the journey of being an international official can start at any age."
Ash Wehrly for the World Athletics Media Academy
Launched in March, the World Athletics pledge initiative forms part of the organisation’s contribution to the International Women’s Day 2026 global campaign, #GiveToGain, which calls on individuals and organisations to give their time, resources and support to help forge gender equality through abundant giving. By encouraging stakeholders to pledge mentoring hours, World Athletics is turning the #GiveToGain message into practical action across the sport. Learn more on the Women in Athletics website .

articles.content_orig:
