The four astronauts of SpaceX’s Crew-12 mission are heading home after nearly 10 months in space.
Crew-12 's Crew Dragon capsule, named "Freedom," undocked from the International Space Station (ISS) on Wednesday (Oct. 7) at 8:05 a.m. EDT (1205 GMT). If all goes according to plan, Freedom will splash down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California on Thursday (Oct. 8) at 11:34 a.m. EDT (1534 GMT).
Return-to-Earth coverage will begin on Thursday at 10:20 a.m. EDT (1420 GMT). Freedom will conduct its deorbit burn around 10:46 a.m. EDT (1446 GMT), then splash down in the Pacific at 11:34 a.m. EDT (1534 GMT). You can watch that coverage here when the time comes, courtesy of NASA.
Then, at 1:15 p.m. EDT (1715 GMT) on Thursday, NASA and SpaceX will hold a press conference to discuss Crew-12's homecoming and the launch of the company's robotic CRS-35 cargo mission to the ISS, which is targeted for Oct. 13. Participants in the briefing are:
The Crew-12 astronauts are Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway of NASA, ESA's Sophie Adenot, and Andrey Fedyaev of the Russian space agency Roscosmos . Meir and Fedyaev had each been to space once before, while Crew-12 was the first mission for Hathaway and Adenot.
The quartet launched to the ISS atop a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket on Feb. 13 . Their arrival brought the station up to its normal complement of seven crewmembers. It had been operating with a skeleton crew of three since Jan. 15, when SpaceX's Crew-11 mission headed home a month early to deal with a medical issue experienced by one of its astronauts, NASA's Mike Fincke .
That was the first medical evacuation in the long history of the ISS. But it was not an emergency situation, NASA officials stressed at the time, and Fincke is doing fine now here on terra firma. (He retired in August with a total of 549 days in space, the fourth-most ever for a NASA astronaut.)
Crew-12, in turn, has been relieved by the four-person Crew-13 , which arrived at the ISS on Thursday (Oct. 1). Crew-13 made it to the station less than eight hours after launch — the quickest-ever ISS trip for an American spacecraft. (The world record is just over three hours , by a Russian Soyuz crewed vehicle.)
Crew-13 was originally supposed to launch on Sept. 12. However, an issue with the propulsion system on its Crew Dragon capsule, named "Grace," pushed things back, giving Crew-12 a few extra weeks in orbit.
The Crew-12 astronauts were very busy during their nearly 10 months off Earth, performing a variety of maintenance work and dozens of scientific experiments.
Then there were the spacewalks . Meir performed four of them, bringing her lifetime total to seven. And on Aug. 18, Adenot stepped outside the ISS, becoming the first French woman ever to walk in space. She did two more over the next two weeks, including one with Meir, which was just the sixth all-female extravehicular activity in the station's history.
The Crew-12 astronauts are doubtless feeling a mix of emotions about their homecoming, as big transitions are always bittersweet. Indeed, Meir gave us a sense of this a few weeks back.
"What I'm looking forward to most is seeing my three-and-a-half-year-old daughter,” Meir said during a Sept. 16 call with reporters from the station.
"I'm so looking forward to seeing nature again," she added, "feeling the breeze on my face, the wind rustling through the leaves, experiencing all those things that we don't have up here. But I will very, very much miss being weightless all the time and the incredible views that we have."
Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

NIJMEGEN, The Netherlands – 7 October 2026 – Byondis B.V., a private biopharmaceutical company engineering antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) to tackle the cancers that current therapies cannot reach, will share progress from its platform technology portfolio at World ADC San Diego, the world's largest ADC conference, being held from 12-15 October in San Diego, USA.
With more than 20 years of in-house ADC expertise, Byondis is evolving the ADC field with novel payload platforms, advanced masking technology and optimized linker and conjugation strategies. These enable ADC solutions that can overcome the critical limitations of current and next-generation therapies with the potential for superior efficacy, duration of response and safety, to improve clinical outcomes in patients with difficult-to-treat tumor types.
Overcoming ADC Resistance The company is advancing an IND-enabling (regulatory non-clinical) package to completion for its lead proprietary ADC candidate, BYON14156, marking a key step towards clinical trial authorization. Harnessing the company's first-in-class antifolate payload and targeting an antigen highly expressed across multiple tumor types, BYON14156 is engineered to overcome the major challenge seen in current and next-generation ADCs with payload resistance. Dose range-finding toxicity studies in non-human primates have shown a benign toxicity profile and a favorable therapeutic window. Earlier studies have demonstrated efficacy across a range of tumor models in vitro and in vivo , including topoisomerase and tubulin inhibitor-resistant models.
Wim Dokter, PhD, Chief Scientific Officer at Byondis, will share a presentation at World ADC entitled Spotlighting Comprehensive Preclinical Development of Antifolate ADCs to Enter IND Phase for a Novel Drug-Linker Mechanism on Wednesday 14 October at 11.00am PDT , in which he will profile the development of BYON14156, ahead of its advancement into the clinic, anticipated in 2027.
The advancement of BYON14156 is a key part of the company's strategy to establish itself as a leader in the development of ADCs, through its platform technologies and the modular, end-to-end capabilities that underpin the company.
A Universal Solution to Reduce Off-Tumor Toxicity Byondis' best-in-class steric masking technology, ByonGuard™, which is designed to improve the therapeutic index of ADCs, T cell engagers and other antibody-based therapies, and provide a universal solution to reduce off-tumor toxicity, will be highlighted on Monday 12 October at 10.30am PDT in the presentation, Introducing ByonGuard: Conditional Activation Technology that Improves the Safety Profile & Therapeutic Index of ADCs . Wim Dokter will explore the rationale to develop conditionally active ADCs to overcome challenges with target-mediated toxicity and improve therapeutic index, and share safety and efficacy findings from Byondis' latest research.
Christoph Korpus, PhD, MBA, Chief Executive Officer of Byondis, said: "The progress of our first-in-class antifolate payload ADC candidate towards the clinic is a clear demonstration of the strength of our platform technologies in action. It reflects the focused strategy we have built over the past year: prioritizing the proprietary platforms with the greatest potential to address the limitations of current and next-generation ADCs, while pursuing partnerships that can accelerate the impact of our technologies for patients. This candidate brings forward Byondis' most advanced platform technology, and its progress reinforces our conviction as we continue to engage with potential partners across our platform portfolio."
Under the leadership of Christoph Korpus, PhD, MBA, who was appointed as Chief Executive Officer in April 2026, Byondis has sharpened its focus on the continued development of its proprietary technology platforms, each of which are engineered to work independently or in combination to address multiple hallmarks of cancer, alongside the pursuit of partnering, licensing and co-development opportunities to maximize value.
Byondis' fully integrated discovery, development and manufacturing capabilities give the company the flexibility to advance its proprietary pipeline independently, while its modular platform approach enables broad partnering flexibility through co-development, licensing and strategic collaboration. The company continues to actively engage with prospective partners across its antifolate, immunostimulatory phosphonate and dual payload platforms, and its steric masking technology.
About Byondis Byondis B.V. is a private biopharmaceutical company engineering antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) to tackle the cancers that current therapies cannot reach. Grounded in more than 20 years of ADC expertise, Byondis is evolving the field with novel payload platforms, advanced masking technology, and optimized linker and conjugation strategies, enabling the development of ADCs with superior efficacy, duration of response, and safety to improve clinical outcomes and bring hope to patients.
Its broad platform technology portfolio includes a first-in-class antifolate payload designed to overcome resistance to existing ADCs, a best-in-class steric masking technology providing a universal solution to reduce off-tumor toxicity, and a first-in-class immunostimulatory phosphonate payload to address a critical need for patients who do not respond to immunotherapy. Each is engineered to work independently or in combination to address multiple hallmarks of cancer. The company's lead proprietary program, BYON14156, is advancing towards the clinic.
Byondis' modular approach to ADC design facilitates broad partnering flexibility through co-development, licensing, and strategic collaboration. With end-to-end capabilities spanning pre-clinical and clinical R&D, GMP delivery and regulatory engagement, Byondis operates from state-of-the-art facilities in Nijmegen, the Netherlands. For more information, visit www.byondis.com .

articles.title_orig: Webb finds a surprising atmosphere on a scorching lava world
articles.title_zh: Webb finds a surprising atmosphere on a scorching lava world
articles.content_orig:
For scientists searching for life beyond Earth, rocky planets with atmospheres are among the most promising places to investigate. An atmosphere is essential for maintaining liquid water on a planet's surface. Yet among the more than 6,300 exoplanets cataloged thus far, most are not rocky, and only a small number of known rocky planets appear to possess atmospheres.
Now, researchers have added another world to that short list. In a study published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters , a team led by University of Chicago scientist Brandon Park Coy reports evidence of an atmosphere surrounding HD 3167 b, a rocky super-Earth located 154 light-years away in the constellation Pisces. The intensely hot planet, classified as a "lava world," completes an orbit around its star in only one Earth day.
"What's so surprising is that the closer a rocky planet orbits its star, the harder it should be to have an atmosphere, because it's bombarded by stellar wind and gets more high-energy photons from the star. But it seems that many of these lava worlds do," explained Edwin Kite, UChicago associate professor of geophysical sciences and co-author of the study. "These planets are too hot for life, but by studying them, we can say something about the processes that matter for other rocky worlds."
In the Q&A below,Coy, a graduate student in Kite's group and first author on the study, explains why atmospheres on lava worlds are scientifically valuable, how researchers detected evidence for this one, and what they hope to learn next.
What was the goal of the survey that found this atmosphere-bearing exoplanet?
One of the driving questions that the James Webb Space Telescope is being used to answer is whether planets orbiting stars much smaller than the sun have atmospheres. It appears that most of those terrestrial planets don't -- they're just bare rock.
But surprisingly, we've found evidence that the majority of lava worlds -- similar in composition to Earth and Venus but much, much hotter -- might have atmospheres. Five terrestrial planets found with atmospheres, including the one described in this study, have been ultra-hot.
This planet, however, is the coldest lava world found so far with evidence of an atmosphere. This is interesting because we're trying to understand the temperature transition between planets with and without atmospheres.
The result is the first from a program led by Megan Weiner Mansfield, PhD'21, who's now at the University of Maryland. The goal of the program, which is looking at 10 ultra-hot lava worlds, is to see if there's a critical temperature over which you start seeing planets with atmospheres.
"We're interested in studying these kinds of planets because we think early Earth might have looked a lot like a lava world." -- Study author Brandon Park Coy
How can you tell if an exoplanet has an atmosphere?
Right now, directly looking at Earth-like planets for signs of life is out of reach. Instead, we can use the Webb telescope to detect light in the mid-infrared wavelength range to estimate the temperature of exoplanets, which can tell us if they might have atmospheres.
There are two primary ways that we study exoplanets. One is called transit, when the planet goes in front of the host star. Another called secondary eclipse, which is the method we used for this study, is when the planet passes behind its star, and we can measure how much light is lost. That difference tells us how much mid-infrared light comes from the planet itself, which essentially tells us how hot the planet is.
If a planet doesn't have an atmosphere, its star-facing, day side should be as hot as theoretically possible based on how reflective its surface is and its distance from the star. But an atmosphere would help redistribute heat from the day side to the night side. We see this happen on Venus -- there's almost no difference in surface temperature between the day and night sides, or between the poles and the equator. If a planet has an atmosphere, it might also have clouds that reflect incoming starlight and cool the dayside. So if a planet's day side is cooler than the maximum possible, it likely has an atmosphere.
The subject of this study, HD 3167 b, is noticeably cooler than its expected maximum, providing strong evidence that it has an atmosphere.
What do you think HD 3167 b's atmosphere is made of?
These lava worlds are so-named because the surface facing their star is likely melted rock. We think that HD 3167 b might have a silicate-rich composition, with a similar mixture of minerals that make up Earth's mantle. Before this study, we expected that any atmosphere on these ultra-hot planets would be composed of vaporized rock, but we're starting to see evidence that some might have heavier gases like carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, or water in their atmospheres.
The makeup of HD 3167 b's atmosphere is still up in the air. That's one reason we're so interested in getting new observations.
Why is this result important?
Because the four other lava worlds found to have atmospheres are in the ultra-hot regime, it raises questions about whether there's a critical transition temperature when silicate atmospheres start becoming very thick. Is there a temperature where these planets form silicate cloud decks that might reflect incoming radiation to space and cool its day side? This relatively cooler planet helps us better characterize and nail down this transition.
Despite how inhospitable they are for life, we're also interested in studying these kinds of planets because we think early Earth might have looked a lot like a lava world. We think that very early in the solar system's history, when the terrestrial planets formed, they were extremely hot due to the energy from all of the planetesimal collisions. Earth had what's known as a magma ocean stage with an entirely liquid surface. This result gives us a window into studying what conditions may have been like in Earth's first couple of million years.
Materials provided by University of Chicago . Original written by Maureen Searcy. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title_orig: At $1,279, Google’s Xreal Aura will go head-to-head with Meta’s VR Glasses
articles.title_zh: At $1,279, Google’s Xreal Aura will go head-to-head with Meta’s VR Glasses
articles.content_orig:
The first transparent Android XR glasses are “weeks” away — if you made a reservation.
The first transparent Android XR glasses are “weeks” away — if you made a reservation.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Two weeks ago, journalists in the San Francisco Bay Area got to try two hot new wearables that weigh only around 100 grams: the just-revealed Meta VR Glasses , and the long-awaited transparent Google XR glasses built in partnership with Xreal. It turns out they’re going head-to-head. Xreal has just opened Aura pre-orders starting at $1,279 , $20 less than the Meta VR Glasses.
That’s for the Xreal Aura with 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage; there’ll also be a 16GB / 512GB config for $1,499. (Xreal couldn’t tell us whether the 16GB of RAM would be important for some apps by publish time.)
Both the Google / Xreal Aura and Meta’s VR Glasses let you overlay virtual objects and desktops on the real world. Both are relatively lightweight because they’ve got a cord — their Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite chips and batteries both live in a compute puck, which runs either Meta’s Horizon OS or Android XR. Both greet you with a grid of floating app icons to choose from.
But they’re very different experiences in practice, primarily because the Google / Xreal Aura has transparent lenses, while the Meta VR Glasses use passthrough vision to let you see the real world and offers more immersion. While the Xreal Aura has one of the largest transparent fields of view yet at 70 degrees diagonal, it’s still smaller than Meta’s passthrough glasses. I wrote all about it in this story , and it’s just one of many differences.
The Meta VR Glasses also have eye tracking, like the Apple Vision Pro, so you can select things just by looking at them and pinching fingers resting on your lap; the Google / Xreal Aura has a touchpad built into the compute puck and hand-tracking to give you virtual laser pointers. (Both let you connect to other peripherals and display other devices too — and you can plug devices with USB-C DisplayPort video right in.)
And, of course, you’ve got your Android apps inside the Xreal Aura, or your Quest games inside the VR Glasses.
I don’t think any journalist can tell you which is better yet; you may want to wait for reviews. We also have yet to test Android XR extensively: while Samsung and Google did technically ship the $1,799 Galaxy XR with Android XR last year, they didn’t send one to The Verge for review.
The Meta VR Glasses aren’t due until spring 2027, but Xreal isn’t necessarily shipping lots of pairs before then. Today, the only people who can preorder the Xreal glasses are those who already put in a reservation , and only the first 2,000 “Founder’s Edition” pairs are necessarily coming at “launch.” Those will ship this year, Xreal CEO and co-founder Chi Xu tells The Verge .
It might not take till the end of the year. Xreal’s press release does say they “will begin shipping soon” and that the “launch” is “now just weeks away,” but those are wiggly, and again, those timeframes are just for early adopters. If you don’t have a preorder, “Orders will open to the general public in the coming weeks.” The glasses will also only ship in the US, Canada, Japan, and South Korea to start, before expanding to other regions in 2027.
I’m already a fan of Xreal’s glasses and how they let me watch my 3D movies with a 57-degree field of view, and I’m intrigued by the puck. I’d love to see how much more useful these glasses are with a 70-degree view.

articles.title_orig: Quiles will become Moto3 World Champion if...
articles.title_zh: Quiles will become Moto3 World Champion if...
articles.content_orig:
Quiles heads to Indonesia for his next chance at match point, but what does the #28 need to do to clinch the title?
It’s a big weekend for Maximo Quiles (CFMOTO Gaviota Aspar Team), who has another opportunity to be crowned Champion this weekend. Quiles enters the weekend with a 127-point advantage over his rivals, and with just 125 points remaining up for grabs after Indonesia, the #28 is now faced with another opportunity to be crowned Moto3 World Champion.
Simply put, if Quiles leaves Indonesia with at least a 125-point advantage, then he will be crowned 2026 Moto3 World Champion. Four riders remain in mathematical contention, with Quiles, Alvaro Carpe (Red Bull KTM Ajo), David Almansa (Liqui Moly Dynavolt Intact GP) and Brian Uriarte (Red Bull KTM Ajo) all facing a pivotal weekend.
Ultimately, Quiles has the opportunity to control his own destiny. A victory would crown him World Champion regardless of other results, whilst P2 would also be enough if Almansa finishes P3 or lower. Meanwhile, a third-place finish will secure Quiles the title if Almansa were to finish P4 or below on Sunday.
Finishing outside the podium positions brings Carpe into contention. If Quiles finishes fourth, Carpe would need to score P2 or worse, while Almansa would need to finish P5 or lower. Anything outside of the top five (P6 or lower) for Quiles brings Uriarte back into the picture, increasing the complications.
It has already been an incredible season for Quiles, who has earned nine race wins and 14 podiums from the opening 16 rounds. The #28 has already scored 52 points more than his entire 2025 campaign, underlining just how impressive his form has been this year.
Join us this weekend for a potential title-deciding weekend at the Indonesian GP. The Moto3 grid heads lights out at 12:00 Local Time (UTC +8) on Sunday, so don’t miss out!

articles.title_orig: Bigger than Manhattan: The record-breaking airport megahub that conquered the world
articles.title_zh: Bigger than Manhattan: The record-breaking airport megahub that conquered the world
articles.content_orig:
EDITOR’S NOTE: This CNN Travel series is, or was, sponsored by the country it highlights. CNN retains full editorial control over subject matter, reporting and frequency of the articles and videos within the sponsorship, in compliance with our policy .
Standing at the crossroad of continents, Istanbul has long been a global linchpin.
As Byzantium and then Constantinople, it controlled trade routes along the Silk Road and maritime passage from the Black Sea to the Mediterranean.
In the golden age of railways, Istanbul was the end point of the Orient Express, at the very cusp of Europe and Asia.
Now, in the 21st century, iGA Istanbul Airport is ruling the skies, having just overtaken London Heathrow as the best-connected airport on the planet.
“They’ve finally got the number one position,” says John Grant, chief analyst at OAG, a global travel data provider which has just released its Megahubs 2026 Index, comparing the world’s top airports.
The rankings are generated by comparing the number of scheduled connections to and from international flights , with the number of destinations served from the airport. They do this through a snapshot look at the busiest day of the year, which this year was August 2.
Gaining the top spot is “an important achievement for iGA Istanbul Airport and reflects the position we have built as a global aviation hub,” airport CEO Selahattin Bilgen tells CNN. “Today, we already serve approximately 350 destinations around the world, with significant room to grow further.”
Amsterdam Airport Schiphol is third place in this year’s ranking, followed by Kuala Lumpur at No.4 and Chicago O’Hare at No.5.
It’s been a swift and impressive rise for the award-winning $12 billion Istanbul Airport, which opened to much fanfare in 2018, about 20 miles outside Istanbul on the European side. This is a hub built for scale: Its huge 1.4-million-square-meter terminal is the world’s largest under one roof and the whole 76.5-million-square-meter site is bigger than Manhattan.
More than 84 million passengers pass through each year, making it the eighth busiest airport in the world. However, the long-term plan is to increase capacity to 200 million passengers per year, which is double the annual number currently handled by Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta, the world’s busiest airport.
“They’re going to be unassailable in the coming years,” says Grant. “They’ve got runway capacity. They’ve got a national airline that is hugely successful and continues to grow with new fleet orders. They’re very close to some of the most emergent markets in the world, such as Central Asia. They’ve benefited partly from the Middle East situation. They’re just very well placed.”
Istanbul Airport opened its fourth main runway last month and the end goal is for the hub to have nine: six main and three reserve.
The new  2,820-meter-long runway is its first to run east to west, meaning a reduction in taxiing and airborne times for westbound aircraft, saving time and fuel.
“They’re the only airport in the world that is licensed for three simultaneous runway operations,” says Grant, “You can build more frequency at those peak hours, and it gives you more operational flexibility. If you’ve got three runways, then you’re likely to improve your punctuality.”
Secrets of the sultan’s palace where concubines and eunuchs lived
Turkish Airlines has an 80% share of flights at Istanbul Airport and plays a key role in the hub’s success. Two years ago, it entered Guinness World Records for its achievement in flying to more countries than any other airline: 130 in total, as of 2026.
It operates a modern and rapidly expanding fleet of more than 500 Boeing and Airbus aircraft, including a diverse mix of narrow and widebody planes.
A younger fleet makes “a better impression” on customers, says Viktoriia Myroniuk, a senior lecturer in air transport management at the UK’s Cranfield University, reflecting on the polished service that helped earn Turkish Airlines its recent Skytrax award for Best Airline in Europe .
Newer aircraft are also more efficient, which, in this time of rising fuel prices, gives the airline a competitive edge, allowing them to lower ticket prices.
Selahattin Bilgen, CEO of iGA Istanbul Airport, tells CNN, “The efficiency and cost advantages we provide continue to attract new airlines to our network each year, and today we are one of only two major hubs worldwide serving the largest number of airlines.”
Infrastructure is equally key to that connectivity. “As a relatively new airport, iGA İstanbul Airport was designed from the outset with growth in mind, providing the capacity and flexibility to accommodate increasing passenger demand and support our role as a major international transfer hub.”
OAG’s 2026 Megahub rankings are inevitably affected by the ongoing disruption in the Middle East, as well as the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.
While other airports and regions have suffered, Istanbul Airport and Turkey’s geographical position and diplomatic relations have by chance granted it better fortune.
Istanbul Airport has the flexibility and capacity for growth that its competitors in the region lack. London Heathrow’s plan for a third runway remains highly controversial, due to the environmental impact in a highly built-up corner of southeast England. Amsterdam Schiphol, the world’s third best connected, has a flight cap of 488,000 movements a year.
“The fact that Istanbul Airport is slightly on the outskirts” means “they can operate 24/7,” says Myroniuk.
She also praises Turkish Airlines’ stopover program , which allows connecting passengers to take a break to explore Istanbul and enjoy free accommodation in partner hotels.
“I’m one of those unlucky passengers who really can’t sleep on board” and struggle on economy flights, Myroniuk says, but “your luggage stays with Turkish Airlines. You go to the perfect night’s rest.”
She married her brother, then he died. The monument to her grief was a Wonder of the Ancient World
It’s a form of sustainable tourism, she says, allowing travelers to embrace slower travel and to connect with local culture, rather than notching up cheap connecting flights with no experiences to show for it.
For many passengers it is also easier to get a visa to stop off in Turkey than it would be to take an exploratory tour from an EU airport, so that’s another advantage Istanbul Airport enjoys.
Although it’s hard to make any predictions in these turbulent times, Grant says that “all things being equal,” Istanbul will continue to hold onto its position in 2027.
“I think we’re going to see over the next three or four years the Chinese airports strengthen in their positions. We’re seeing more international growth from Chinese airlines, and that will help them,” he says.
International airlines including British Airways have yet to resume flying to the Middle East, but airports in the region will hopefully “get back to where they were,” says Grant. “All of which will continue to chip away at the position at Heathrow and Amsterdam Schiphol, and Paris, where we have European airports” that are reaching capacity.

articles.title_orig: Shock gloves purchased by ICE cause intense pain and quick compliance, Army study finds
articles.title_zh: Shock gloves purchased by ICE cause intense pain and quick compliance, Army study finds
articles.content_orig:
The shock gloves immigration agents could soon use to control detainees and protesters worked so powerfully during a military exercise that participants felt intense pain, stopped fighting immediately and feared additional exposures, according to a previously unreleased Army study.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement leaders were aware of the findings before signing a $16.7 million contract to purchase 6,000 pairs of shock gloves in August, according to records obtained by the watchdog group American Oversight and shared with The Associated Press.
The shocks had a profound impact on Army employees who played the role of combative prisoners during the exercise, which took place at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas in October 2024. The participants, several of whom were large-statured men, stopped resisting seconds after officers applied shocks by touching gloves to their skin, and were left with "fatigue, soreness and excessive apprehensiveness to being shocked again," the study found.
"After experiencing the effects of the GLOVE ... participants stated just seeing the GLOVE was enough to make them want to comply," the authors wrote.
In contract paperwork released on a federal database in August, ICE called the gloves "distraction and de-escalation devices" that will be safer than other non-lethal options to subdue targets for arrest and deportation and protesters who create civil disturbances. The agency has argued the rapid compliance the gloves cause will keep officers safer and prevent incidents from requiring potentially lethal force.
"ICE does not currently have an empty hand use of force device to provide to the field amid unprecedented levels of threats and violence against ICE officers and agents to help ensure they can de-escalate tense situations before they turn violent," the agency wrote in procurement documents.
But critics have warned the gloves will give ICE another weapon to intimidate and brutalize people even as the agency is under fire for excessive force that has left a trail of deaths and injuries across the nation. The gloves, they note, are easy to discharge, do not leave a mark and have not been extensively used in settings outside of jails. The manufacturer warns they should not be used on high-risk populations such as children, pregnant women or disabled people.
"The military assessment in ICE's own files shows that these gloves can cause 'intense pain' and force compliance. It does not establish that they are safe," said Chioma Chukwu, executive director of American Oversight. "Everyone should be alarmed that ICE is preparing to deploy a tool designed to inflict, at best, intense pain, without showing that it is safe for the people who will be subjected to it."
ICE released the study and other documents to American Oversight as part of the group's Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the agency seeking records related to its use of force.
The military prison study assessed whether the gloves could be used effectively to forcibly remove combative prisoners from their cells, to respond to disturbances in common areas and to transport uncooperative inmates. Role-playing employees conducted several scenarios with and without the gloves to test their impact, including violent encounters in which inmates were to fight as hard as they could.
The study found the devices "increased the efficiency" of teams carrying out forced cell extractions and responding to disturbances by reducing the length of physical encounters, keeping guards from becoming exhausted and preventing injuries. They did not "significantly change" the time it took to control inmates during escorts but required less effort.
"GLOVE provides a boost in confidence to smaller or less trained members," the study found. "Inmate compliance was immediate" compared to other methods, it added.
The electric jolt does not cause the body to freeze like a Taser shock does, but instead "works by overloading the peripheral nerve endings" of the skin to cause pain, the study said. Participants who were wet or had oil on their skin described even more powerful shocks, with one reporting discomfort for 30 minutes afterward.
ICE's contract requires the manufacturer, Compliant Technologies LLC, to deliver the gloves within six months. Its owner, Jeff Niklaus, said he was unavailable for an interview, citing a busy workload.
The six-month deal includes the gloves, support equipment and services. The gloves themselves cost $2,495 apiece.
Compliant Technologies' instruction manual says users of the gloves should "always give the subject(s) a reasonable opportunity to comply before force is used." It suggests using them for up to 15 seconds, unless the subject becomes more violent or endangers people.
White House border czar Tom Homan has said it could "be awhile" before the gloves are in the field because ICE is still ironing out training and policy issues. A statement released Tuesday by ICE did not address questions about the study and the status of the rollout, but said "officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics."
U.S. Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said ICE has not responded to an Aug. 27 letter in which she and 15 other Democratic Senate colleagues called for ICE to abandon its plan to buy the gloves or explain how they would be used and managed to avoid abuse. She said she still wants answers.
"Without ICE's responses to legitimate questions from 16 United States Senators, the American public is being left in the dark about how these electric shock gloves are being deployed and what, if any, training the agents who use them have received," she said.
The Department of Homeland Security has defended the purchase, accusing critics of trying to deny federal law enforcement officers safety equipment. In a statement to CBS News in August, a DHS spokesperson called the pushback from Democrats "despicable and a deliberate attempt to undermine and endanger our officers."
"ICE is constantly assessing the needs of our officers in the field to ensure they have the tools and equipment necessary to safely arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens from our country. Every decision is made with careful consideration and appropriately reviewed to ensure that any technology ICE utilizes is consistent with all applicable law enforcement policies and standards," the spokesperson said, adding that personnel are "highly trained in de-escalation tactics."
Joe  Walsh and Nicole  Sganga contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft, Nvidia CEOs to unveil new AI laptop at San Francisco event
articles.title_zh: Microsoft, Nvidia CEOs to unveil new AI laptop at San Francisco event
articles.content_orig:
The Surface Laptop Ultra runs on Nvidia's RTX Spark chip and is designed to handle AI tasks locally, without relying on cloud servers
Microsoft $MSFT and Nvidia $NVDA unveiled the Surface Laptop Ultra on Wednesday at a company-hosted event in San Francisco, with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang presenting the machine together.
The laptop is built around Nvidia 's RTX Spark chip, which enables AI workloads — from coding assistance to demanding business applications — to run locally on the machine instead of being sent to cloud servers. For Microsoft , the device advances its goal of moving at least a portion of AI processing out of Azure data centers and into the hands of Windows users. For Nvidia , the Surface Laptop Ultra opens a path into a segment of the processor market that Intel $INTC and Advanced Micro Devices have controlled for decades, according to Reuters.
Pricing is a significant variable. Memory costs have driven up prices across AI-capable hardware, and Nvidia recently raised the price of its DGX Spark AI desktop by roughly 75% to $6,950. According to Reuters, Moor Insights & Strategy analyst Anshel Sag said the hardware has moved beyond the price range of many potential buyers. "The software wasn't ready, but the hardware was. Now the software is ready and the hardware is too expensive to actually run it locally," Sag said. "So it's becoming this thing where only the people who have the budget can really afford to run AI locally."
The event also featured Windows and Devices chief Pavan Davuluri, according to Engadget . The Surface Laptop Ultra was first shown at Microsoft 's Build developer conference earlier this year. Its display is a 15-inch mini LED panel, it carries the biggest trackpad Microsoft has ever shipped, and its port lineup spans USB-C, USB-A, and a full-sized SD card reader, according to Engadget.
Nvidia announced the RTX Spark chip in June, describing it as its first processor designed to serve as the main chip in Windows PCs. The chip fuses a Blackwell graphics processor with a custom Arm-based CPU called the N1X, designed by MediaTek, connected through Nvidia 's NVLink interconnect. It offers up to 128GB of unified memory and delivers 1 petaflop of AI compute, the company said. The chip is built on TSMC $TSM 's 3-nanometer fabrication process.
Microsoft and Nvidia are also building security tools for running AI agents on the devices, including new Windows security features and a runtime called Nvidia OpenShell that lets users control what agents can access and how queries are routed based on privacy preferences, the company said. The effort follows a cyberattack on AI startup Hugging Face carried out by an out-of-control OpenAI agent, which sharpened industry concern about AI agent security.

New information reveals that, over the weekend, the U.S. removed all long-range bombers from the British air base near where five men were arrested last week in a suspected terror plot. A U.S. official who is not authorized to speak publicly told NPR that the decision to abruptly send home a dozen B-1 bombers from Royal Air Force base Fairford was due to a "credible threat" from Iran, which potentially involved a drone attack.
F15's maneuver at RAF Lakenheath on Sept. 28, 2026, in Lakenheath, England. Dan Kitwood/Getty Images hide caption
High school students in France are blocking schools today , after hundreds of thousands of them marched across the country yesterday. They are joined by teachers, parents and labor union members. The movement, which began in a particularly run-down high school facing teacher absenteeism, aims to improve learning conditions and address inequalities in the French education system.
A former head of Germany's foreign intelligence agency will appear before a federal judge today to face charges of espionage and attempted treason. Federal prosecutors accuse August Hanning of using classified information to brief a foreign intelligence agency. He served as the head of Germany's CIA equivalent for seven years from 1998 to 2005. Prosecutors allege he shared sensitive political information for 12 years after leaving office. They have not yet disclosed who Hanning's alleged clients were.
As Israel marks three years since Hamas' surprise Oct. 7 attacks , new reports in Israeli and U.S. media say regional allies warned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Hamas was planning to attack. Four people in the Middle East with direct knowledge of the warnings told NPR that Netanyahu was personally informed about the potential attacks and his security agencies were notified multiple times in the weeks and days leading up to Oct. 7, 2023. Netanyahu has denied this, labeling the reports "fake news" and recently filing a defamation lawsuit against the news outlets that first published the information. He and his defense minister now warn that Hamas might attempt to attack again on this Oct. 7 memorial day and leading up to Israel's national elections later this month.

articles.title_orig: Half a billion dollars in GOP spending does little to move polls
articles.title_zh: Half a billion dollars in GOP spending does little to move polls
articles.content_orig:
Republicans are swamping House and Senate races with an unprecedented flood of late ad spending as the party tests whether hundreds of millions of dollars can buy it some reprieve from the eroding political environment that’s threatening longtime Republican states and districts.
Since the start of September, Republicans have made more than $700 million worth of new advertising bookings in congressional races alone, according to an NBC News analysis of data from AdImpact, a political ad-tracking firm. That’s new money on top of what had already been committed to those races in ad reservations made over the summer.
By comparison, Democrats booked more than $430 million in new ad reservations across those races last month.
The disparity is greatest in the battle for the Senate majority, where almost 7 of every 10 newly booked advertising dollars are coming from Republicans. That’s led by a massive, late investment in the Senate race in Texas, where Democrat James Talarico is threatening a longtime Republican seat and the GOP has poured in almost $150 million in new ad dollars to back up its nominee, Ken Paxton.
The gap is smaller in the House, where a bit less than 6 in 10 of those new ad dollars are coming from the GOP.
Democrats still have a number of advantages in their corner, including President Donald Trump and his party’s eroding standing among voters, Democrats’ own well-funded candidates, and help from outside groups. Candidates can take advantage of a rule that allows them to buy television ads at cheaper rates than outside groups, too.
But the color of the outside money flood shows how Republicans, increasingly on defense in both the House and the Senate, are able to lean on their financial advantage in hope of defying political gravity, as party bastions like Texas and even Kansas look more competitive than usual.
On Tuesday morning, South Carolina — where a Democrat has not won a Senate race since 1998 — became the latest state to see a new infusion of Republican money, with the super PAC aligned with Senate Republicans planning to spend $5 million there, according to a source familiar with the spending. Axios first reported the spending in the state.
“With the environment not on our side and an incumbent presidency, the three things we have going for us are good candidates, a good map and a lot more money than they do,” said a Republican strategist involved in Senate races.
Everything about the late flood of ad spending is bigger in Texas, where a new group called Texas PAC has booked more than $115 million over the last month alone aimed at boosting Paxton, the state attorney general. Democrats haven’t won a statewide election in Texas in more than 30 years.
But because Republicans are spending largely through outside groups, they have to pay a premium on the rates for each ad, while Talarico’s flush campaign is able to capitalize on those lower candidate ad rates. That means the spending disparity is greater than the actual number of ad airings or their reach.
Senate races in Ohio and Michigan also drew more than $75 million in new ad dollars in September, mostly from Republican-aligned groups. They include a super PAC funded by cryptocurrency interests, Trump’s aligned super PACs and other groups aligned with the national party or Senate Republican leadership.
Again, both states have Democratic candidates — former Sen. Sherrod Brown in Ohio and former county health official Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan — who have been spending significant money on their advertising campaigns.
No Going Back PAC and Safety and Affordability PAC have made more than $150 million in new ad bookings since the start of September across dozens of races. While the groups haven’t confirmed where they’ve gotten their war chest from, The New York Times recently confirmed that MAGA Inc., Trump’s main super PAC, is primarily funding the effort with the hundreds of millions of dollars it has banked over the last few years.
Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina, chair of the Senate GOP’s campaign arm, touted the party’s spending advantage as key to helping Republicans hold on to their majority and credited Trump’s deep-pocketed political operation with ensuring the flood of cash continues.
Scott told reporters that he met last week with Trump’s chief of staff, Susie Wiles, and that the message from Wiles was “money will not be our problem.”
“That’s exciting news to me,” Scott said, adding later, “Knowing that they are going to invest completely in these races is incredibly helpful, because cash is king.”
“We finally find ourselves at a cash advantage because of MAGA Inc. It’s a powerful tool that is providing us with the firepower necessary to really share our message,” he said.
Democrats take some solace in where the new spending is going. The vast majority is plowing into states and seats Trump carried in 2024, including congressional districts Trump would have won by double digits that year, like North Carolina’s 1st District, Texas’ 35th District and Alaska’s at-large congressional district.
The money is also going to races in which Republicans felt comfortable until recently, like the Senate race in Kansas, where the top Senate Republican super PAC just reallocated millions initially meant to be spent in North Carolina.
“The money is not because there is this swell of Republican momentum; the money is because of a swell of Republican panic,” said Lauren French, the communications director at Senate Majority PAC, the super PAC aligned with Senate Democratic leadership. “Voters don’t like anything they are selling — that includes the message, the candidates and the president.”
Meredith Kelly, a longtime Democratic strategist who works on House and Senate races, said, “When you are defending in such deep-red territory, the technical term for that is: ‘You’re f---ed.’”
“Republicans, if they have one advantage, it’s that they have more money, and they are putting that money to the test right now post-Labor Day,” Kelly added. “However, the big question is: Is that money enough to counteract the fact that Donald Trump’s coalition is falling apart?”
Still, Democrats are uncomfortable watching their party get outspent to such a degree.
“It’s a huge problem, and it will be an ongoing problem, and you see all the lists of high-value donors for both parties and we get swamped every time,” Kelly said. “It creates such an initial advantage for the Republicans that we have to close the gap on in a variety of ways — candidate money, better message, better candidates. We are setting ourselves up for an uphill battle every single time because of the Republican donor strength in terms of the billionaire class.”
Ben Kamisar is a national political reporter for NBC News

articles.title_orig: Tropical Storm Isaias forms in Gulf, could reach U.S. as hurricane this weekend. See maps, possible path.
articles.title_zh: Tropical Storm Isaias forms in Gulf, could reach U.S. as hurricane this weekend. See maps, possible path.
articles.content_orig:
Tropical Storm Isaias has formed in the Gulf and is expected to approach the U.S. northern Gulf Coast on Friday after becoming a hurricane, according to the National Hurricane Center .
Isaias would be the Atlantic Basin's first hurricane of the season and is its ninth named storm. El Niño continues to bring a more active season in the Pacific. The storm formed with less than two months remaining in the 2026 hurricane season , which ends Nov. 30.
Tropical Storm Isaias, which grew from Tropical Depression Nine on Wednesday and is pronounced "ees-ah-EE-ahs," is expected to pass to the north of Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula on Thursday before approaching the U.S. Gulf Coast the following day, according to forecasters. It is expected to rapidly strengthen.
"Hurricane watches will likely be required for a portion of the U.S. northern Gulf coast later today," the hurricane center said Wednesday. Tropical storm-force winds were extending outward up to 45 miles from the storm's center.
Isaias is forecast to bring moderate to heavy rainfall to the Gulf Coast and into the rest of the Southeast this weekend into early next week. The hurricane center forecasts 3 to 6 inches of rain and as much as 10 inches in some places on the central Gulf Coast from southeastern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle.
Some longer-range forecast models also see this moisture eventually reaching the Ohio Valley and Northeast by midweek next week.
The hurricane center on Thursday warned of "an increasing risk of dangerous wind and storm surge impacts" along parts of the northern Gulf Coast and urged people living in Louisiana, Alabama, Mississippi and northern Florida to "closely monitor the latest forecast updates and ensure they have their hurricane plan in place."
In addition to rain, the hurricane center said Isaias could potentially bring urban flooding and isolated river flooding to places in its path.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis on Tuesday signed an executive order declaring a state of emergency for 25 Florida counties ahead of the storm's arrival. DeSantis said in a statement that the order "ensures communities have the time and resources necessary to prepare for potential severe weather impacts to the Panhandle and Big Bend region of Florida."
While tropical storm and hurricane formation and frequency vary throughout the season, the "I"-named systems tend to be the most retired names within the Atlantic basin.
The most commonly known retired "I"-named storms are Ian (2022), Ida (2021), Irma (2017), and Irene (2011).
When Ike was retired in 2008, Isaias replaced the "I" name on the Atlantic tropical cyclones list, which rotates every six years.

On 25 September 2026, World Lung Day highlighted the importance of respiratory health as a public health priority, calling for stronger prevention, earlier detection, equitable access to care and healthier environments.
Respiratory diseases remain a major public health challenge across Europe. While many lung diseases are preventable, addressing their impact requires coordinated action from policymakers, healthcare professionals, researchers and communities.
This year’s message, “Healthy Lungs, Healthy Populations,” emphasised the need to translate scientific evidence into effective public health action.
These priorities closely align with the objectives of the Joint Action on Respiratory Diseases (JARED), which brings together European partners to improve respiratory health, strengthen prevention and reduce health inequalities.
World Lung Day serves as a reminder that protecting lung health requires sustained commitment and collaboration across sectors.

articles.title_orig: The economic path to climate finance
articles.title_zh: The economic path to climate finance
articles.content_orig:
While policymakers often frame decarbonisation as a climate imperative, some of the fastest energy transitions are being driven by economics, affordability and energy security
As the world pursues decarbonisation, the concept of a ‘just transition’ has become ubiquitous, particularly when describing the shift away from fossil fuels in emerging and developing economies. Emissions targets at the global and national levels are viewed as the main drivers of the energy transition, and the climate policies developed to meet those targets must balance environmental and social objectives. But decarbonisation is not always the product of a planned emissions-reduction pathway. In fact, with the cost of renewables continuing to fall, many emerging and developing countries now see phasing out fossil fuels as a matter of economic survival and energy security. For example, in January 2024, Ethiopia banned the import of petrol and diesel vehicles with immediate effect. The move was striking precisely because it was framed not as a climate commitment, but as a way to reduce its annual fossil-fuel import bill of more than $5bn, which consumed a huge share of the country’s scarce foreign-currency reserves.
With the country constructing Africa’s largest hydroelectric dam, it made little economic sense to remain dependent on expensive fuel imports to power transport. Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) quickly filled the market gap created by the ban; the streets of Addis Ababa are now teeming with BYD cars. Tax exemptions and import duty waivers for EVs, coupled with the rising costs of second-hand internal-combustion-engine vehicles, have accelerated this shift in consumer behaviour. The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, which was officially opened in September 2025, produces enough surplus hydropower to run these EVs cheaply.
Swift update of solar power Crucially, economic and energy-security concerns, not a formal emissions-reduction framework, were responsible for such rapid decarbonisation. A similar pattern seems to hold in Pakistan.
The country’s swift uptake of solar power reflected factors that created an opportunity for disruptive change, not green advocacy or a national climate plan. In 2022, a massive flood left roughly one-third of the country under water and caused more than $30bn in economic damage, straining government budgets, reducing household incomes, and undermining the state’s ability to operate public utilities. With energy costs rising, there was a clear need for an alternative to diesel generation.
Meanwhile, China had surplus solar-panel production, and the US had imposed import restrictions. Pakistan took advantage of China’s discounted solar panels to adopt renewable generation at a rapid clip. Between December 2021 and December 2025, the share of Pakistan’s electricity generated by solar increased five-fold. A late mover confronting unique energy-security challenges, Pakistan benefited from cost advantages created by global trade dynamics.
While South Africa has been following an emissions-reduction pathway for decades, an affordability crisis ultimately drove widespread decarbonisation. These countries are moving away from fossil fuels largely because of mounting economic and energy pressures, rather than a narrow focus on emissions reductions. But this does not mean that the question of justice disappears. Lower-income households account for a smaller share of the roughly eight gigawatts of rooftop solar installed in South Africa, reflecting high upfront costs. Crisis-driven decarbonisation still requires efforts to improve affordability and ensure that people from all walks of life can participate in the energy transition.
Systemic change is required Policymakers have used the concept of a ‘just transition’ to make a morally and emotionally compelling case for decarbonisation. But they should be focusing on how to foster systemic change. Understanding that the primary drivers of solar uptake in South Africa and Pakistan or EV adoption in Ethiopia are structural and economic could help policymakers develop better tools and systems. This also has direct implications for how philanthropists and governments allocate resources. Channelling funding toward grid capacity, storage infrastructure, and affordable financing mechanisms will likely produce more durable results than funding for climate education and communication.
Investing in efforts that aim to improve people’s lives, from lower energy bills to unfettered electricity access, will do more to accelerate decarbonisation – and to change hearts and minds. To be sure, the world must reduce emissions to prevent the planet from overheating. To achieve that goal, it should focus on expanding energy access and ensuring affordability. That means recognising and adequately responding to the external pressures that can support decarbonisation pathways in emerging and developing economies. Ethiopia, Pakistan, and South Africa have shown that economic factors can provide better entry points for scaling green solutions and catalysing systemic change than top-down, morally driven transition plans.

articles.title_orig: US death row inmate Christa Pike awake and speaking after failed execution, lawyers say
articles.title_zh: US death row inmate Christa Pike awake and speaking after failed execution, lawyers say
articles.content_orig:
US death row inmate Christa Pike is "conscious and speaking" after surviving a failed execution attempt in Tennessee last week, her lawyers say.
Pike, 50, continues to receive critical medical care while "handcuffed and shackled to the bed" in hospital, her lawyers said in a statement on Tuesday. An anaesthesiologist advising her team told the BBC that Pike was able to communicate in a "basic way" but did not seem to recall the execution attempt.
Pike, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two lethal injections on 30 September in Tennessee.
Experts and her legal team say her apparent recovery is unprecedented.
Pike is believed to be the only person to survive a lethal injection. The execution attempt was described immediately afterwards as a "mess" by Slemmer's mother, who had pushed for Pike to be put to death.
After it became clear Pike would not die, she was taken to hospital, where she remained unconscious for days as medical staff cleared her body of the injected chemical.
In their statement on Tuesday, her lawyers said her prognosis remained unclear, but that "at a minimum, we expect a long recovery".
In additional comments made to the BBC, the anaesthesiologist advising her team said Pike had been taken off a ventilator.
"She has some memories of being in the hospital but no memory, I believe, of the execution attempt," Dr Joel Zivot said of the limited communication that had taken place.
Zivot said Pike was able to recall her name and had made an incorrect guess at the date, believing that the month was still September.
In an earlier interview, Zivot said the likelihood of recovering from lethal injection was low. "Most people who get lethal injection die from it," he explained.
There remained many unknowns, he said, including how much of the drug used by the prison authorities, pentobarbital, got into her system.
"I would not, in any way, say at this point that all the big risks are behind her," he said.
Deborah Denno, a criminologist and professor at Fordham Law School, said she was "absolutely astonished" that Pike was conscious and speaking.
There had been seven other cases where prisoners survived executions but in those cases, executioners were not able to inject anything into the inmates' veins, Denno told the BBC.
Pike "is the only person for whom some kind of toxin has been injected", she said.
"They did everything they were supposed to do as part of the execution process, and it simply didn't work," Denno said. "This has never happened before."
Speaking to Radio 4's Today programme, a local journalist who witnessed the attempted execution said that he, too, did not know of "an exact precedent".
Steven Hale, a journalist for the Nashville Banner, said the case raised many questions, including "what must this be like for the victim's family, who for 30 years has been told we are gonna give you justice and justice is us executing Christa Pike".
Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong after twice injecting her with the chemical pentobarbital.
Zivot has suggested the pentobarbital was more likely to have spread across the tissue under Pike's skin than to have entered her bloodstream in a quantity that was sufficient to kill her.
Pike's lawyers previously warned that her medical history and anatomy - including thrombocytosis (a blood-clotting condition) and small veins could scupper the execution and cause her pain.
While the incident is investigated, Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has suspended all executions for the rest of the year - and the head of prisons in the state is resigning.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens.
Shipp was 17 years old at the time, meaning that he was spared the death penalty for his part in the attack because he was not yet legally an adult at the time. He remains in prison.
Pike's lawyers are scheduled to appear in court in Nashville on Wednesday. They also plan to hold a news conference outside the court.
In their latest update, they repeated their call for Lee to use his powers to commute Pike's sentence to the lower punishment of life in prison without parole.
In 2022, more than a third of executions across the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which tracks information about such cases.
For lethal injections, such incidents have typically occurred due to difficulty obtaining reliable IV access to the veins, though the underlying reason differs from person to person.
In cases the centre has documented, all failures happened before the lethal  drugs could be administered. The last failed lethal injection that was tracked happened earlier this year - also in Tennessee.
The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein for a lethal injection. He was granted a year's reprieve by the governor.

articles.title_orig: Real-world VOYAGER data on faricimab in nAMD, DME, RVO at EURETINA 2026
articles.title_zh: Real-world VOYAGER data on faricimab in nAMD, DME, RVO at EURETINA 2026
articles.content_orig:
Real-world VOYAGER data at EURETINA 2026 show vision and anatomic outcomes with faricimab across nAMD, DME, and RVO.
New 12-month real-world data from the global VOYAGER study suggest that outcomes with faricimab-svoa (Vabysmo; Genentech) in routine practice are broadly consistent with those reported in its phase 3 trials, with treatment-naive eyes gaining vision and previously treated eyes maintaining or modestly improving vision alongside reductions in retinal thickness and fluid. 1 The findings, which span neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD) , diabetic macular edema (DME) , and macular edema following retinal vein occlusion (RVO) , were presented at the 26th EURETINA Congress in Vienna, Austria, held October 1–4, 2026. 1-4
The data are of particular interest to retina specialists because much of faricimab's real-world use involves patients switched from other anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) agents—a population that was largely excluded from, or underrepresented in, the pivotal trials. 5-7
VOYAGER ( NCT05476926 ) is a prospective, noninterventional study of more than 5,000 patients initiating faricimab 6 mg for nAMD, DME, or RVO across 28 countries in Asia-Pacific, Europe, North America, and South America. 2-4 Treatment followed usual care, with no mandated visit schedule or imaging protocol. 2 Investigators collected visual acuity (VA) in Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) letters, central subfield thickness (CST), investigator-determined subretinal fluid (SRF) and intraretinal fluid (IRF), and ocular safety events. A subset of spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) scans was additionally analyzed using an in-house deep learning segmentation algorithm (ROSA) to quantify fluid volumes in the central 1-mm field. 3,4 All analyses were descriptive. 2-4
“The strength of VOYAGER lies in both its pragmatic design and its broad global inclusion,” Robin A. Vora, MD, a retina specialist at Kaiser Permanente Oakland Medical Center, said in an email interview with the Eye Care Network.
“By omitting protocol-driven appointment and imaging schedules, the study closely mirrors real-world community practice, including high-volume integrated health systems like Kaiser Permanente. Furthermore, by enrolling patients across 28 countries, the dataset aligns well with the diverse patient demographics we care for in Northern California.
As a result, the overall real-world outcomes across all three indications—wet AMD, DME, and RVO—closely resemble what we see in our practice, particularly within the previously treated (switch) population. Where real-world U.S. clinical practice differs from global observational trial data, however, is in the treatment-naïve cohort. In the U.S., insurance coverage preferences and mandated first-line step therapy (such as bevacizumab) often make it difficult for practices to immediately initiate newer generation agents in naïve eyes and, as such, not achieve the rapid early gains reported in VOYAGER.”
In the DME cohort—reported in an abstract by Veeral Sheth, MD, and colleagues—506 treatment-naive and 413 previously treated eyes had at least 12 months of follow-up between November 2022 and January 2026. 2 Among treatment-naive eyes, mean VA improved from 64.1 to 71.1 letters, and mean CST decreased from 415.2 µm to 292.6 µm at month 12. The proportion of eyes with SRF fell from 17.3% to 2.4%, and IRF from 60.8% to 26.8%. 2 In previously treated eyes, VA rose from 66.9 to 69.1 letters and CST decreased from 367.6 µm to 314.2 µm; SRF fell from 10.6% to 4.1% and IRF from 46.3% to 39.1%. 2
Injection frequency declined in the second half of the year, from a mean of 4.3 injections in months 1–6 to 2.1 in months 7–12 in treatment-naive eyes and from 4.1 to 2.7 in previously treated eyes. 2 Per-injection rates of intraocular inflammation (0.05%) and endophthalmitis (0.02%) were low and described by the authors as aligned with the phase 3 program. 2
Genentech's announcement reported somewhat different DME figures, including a mean gain of 8.2 letters and a CST reduction of 127.8 µm in treatment-naive eyes and a 2.7-letter gain in previously treated eyes; the release did not specify the analysis population or explain the difference from the abstract Sheth presented at EURETINA. 1
A separate abstract led by Adrian Koh, MD, applied machine learning segmentation to DME scans from a smaller subset of 28 treatment-naive and 36 previously treated eyes from 14 countries. 3 In treatment-naive eyes, mean total fluid volume decreased from 61.1 nL to 14.3 nL over 12 months, driven by reductions in both SRF and IRF. In previously treated eyes, total fluid fell from 46.7 nL to 26.5 nL, almost entirely through IRF reduction, while SRF volume was minimal and unchanged. 3
In nAMD, the company reported a mean VA gain of 4.6 letters and a CST reduction of 110.5 µm in treatment-naive eyes after 12 months and essentially stable VA (−0.1 letters) with a 26.1-µm CST reduction in previously treated eyes. 1 The proportion of treatment-naive eyes with SRF fell from 72.1% to 25.3%, and with IRF from 48.5% to 20.6%. 1
An imaging abstract led by Clare Bailey, MD, analyzed 136 treatment-naive and 174 previously treated nAMD eyes from 17 countries using the same segmentation approach. 4 Among treatment-naive eyes, mean total fluid volume decreased from 33.1 nL to 3.7 nL and mean pigment epithelial detachment (PED) volume from 43.8 nL to 30.7 nL. In previously treated eyes, which began with lower fluid burden, total fluid decreased from 11.6 nL to 6.4 nL and PED volume from 63.1 nL to 52.7 nL. 4 According to the release, eyes in both the nAMD and DME cohorts received fewer injections in months 7–12 than in months 1–6. 1
RVO results were reported at 6 months and only in the company release. 1 In branch RVO, treatment-naive eyes gained a mean of 10.0 letters with a 171.3-µm CST reduction, while previously treated eyes gained 2.0 letters with a 59.0-µm reduction. In central/hemiretinal RVO, treatment-naive eyes gained 16.6 letters with a 287.4-µm CST reduction, and previously treated eyes gained 3.9 letters with a 63.4-µm reduction. 1 Cohort sizes were not reported.
Faricimab is a bispecific antibody that binds both VEGF-A and angiopoietin-2 (Ang-2); the Ang-2 component is thought to promote vascular stability, although its contribution to clinical response has not been established, according to the prescribing information. 8 The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved faricimab for nAMD and DME in January 2022 as the first bispecific antibody for the eye, followed by approval for macular edema after RVO in October 2023. 8,9
Approval was based on phase 3 trials demonstrating noninferiority to aflibercept 2 mg. In TENAYA and LUCERNE, treatment-naive patients with nAMD gained 5.8 and 6.6 letters, respectively, at the primary end point with dosing up to every 16 weeks. 5,8 In YOSEMITE and RHINE, patients with DME gained approximately 11 to 12 letters at year 1.6,8 In BALATON (branch RVO) and COMINO (central/hemiretinal RVO), mean gains were 16.9 letters in each trial at week 24 with monthly dosing. 7,8 The 72-week extension of those trials evaluated treat-and-extend dosing, and the US label was updated in April 2026 to address RVO treatment beyond 6 months. 8,10
Direct comparison with the trials is limited. Pivotal-trial patients were newly diagnosed and largely treatment naive, whereas VOYAGER includes switched eyes with variable treatment histories and baseline characteristics. The release quoted Robyn Guymer, MBBS, PhD, chair of the VOYAGER steering committee and deputy director of the Centre for Eye Research Australia, who noted that patients in routine practice often do not meet the strict entry criteria of phase 3 trials. 1
VOYAGER is a single-arm, observational study without a comparator, so the results cannot establish relative efficacy against other anti-VEGF agents. Treatment intervals and imaging were le
