articles.title_orig: The World October 7 Made. Plus. . .
articles.title_zh: The World October 7 Made. Plus. . .
articles.content_orig:
It’s Wednesday, October 7. Today, we’re bringing you a different Front Page . It’s dedicated to one thing: the third anniversary of Hamas’s attack on Israel—what it meant then, and what it means now.
Many of the ways in which the world changed over the last three years are by now familiar. A disorienting new normal for Israelis, who suddenly found themselves in a fight for national survival. A region turned upside down by the attack and the wars that followed. The celebration in the West of terror attacks as “resistance.” The emergence of Israel as a litmus test in American politics. The explosion of antisemitism across the world.
But on that terrible day three years ago, none of these consequences were clear.
Today, we bring you stories on the world October 7 made. Douglas Murray on Israel’s determination to fight on—and why it is winning. Eli Lake on how the American foreign policy establishment is rewriting the history of the Gaza war. Simon Sebag Montefiore on the October 7 wars and how they will change the Middle East. Former British prime minister Tony Blair on the latest example of how October 7 has helped mainstream antisemitism in Western politics. And MIT engineering systems professor Yossi Sheffi on what happened after he published a book about antisemitism on campus following the attacks.
But first we want to tell you about the people on the ground who October 7 left behind, starting with those who survived the day, but never fully recovered.
Some 1,200 people were slaughtered three years ago today, and 251 taken hostage. But there were countless others whose lives were forever changed.
Today, Polina Fradkin talks to the families of those lost to suicide in the wake of October 7, the therapists who work around the clock to spot suicidal ideation before it’s too late, the lingering fear among Israelis that their loved ones could be next—and the people who refuse to lose hope in their home. Read her story about the long psychological shadow cast by the atrocity.
For Avinatan Or , October 7 was the start of what would become 738 days in Hamas captivity, after he was abducted from the Nova festival. Last month, his memoir was published in Hebrew in Israel, and swiftly became a No. 1 bestseller. Today, we’re proud to bring you an exclusive English excerpt from the book—about the experiences that led him, five months into captivity, to literally dig his way to freedom. His tale is one of extraordinary resilience and bravery in the darkest circumstances imaginable. Read Avinatan on his time in the tunnels.
And now we turn to the Palestinian people, for whom the shadow of October 7 is impossible to escape. They live among its consequences: Much of Gaza has been reduced to rubble, their cause has been warped into a Western protest movement and, somehow, Hamas still operates amid the wreckage. The attacks three years ago, writes Ahmed Fouad Alkhatib , a Gazan who himself lost family members and his childhood home in Israel’s retaliatory response, triggered “the most catastrophic chapter in contemporary Palestinian history.” Read his piece on how Hamas turned Gaza into the “fulcrum for instability, devastation, and conflict in the Middle East,” and what Gazans—and their ostensible allies across the West—must do to chart a path forward.
Last week, the world was captivated by an extraordinary act of bravery, when ordinary Israelis stormed the cockpit to avert a hijacking on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. (Read our exclusive interview with one of the heroes.) For Douglas Murray , these heroics were emblematic of Israel’s approach to its enemies over the past three years: “The Israelis saw an existential threat, took matters into their own hands, and decided their own course,” he wrote. “The rest of the West will have to decide whether it will follow the Israeli model or let its own future be dictated by terror and the hijacking of its entire society.”
Read his full column on how Israel put victory ahead of the approval of its critics:
Here in the United States, Israel is at the center of debates about American foreign policy—and the tide turned against the Jewish state almost immediately after October 7. A new book, Crossing the Red Line by Akbar Shahid Ahmed, claims to offer an objective view of the divide within the Democratic Party on the issue, but Eli Lake says it does nothing of the sort. Read Eli on the fight over Israel—and whether there are any pro-Israel voices left in the Democratic foreign policy establishment.
As for how the wars that followed October 7 changed the Middle East, don’t miss Simon Sebag Montefiore ’s latest essay in our pages. It’s a deep dive into the war that upended everything, and which regional power is likely to come out on top.
As we at The Free Press have documented over the last three years, October 7 and its aftermath revealed disturbing truths about our own societies here in the West. An antisemitism lingering just beneath the surface, now paraded without embarrassment; a surprisingly widespread sympathy for movements and ideologies defined by their hatred of America.
Today, we offer two stories unpacking recent examples of these trends.
This weekend, the UK’s Green Party passed a motion entitled “Zionism is Racism,” which commits the party to a single Palestinian state and a world where Israel does not exist. The motion isn’t trivial, nor is it an instance of simple virtue signaling, argues former British prime minister Tony Blair —it’s an adoption of antisemitism as party policy. Read his essay on why the moral confusion of a once-marginal political party is something no one worried about the future of the UK, or the future of the Holy Land, can ignore.
In the wake of October 7, MIT engineering systems professor Yossi Sheffi published a book about antisemitism on campus following the attacks. But shortly after the book was published, MIT’s administration told Yossi to stop promoting it. Then they accused him of conducting an unauthorized experiment by interviewing Jewish students about their campus experiences. What happened exposed an institutional rot that made Yossi’s book all the more urgent, and is a revelation about higher education post–October 7 that still stings every year thereafter.
The Free Press has published many more stories about October 7 and its aftermath. If you want to revisit some of them today, start with the collection we put together on the first anniversary of the attacks:
VH Blackinton used Claude to turn institutional knowledge into a living record for the team.
Bari Weiss, this was on the CBS instagram this morning. You should be embarrassed…
https://www.instagram.com/p/DeMXMeggJKN/?stkn=MXg1NzZmajZhbm1vOQ==
Palestinian leadership has been rolling from one nakba decision to the next for 100 years. Each one has been rooted to the hatred and phobia of Jews.
Every attack on Israel, every denial by Mamdani of Israel’s right to exist, every AOC accusation of genocide, every scream for a global intifada or a free Palestine from the river to the sea, every swastika scrolled on a Jewish school in the United Kingdom, every attack on Jews by terrorists makes the case for Israel to not only exist but to dig in, spread out, build up and push back.
The antisemites now roaming and ruling in the halls of parliaments, kingdoms, senates, war rooms, and tunnels around the world are making a very strong case for Israel.

articles.title_orig: As measles rages, one clinic leans on years of hard-won trust to keep vulnerable people safe
articles.title_zh: As measles rages, one clinic leans on years of hard-won trust to keep vulnerable people safe
articles.content_orig:
Main Street is bustling on a Wednesday afternoon in late September. Cars mix with horse-and-buggy carriages on the road, many coming and going from the weekly Sale Day — a market spread over 10 acres with livestock, fruits and vegetables, flowers and other goods for available to purchase. Lively conversations in English and Pennsylvania Dutch fill the barn where a produce auction stretches until lunchtime; bids for a pint of bright red cherry tomatoes run from 90 cents to $1.30.
As dozens of people mix and mingle through the afternoon — Amish and other Plain people, so named for their simple way of dressing, as well as “English,” as they refer to folks outside of their community — there are no direct indications that a measles outbreak is raging in the area. Only one woman has a mask on, which she says she’s been wearing any time she’s left home since the start of the Covid-19 pandemic. One vendor is closed for “unexpected family obligations,” and one regular auction attendee is mourned after her recent sudden death after having “flu-like symptoms.” Tourists are visiting from Brooklyn.
But less than a mile away at the Central Pennsylvania Clinic, measles is front and center.
A turn off of Main Street quickly opens up to an idyllic rural valley, filled with lush farms set to a backdrop of rolling green mountains. An unlined road leads across a babbling river to reveal a striking gray building up on a hill, a massive barn raised in the traditional style that uses only wood pegs — no nails — to hold the structure together.
The front door is locked, with a photo and description of measles hanging in the window, along with a notice asking visitors to “ring doorbell for service.” Dr. Katherine Mascia swings the door open with a big smile and a quick question: “Any measles symptoms today?”
Beneath the genuine smile is true heartbreak. A massive measles outbreak in the area — now the deadliest and nearly the largest the United States has had in decades — is bringing significant pain and suffering to the families she cares for.
“In the five years that I’ve worked here, I don’t think we’ve had so many patients admitted to the hospital all within the span of a few weeks,” Mascia said. “We might usually have maybe one patient who’s admitted for their complex care needs, but to have so many all at the same time, it’s really unprecedented.”
About 1,000 measles cases have been reported by the Pennsylvania Department of Health since the outbreak started in April, nearly surpassing the record number recorded in South Carolina during an outbreak that started last year and that became the largest in the US since 1992. The clinic’s home of Mifflin County is one the hardest-hit, near the epicenter in neighboring Lancaster County.
The patients who the Central Pennsylvania Clinic serves are especially vulnerable to the severe effects of a measles infection. The nonprofit is centered around caring for children and adults with genetic disorders that are especially common among the Amish and broader Plain community, a group that also tends to have lower vaccination rates than average.
The Plain people are known for their ​caution toward government and other nonreligious authority.
But as measles tears through many of their hometowns in central Pennsylvania, the national conversation has become paradoxically politically charged.
Leaders from the federal government and the Pennsylvania government have clashed over the response , with much of the debate centered around the five deaths that have come during this outbreak. Disputes over the definition of what counts as a measles death and how news of the deaths is shared with the public have disrupted public health response plans.
Meanwhile, the Central Pennsylvania Clinic’s staff is focused on how to best keep everyone safe and healthy. They’re leaning on the clinic’s well-forged foundation of trust. It has taken persistence and patience — sometimes years — for the clinic to build those relationships, and the strength of that trust has faced some of its greatest tests over the past few months.
When Pennsylvania reported a measles-associated death in an 18-year-old in Mifflin County, Mascia said, the clinic started to get tons of calls — from patients they knew and other members of the broader community — who just wanted to know what happened. They weren’t paying attention to what government officials were arguing about on social media, she said. They wanted a clear understanding of how the young person died.
“I’m quite honored that they’re calling us and asking those questions. It helps me feel like they really trust us,” Mascia said. “But it puts pressure on us, too.”
She said she reached out to the county coroner directly to get a formal statement on the cause of death, and she references that statement when patients have questions.
“We want to keep that line of communication open with the community, and it’s so important to provide accurate information and be consistent with the messaging,” she said.
Central Pennsylvania Clinic leaders have been thinking about and planning for a measles outbreak in the community since the start of the West Texas outbreak in January 2025, Mascia said. Their patients are vulnerable, and their offices, while incredibly well-equipped in many ways, are not built to treat measles patients.
“We don’t have advanced ventilation systems, and we don’t have negative-pressure rooms, so if a person who is infected with measles comes in, our entire building is compromised for two hours,” Mascia said.
Pennsylvania requires a throat swab, a blood sample and a urine sample to confirm a measles case — arduous tasks for both ill patients, who often had to take a taxing horse and buggy ride to the clinic, and for clinic staff who have to work within the constraints of their facility.
The rear entrance to the clinic building, which also hosts a federally qualified health center, has become a makeshift triage center for people with suspected measles cases. The back parking lot is large enough for cars and buggies to spread out, and clinic staffers meet families at the door, where they can lead the patient into a small storage barn to collect urine samples.
It was important to have a logistical plan to keep operations safe, Mascia said, but she pointedly explains that the most critical way to protect their patients is to raise vaccination rates.
The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is extremely effective. One dose is 93% effective against measles, and the recommended second dose bumps that protection up to 97% — and the immunity is lifelong. Extensive research has also demonstrated the vaccine’s safety .
Childhood vaccination rates have been falling nationwide, with a record share of parents opting to exempt their new kindergartners from the required shots last school year.
Vaccination rates tend to be lower among Plain people, but it’s not because of an inherent opposition, experts say.
There are certain shared values within the community, but there are also varied individual beliefs and opinions about vaccines, as there would in any broad group of people, Mascia said. Consistency in the clinic’s messaging around vaccination has been the key to raising coverage rates.
If the patients sense any type of coercion from doctors or if they feel forced into a decision about something like a vaccination, they’ll completely disengage from all health care – an outcome that would be particularly troublesome for the vulnerable patients they care for.
“We share that it’s our strong recommendation that everyone be fully vaccinated,” Mascia said. “And if they’re not interested, we repeat our recommendation and say ‘we’re here to help if and when you change your mind.’”
In the Amish and broader Plain community, the experience of a neighbor and advice from a family member carry significantly more weight than findings from a study published in the most prestigious medical journal or recommendations from the leading clinical soci

articles.title_orig: Investors pick new darlings and duds as selloff rocks Europe's bond market
articles.title_zh: Investors pick new darlings and duds as selloff rocks Europe's bond market
articles.content_orig:
France's student protests took a breather on Wednesday after weeks of unrest, but market pressure on the French government intensified ahead of crucial budget negotiations due to start next week.
The student rallies, now stretching into their third week after violent clashes with police, mass school closures and thousands of arrests, are expected to resume on Thursday. What began as a Parisian student protest pressuring the government to address teacher shortages, lengthy timetables and derelict schools has evolved into a nationwide movement that has garnered support from people of various ages.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said Wednesday morning that officials would use the pause in demonstrations to open dialogue with high school students. He is due to address the nation on Wednesday evening.
"The demands [of students] are numerous and vary from one high school to the next. They must be assessed objectively, school by school," he said in a post on X on Tuesday. "Substitutes, the state of the buildings, guidance, organization of school time, high school democracy: all topics must be put on the table."
But he added that conversations must be had "without giving in to politicized manipulations."
Lecornu's government has accused radical-left party La France Insoumise (LFI) of hijacking the student movement. Some of the party's sitting politicians have publicly backed the student protests.
LFI did not respond to CNBC's request for comment.
The unrest in France has highlighted and intensified the economic and political challenges facing the country.
In the coming weeks, the French government faces tough budget negotiations, during which it must convince lawmakers in the politically divided National Assembly — which includes the far-right National Rally , the left-wing New Popular Front and Lecornu's center-right grouping — to agree to a fiscal adjustment worth tens of billions of euros.
Since France's July 2024 snap election delivered no parliamentary majority, budget disputes have sparked political discord, with two administrations being ousted in no-confidence votes. It took incumbent leader Lecornu until February this year to pass the 2026 budget, which he only achieved by drawing on emergency legislation that allowed him to bypass parliament and force the policy through.
Further political shifts are expected after the presidential election next spring, with far-right candidate Marine Le Pen currently the frontrunner. In a speech on Tuesday, Le Pen pledged to reduce France's deficit to 3% within 18 months of the election should she win – but critics questioned whether her plans were feasible. The French budget deficit topped 5.1% of GDP last year.
The political instability, deficit concerns, and doubts over the minority government's capacity to deliver the necessary scale of spending cuts have also rattled investors trading French government debt. Yields on French government bonds, known as OATs, have surged to multi-decade highs this year, sparking concerns the country could be headed toward a sovereign debt crisis.
Bond yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Bank of France Governor Emmanuel Moulin, who sits on the European Central Bank's Governing Council, threw cold water on the notion that France might soon need assistance from European Central Bank policymakers in Frankfurt.
The ECB does not exist to "deal with the fiscal problems" of individual countries, he told radio station France Inter.
"It's there to fight inflation and keep inflation around 2%," he said. "So the conditions are not met today for an intervention from the ECB."
The yield on France's benchmark 10-year OAT gained 16 basis points on Wednesday, rising sharply after a decline the previous day. The 10-year OAT's yield has surged by more than 100 basis points since the start of the year.
Emmanuel Roman, CEO of asset management giant Pimco, told French newspaper Le Monde that "the situation is critical" in France's bond market, which he said was "sending a serious signal" to the government.
"The deficit needs to be reduced – a budget is needed, and that budget needs to be passed," he said in an interview published Wednesday. "France needs a credible political policy, which it currently lacks."
Roman added that the country "needs reforms like the ones Italy had to implement when its back was against the wall."
"There's an urgent need to take serious measures," he said.
Anthony Brinkman, a high-yield portfolio manager at Principal Asset Management, told CNBC in an email Wednesday that French debt markets could still come under more pressure.
"We remain cautious on French credit: the OAT sell-off does not look exhausted, and we do not believe the curve has found its clearing price," he said.
"This looks like a repricing of deteriorating fundamentals, rather than a disorderly market move. A worsening deficit and debt-to-GDP outlook have driven incremental widening as negative news lands. With upcoming reviews from both Moody's and S&P in Q4, rating downgrades could amplify selling pressure."

articles.title_orig: China vs. Crypto Isn’t Over Yet: Solana CEO Says Beijing Is Studying the Technology ‘Very Closely’ — 'The
articles.title_zh: China vs. Crypto Isn’t Over Yet: Solana CEO Says Beijing Is Studying the Technology ‘Very Closely’ — 'The
articles.content_orig:
Joseph Chee , CEO and Chairman of Solana Company (NASDAQ: HSDT ), said on Tuesday that China is “very closely” monitoring cryptocurrency and blockchains, while continuing to have reservations about how the technology is used.
During an interview with CNBC, Chee said that there are Chinese think tanks, academics and other groups who are familiar with the technology.
Chee, formerly head of UBS Asia investment banking and with extensive experience in China, said officials are still “very worried” about ordinary people getting exploited by the new technology.
“But they know that’s not the technology they can ignore,” he added.
Chee said China is using Hong Kong as a testing ground for how cryptocurrency-related systems might be implemented and managed.
Notably, Hong Kong is a growing hub for digital asset innovation, wealth and talent, ranking as one of the world’s most cryptocurrency-friendly cities
Chee said China should prioritise education first, so that those responsible for managing cryptocurrency fully “understand how to manage” the technology before any wider rollout.
He said that China could continue restricting cryptocurrency trading and stablecoin issuance on the mainland, while allowing blockchain tools to support business and government operations.
Bitcoin may reach $132,750 by 2027 and $275,000 by 2029; well-run BTC treasury firms could outperform Bitcoin by ~50%.
Beijing issued multiple restrictions between 2013 and 2021 that ultimately banned all cryptocurrency transactions and mining. China’s central bank formally declared all digital-asset trading illegal in September 2021, and providing such services to Chinese citizens from abroad is also prohibited.
The central bank reaffirmed the enforcement last year, voicing specific worries about dollar-pegged stablecoins. Instead. Instead, China has focused on advancing its central bank digital currency , the Digital Yuan.
Interestingly, President Donald Trump has consistently used China as a justification for advancing pro-cryptocurrency policies in the U.S.

articles.title_orig: Greetings abound as Bossey turns 80
articles.title_zh: Greetings abound as Bossey turns 80
articles.content_orig:
Global religious leaders shared greetings during the celebration of the 80th anniversary of the Ecumenical Institute at Bossey on 7 October.
His All-Holiness Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew video message being presented during the commemorations of the 80th anniversary of Bossey.
His All-Holiness Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew, in a video message, expressed affection for the institute, recalling his own studies there.
“Since October 1946, the Chateau de Bossey has welcomed students from every Christian  tradition and from every corner of the world,” he said. “ It is fitting therefore that this anniversary should be marked by the gathering of Bossey ’ s alumnae and alumni, for they are the truest measure of what these 80 years have accomplished.”
Cardinal Kurt Koch, prefect of the Dicastery for Promoting Christian Unity, in a written greeting, noted that the history of Bossey is closely interwoven with the deepening relationship between the Catholic Church and the World Council of Churches. “ The establishment of the Joint Working Group in 1965, the first meeting of which was held at Bossey in May 1965, opened a new and enduring chapter of dialogue and practical cooperation, ” he wrote. “ Bossey soon became one of its particularly fruitful expressions.”
H.E. Metropolitan Anthony, chairman of the Department for External Church Relations of the Moscow Patriarchate, in a written greeting, reflected that a number of Russian Orthodox Church representatives have gained invaluable experience of inter-Christian dialogue at Bossey.
“ I would also like to mention high academic standards maintained by the Ecumenical Institute at Bossey, which implements its educational programs in collaboration with the University of Geneva,” he wrote. “ On this memorable occasion, I wish you God's help and blessed success in your further ministry.”
Most Rev. Dr Olav Fykse Tveit, presiding bishop of the Church of Norway, expressed deep thanks for all that Bossey represents and continues to offer as a place of study and reflection, a space where people from different traditions and backgrounds come together in dialogue, and a living symbol of the ecumenical movement.
“ Over the years, Bossey has been much more than an academic institution,” said Tveit. “ It has been a place of encounter, friendship, learning, and transformation—a place where differences can be explored with openness and respect, and where the shared calling to build greater understanding and unity can take root.”

articles.title_orig: California pair charged with abusing at least 14 surrogate-born children
articles.title_zh: California pair charged with abusing at least 14 surrogate-born children
articles.content_orig:
A California pair has been charged with multiple counts of abusing at least 14 surrogate-born children - some as young as two months old - and dissuading a witness.
"The number of children who were subjected to this alleged horrific abuse is unprecedented," Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan J Hochman said in a statement.
Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang, who US media describe as a couple, were arrested at their Arcadia mansion on Tuesday.
The pair pleaded not guilty at a Pasadena courthouse, the BBC's US partner CBS News reported.
Xuan, 66, and Zhang, 39, are accused of conspiring to subject 15 of the 16 children living in their home to repeated physical abuse, after 21 children were removed from their custody last year.
The pair ran their own surrogacy company and are accused of making false statements to at least two women who became surrogates, indicating that Zhang was struggling to conceive, according to the criminal complaint.
As of May 2025, Zhang maintained a spreadsheet that tracked 21 children, including those born to surrogates.
Officials said the investigation began that month when Zhang brought a two-month-old boy to the hospital with a head injury, telling medical staff that the baby had fallen from a bed.
The couple's lawyer Mitchell Krems said the allegation was a "mischaracterisation" based on the evidence he has reviewed, CBS News in Los Angeles reported.
Hospital staff informed law enforcement, and when police arrived at their home they discovered three different rooms called "learning centres" under the supervision of multiple nannies, which Hochman described as a "house of horrors".
The mansion allegedly had 32 motion-activated cameras which Hochman said were used by the couple to monitor the discipline given by the nannies.
Footage allegedly shows the nannies spanking, slapping or hitting the children.
One nanny, Chunmei Li, is accused of hitting the two-month-old baby who suffered the head injury two days before he was brought to the hospital.
Krems said Li was quickly fired, CBS News LA reported.
Li, 58, was previously charged with one felony count of child abuse under conditions likely to cause great bodily injury or death. Hochman said she was on the run with a $105,000 (£88,800) warrant for her arrest.
In July 2025, the couple's home was first raided by authorities, who took 21 children into state custody.
Arcadia Police Department said at the time the couple's house was first raided that the children ranged in age from two months to 13 years old, but most were between one and three years old.
Fifteen of the children were taken from the couple's home while six others were living elsewhere and also later taken into custody.
Krems said his client Xuan was innocent.
"He is being targeted for exercising his constitutional right to have a large family," CBS News quoted the lawyer as saying.
Investigators believe the surrogate mothers were from around the country and they were unaware they were carrying embryos for the couple at the same time.
Melissa Brisman, the attorney for two of the surrogates, told CBS News: "This is wonderful news that people will be held responsible for their actions and there will be consequences if you abuse the surrogacy system".
If convicted as charged, Xuan faces a possible maximum sentence of 17 years and four months in state prison, while Zhang faces up to 11 years and eight months. Li faces up to 12 years.

articles.title_orig: World Day for Decent Work: “Journalists should recognise themselves as workers and fight for our col... - International Federation of Journalists
articles.title_zh: World Day for Decent Work: “Journalists should recognise themselves as workers and fight for our col... - International Federation of Journalists
articles.content_orig:
To mark World Day for Decent Work (WDDW) on 7 October, the International Federation of journalists (IFJ) and its affiliates around the world call on journalists and media workers to recognise their right to decent work, which is a fundamental human right, and to organise and join their union in order to secure dignity at work. “Behind every contract and job title, there is a worker who should enjoy their rights. It is essential that we, as journalists, recognise ourselves as workers, and fight for our collective struggles. Organising together, joining unions and standing for our rights at work are the only ways to defend our profession,” said IFJ President Zuliana Lainez.
According to the International Labour Organization (ILO), decent work means dignity, equality, fair remuneration and safe working conditions. However, all too often these conditions are not met in the media sector. Journalists and media workers often sacrifice their right to decent working conditions in the name of their vocation as a journalist, i.e. to serve democracy and uphold the public's right to information.
Journalists around the world are underpaid and work long hours in precarious working conditions. Often, they do not even have a contract. A recent survey by the Federation of African Journalists (FAJ) , the IFJ’s pan-African group, showed that the working conditions of African journalists have deteriorated dramatically in the last few years. An alarming 61% of respondents reported that their income from journalism does not meet their basic living needs, while only 4% indicated that their salaries adequately cover essential costs.
A survey conducted recently by E tū members in New Zealand found that 60% of respondents did not see themselves still working as journalists in ten years' time. In Brazil, the Federação Nacional dos Jornalistas (FENAJ) published a new study revealing that 50% of journalists and media workers surveyed had experienced symptoms of depression, insomnia and stress associated with workplace violence.
Across the world, unions are demanding decent work in the media sector and the right for journalists to get organised. In Namibia, the IFJ reported employers for threatening media workers from two media outlets, Free Press of Namibia and Namibia Media Trust, with disciplinary action over sick leave. The IFJ also reported these media outlets for monitoring media workers during working hours. In Hong Kong, the BBC bureau dismissed five journalists, following years of pressure over their participation in the Hong Kong Journalists Association (HKJA) . In the United States, media workers employed by Le Monde in Los Angeles staged a one-day protest against unfair management practices in negotiations over their collective agreement.
Recent actions show that unions have played a crucial role in supporting all media workers, strengthening their collective organisation and defending their right to decent and fair working conditions.
In the United States, the Supreme Court ruled in October that the former owners of the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette must pay millions of dollars in compensation to members of the Newspaper Guild of Pittsburgh for implementing pay cuts and other unilateral changes to their working conditions. Pittsburgh Post-Gazette workers, who belong to the News Guild , an affiliate of the IFJ, went on strike for three years due to unfair practices.
In Germany, the country’s public service broadcaster, Deutsche Welle, reversed its decision to abolish the Greek-language service in September, following joint action by the German Journalists’ Union (dju) in ver.di and the Union of Journalists of Athens Daily Newspapers (JUADN) in Greece, among other actors. It will avoid job losses and reinforce the essential role of public service media in informing the public.
In Costa Rica, the Costa Rican Union of Journalists and Communicators (SINAPEC) secured a seat on the National Salaries Council for the workers' sector, alongside other colleagues from the country’s trade union confederation in August. Defending the workers’ interests lies at the heart of union activity.
In Türkiye, journalists and media workers at the AFP bureau in Istanbul ended their 12-day strike in July by securing a 27% wage increase. This followed industrial action led by the Türkiye Gazeteciler Sendikası (TGS) and fully backed by the IFJ.
On World Day for Decent Work, the IFJ and its affiliates are calling on media organisations and governments worldwide to guarantee the rights that every media worker is entitled to, including:
IFJ President Zuliana Lainez said: “Journalists are workers, and decent work is a fundamental right, not a privilege. Unions are essential to defending fair pay, secure employment and dignified working conditions across the media sector, while protecting workers from pressure, harassment and abuse. On World Day for Decent Work, we reaffirm that a strong and organised media workforce is vital to ensuring that journalists can do their jobs with security, independence and dignity."
For more information, please contact IFJ on +32 2 235 22 16
The IFJ represents more than 600,000 journalists in 146 countries
Follow the IFJ on Twitter , Facebook and Instagram

articles.title_orig: STORM-PE subset analysis demonstrates correlation between clinical assessments and real-world functional recovery
articles.title_zh: STORM-PE subset analysis demonstrates correlation between clinical assessments and real-world functional recovery
articles.content_orig:
Penumbra has announced results from a subset analysis of the STORM-PE randomised controlled trial (RCT), which, according to the company, is the first trial to demonstrate a significant correlation between real-world, daily step-based activity as captured on a consumer wearable device and patient performance in the clinical six-minute-walk test. The findings were presented at this week’s at Vascular InterVentional Advances (VIVA; 4–7 October, Las Vegas, USA).
STORM-PE RCT assessed patients with acute intermediate-high risk pulmonary embolism (PE) who were treated with computer assisted vacuum thrombectomy (CAVT) plus anticoagulation compared to anticoagulation alone. Data from the trial showed patients treated with CAVT plus anticoagulation experienced improved right ventricular recovery and achieved greater functional improvement, including walking significantly further and a higher proportion of patients achieving New York Heart Association (NYHA) Class I (no physical limitations) i compared to anticoagulation alone.
A cohort of the trial patients were discharged with a fitness watch to track a patient’s activity, including actigraphy measures during everyday living. STORM-PE investigators performed a correlation analysis between watch actigraphy (daily total step count, walking bout data, and daily peak steps) and made comparisons to the six-minute-walk test performed at 30- and 90-day follow-up visits.
“STORM-PE is the first RCT in PE therapy to incorporate data from a consumer wearable device, representing an important step forward in understanding how office assessed clinical improvements translate into meaningful real-world recovery,” said Robert Lookstein, global co principal investigator of the STORM PE RCT and professor of radiology and surgery at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York, USA. “This innovation enables the scientific community to determine whether improvements observed during office assessments are reflected in patients’ real-world experiences at home.”
Key findings from the study analysed total daily step count, walking bout length, number of walking bouts, walking bout duration and peak 10-minute step count, which each were significantly correlated with 30-day six-minute walk test performance. Correlations were strongest with temporally matched wearable and clinic data at 30 days and attenuated with 90-day follow up data.
“This STORM-PE subset gives us a more complete picture of patient recovery by allowing us to compare data collected in the clinic with information gathered as patients go about their daily lives,” said Rachel Rosovsky, global co-principal investigator of the STORM PE RCT, haematologist at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, USA and associate professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School.
“By generating a more comprehensive view of patient outcomes, these findings have the potential not only to advance our understanding of the role of endovascular therapy in PE, but also to help shape the design of future clinical trials.”
Alongside the STORM-PE findings, investigators presented a new interim analysis of 1,000 prospective patients from the STRIKE-PE trial, looking at one-year functional outcomes and quality of life for PE patients after CAVT during this year’s Venous Endovascular Interventional Strategies (The VEINS) annual meeting (3–4 October, Las Vegas, USA). According to the company, STRIKE-PE continues to support the safety and effectiveness of CAVT, including short device times and low adverse events, for treating PE.
The study also found longer-term functional outcomes and quality-of-life benefits, including sustained reduced dyspnoea, increased walking distance, restored functional status and improved quality of life. STRIKE-PE is a prospective, international, multicentre study evaluating real-world safety, performance and long-term functional and quality-of-life outcomes of CAVT in up to 1,500 patients.
“At Penumbra, we are committed to advancing innovations that are supported by rigorous clinical evidence,” said James F. Benenati, chief medical officer at Penumbra. “By incorporating consumer wearables into STORM-PE, we have a unique opportunity to evaluate whether the clinical improvements observed in traditional assessments are reflected in patients’ day-to-day recovery at home. Together with emerging data from STRIKE-PE, these findings contribute to a growing body of evidence supporting a significant role for CAVT in the treatment of PE.”

articles.title_orig: NASA rover takes striking image of dawn's early light on Mars
articles.title_zh: NASA rover takes striking image of dawn's early light on Mars
articles.content_orig:
The captivating shapes of wind-carved crags called yardangs are revealed in this zoomed-in crop of a broader panorama captured by NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover on Aug. 11, 2026. Scientists are eager to learn more about how the yardang layer formed.
Sunlight illuminates wind-carved cliffs in a dramatic new image.
A newly released panorama captured by NASA’s Curiosity rover offers the most detailed view yet of distant, wind-carved Martian cliffs, highlighting features the mission’s scientists have long been waiting to see up close. The scene was snapped at 8:30 a.m. local Mars time, showing striking blue hues in the foreground as bright morning light illuminates crags known as yardangs on the horizon.
The panorama was captured by Curiosity’s Mastcam on Aug. 11, the 4,982nd Martian day, or sol, of the mission, and comprises six individual images that were stitched together after being sent to Earth. Unlike most of Curiosity’s Mastcam images, this one was processed without white balancing, preserving the early morning appearance.
The six shots that make up this panorama, captured by NASA’s Curiosity on Aug. 11, were stitched together after being sent back to Earth. Unlike most images from the rover’s Mastcam, this one was processed without the usual white balancing — an artistic choice that preserves the early morning appearance.
The yardang layer extends roughly 10 miles (16 kilometers) across the northwestern reaches of Mount Sharp, a 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that Curiosity has been ascending since 2014. In fact, the rover recently passed another milestone in its ascent, reaching 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) of elevation — the most ever climbed on Mars. As it draws ever-closer to the yardangs, mission scientists expect to get even more amazing imagery — and, they hope, answers to how these cliffs were created.
Mount Sharp is made up of layers, each recording a distinct period of Mars’ history. By studying them, scientists have been able to learn more about lakes and streams that covered this part of the Red Planet billions of years ago. Eventually, the water dried up and left salty minerals behind. After new material stopped settling on the mountain, some of it may have been stripped away by wind, giving rise to the yardangs.
This artist’s concept shows Mount Sharp, the 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that NASA’s Curiosity has been ascending since 2014. The location of the yardang layer, which the rover recently captured from a distance, is indicated by an ellipse annotation on the mountain’s northwestern shoulder.
NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover captured this view looking back at the floor of Gale Crater on Sept. 5, 2026. Just nine days prior, the rover had marked 1 kilometer of elevation gain above the crater floor since beginning its ascent of Mount Sharp in 2014.
“The yardang layer looks out of place. It’s the wrong color, the layers tilt at an odd angle, and it almost appears plastered on,” said Ashwin Vasavada, Curiosity project scientist of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “But that’s what makes it exciting to reach. No one is sure exactly what created this layer, but one idea is it may be ash deposited by ancient volcanic eruptions.”
Curiosity is in the second year of its fifth extended mission, which started with an exploration of the spiderweb-like boxwork ridges . The rover will spend most of the next year or so driving through layers enriched with sulfates and carbonates, both signs of ancient drying on the surface. Sometime in 2027, scientists hope to reach the base of the yardangs, where Curiosity will be able to use its robotic arm to collect one-of-a-kind data on these mysterious features.
From Mars to the Milky Way — never miss a discovery! Delivered straight to your inbox.
Curiosity was built by NASA JPL, which is managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California. NASA JPL leads the mission on behalf of the agency’s Science Mission Directorate in Washington as part of its Mars Exploration Program portfolio. Malin Space Science Systems in San Diego built and operates Mastcam.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine Claws Back Land in the Donbas, Thwarting a Russian Push
articles.title_zh: Ukraine Claws Back Land in the Donbas, Thwarting a Russian Push
articles.content_orig:
In January of this year, the "NC13" strike UGV unit of the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade tested a new tactic deep behind Russian lines. Since then, the unit has successfully carried out more than 100 similar operations, turning what began as an experiment into a proven combat system.
The new tactic was named "Gryphon" in honor of a service member from the unit who went missing in action in 2023 while carrying out a combat mission near Andriivka in the Donetsk region. It was in this area, near Bakhmut, that Oscar-winning Ukrainian director Mstyslav Chernov filmed the documentary "2000 Meters to Andriivka" during a different Ukrainian counteroffensive.
The concept behind the new tactic involves deploying kamikaze UGVs, essentially ground robots, deep behind enemy lines using heavy bomber drones. After landing, the robotic systems continue moving toward their targets and can be used to strike key positions, logistics, and personnel while also creating disruption in the enemy rear.
The "NC13" unit was also behind an operation that drew significant international attention about a year ago, when Ukrainian forces captured Russian positions without deploying infantry, using only UGVs and drones.
As a result, two Russian service members surrendered to the robotic systems, after which the machines escorted them to Ukrainian positions as prisoners of war.
Today, the new tactic is part of the Third Army Corps' large-scale operation known as "Vivaldi." Since the start of the offensive, Ukrainian forces have liberated 176 square kilometers of territory (68 square miles ) .
According to the Office of the President of Ukraine, Russian forces suffered more than 5,000 casualties, including those killed, wounded, and captured, during the first three stages of the operation. It is currently known that Ukrainian forces have taken 250 Russian service members as prisoners of war (POWs). The Third Army Corps separately reported 2,000 Russian personnel casualties during the latest stage alone.
Approximately 80% of logistics and 90% of wounded evacuation for Ukrainian troops during all three stages of the operation were carried out by unmanned ground vehicles, or UGVs.
"NC13" commander Mykola Zinkevych, call sign "Makar," explains how the new "Gryphon" tactic works, how the idea of air-dropping ground robots emerged, what happened during the first operations, how Russian forces are reacting to the technology, and why he believes Ukraine is shaping the future of technological warfare.
He also discusses how Western partners are becoming less able to understand Ukrainian military technologies and, more broadly, the needs of modern warfare.
Can you please explain, in general, what this new tactic involves?
In general, this is a sabotage-operation tactic that was fully planned, developed, and implemented by the "NC13" strike unmanned ground systems unit of the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade.
The tactic is genuinely new and has no equivalent anywhere in the world because no one had previously deployed unmanned ground vehicles from unmanned aerial vehicles.
The concept itself is that, using heavy bombers, we drop small ground-based kamikaze systems deep into enemy territory, at a distance of 5 to 15 kilometers (3 to 9.3 miles ) . From there, we carry out different sabotage operations: eliminating enemy personnel, destroying logistics, and so on.
When did you begin using this tactic? Any first operation is essentially a test. How confident were you that it would work?
We carried out the first operation about eight months ago (in January 2026- UP).
We spent quite a long time developing the tactic itself and modifying the equipment because standard ground-based kamikaze systems are not designed for this kind of use.
The engineers spent a great deal of time making it work. The pilots also had to learn how to operate with these systems and deploy them correctly. The planning department, accordingly, spent a lot of time preparing the operation.
But when it worked for the first time, the excitement was incredible. Our first operation went 15 kilometers (9.3 miles ) deep behind enemy lines. We deployed two ground-based kamikaze systems near the target, and from there, the systems themselves moved into the shelter.
It was an enemy staging point where personnel were brought in. They would stop there to rest before moving on to carry out their missions. We eliminated that staging point using two ground-based kamikaze systems.
What was the enemy's reaction? What did it look like from their side?
In fact, the enemy did not understand what had happened, what system had been used, what had struck them, or what tactic we were employing.
Even now, it remains a major surprise for them because we operate in different sectors within the Third Army Corps' area of responsibility.
We combine different technologies in order to change the rules on the battlefield.
We have been able to strike the enemy from the air at significant depth for quite some time. We have also been using unmanned ground vehicles to strike enemy forces for a while.
But this combination (UGV + UAV) allows us to operate at greater depth, in areas where the enemy does not expect to be reached and where they feel relatively safe. So we are going to take that freedom away from them.
How many such operations have been carried out so far?
More than one hundred. We always work systematically. If something works once, twice, or three times, we still do not consider it a fully established capability because it could be accidental.
But when something is carried out more than ten times, it becomes a systematic approach. We have SOPs, standard operating procedures, in place for this tactic: how to use it, where it can be implemented, and what its capabilities are.
It can be used for reconnaissance, mining deep behind enemy lines, striking targets, hunting moving enemy personnel, disrupting logistics, and more. We have fully developed this tactic, identified all of its capabilities, and now use it as a full-fledged tool on the battlefield.
War in general, and especially Russia's war against Ukraine, is a war of speed. Everything depends on who can come up with something new and adapt faster. Are the Russians already trying to do something similar?
I am confident that we are far ahead of the enemy. Even when it comes to the systematic use of strike unmanned ground vehicles on the battlefield, which we have been doing for about a year, the enemy is still far behind.
So when it comes to tactics like "Gryphon," which we are discussing today, there is still a very large gap between us and them.
But I would not rule out the possibility that, over time, the enemy will begin copying this approach and using similar methods.
In fact, during more than 100 successful missions, there have been many almost meme-like moments when the enemy had no idea what they were looking at and would actually approach the robots to inspect them.
There was one occasion when we managed to completely disrupt a Russian mechanized assault that had been planned for foggy weather conditions. At the time, we were actively targeting one of the enemy's logistics routes. We eliminated several personnel over the course of the day.
They started to panic because they did not understand what was happening. They thought a sabotage and reconnaissance group, or SRG, had broken through into their rear. As a result, they canceled the mechanized assault they had planned for that day.
So these small robots can create very significant disruption.
In general, there was serious panic among enemy forces at the depth where we were operating. And panic is actually very important because if we create panic within enemy ranks, they begin to have problems controlling their personnel. Soldiers start refusing to carry out missions, which then creates panic at the command level because commanders do not understand what is happening in their rear, and so on.
That creates destabilization, and all of that works i

articles.title_orig: 3 years on, Israelis grapple with reports Netanyahu was warned before Oct. 7 attacks
articles.title_zh: 3 years on, Israelis grapple with reports Netanyahu was warned before Oct. 7 attacks
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu lays a wreath during a state memorial ceremony in memory of those killed in the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel, at Mount Herzl cemetery in Jerusalem on Oct. 5. Debbie Hill/Pool UPI via AP hide caption
TEL AVIV, Israel — As Israel marks three years since Hamas launched its surprise Oct. 7 attacks, Israelis are reeling from new revelations in Israeli and U.S. media that the country had been repeatedly warned by its regional allies that Hamas was planning to attack.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was personally warned about a potential Hamas attack, and his security agencies were notified repeatedly, in the weeks and days leading up to Oct. 7, 2023, four people in the Middle East with direct knowledge of the warnings told NPR.
The Israeli newspaper Haaretz , The New York Times and The Atlantic first reported about the warnings.
Netanyahu has denied he was warned, calling the reports "fake news" and filing a defamation lawsuit last week against Israeli news outlets that published them. He and his defense minister have issued new warnings that Hamas could try to attack or "challenge" Israel on this Oct. 7 memorial day and leading up to national elections later this month.
But the Oct. 7, 2023, security failure — as well as Netanyahu's repeated refusal to take responsibility for it — has become a lightning rod in Israel as the prime minister seeks a new term in national elections this month.
"You didn't protect my son," yelled out one bereaved Israeli father whose son was killed in the Hamas-led attack, as the prime minister spoke at a memorial ceremony this week for the victims.
One warning came directly from the leader of Hamas in Gaza weeks before Oct. 7, a Palestinian mediator told NPR and other media outlets.
Former Palestinian Authority official Sufian Abu Zaida said he helped mediate secret Hamas-Israel talks for more than a year leading up to Oct. 7. He said Hamas wanted Israel to release Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and offered in exchange to release two living Israeli hostages and the bodies of two Israeli soldiers held in Gaza for years. But he said Israel was unwilling to release as many prisoners as Hamas had demanded.
On Sept. 14, 2023, Abu Zaida said, Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar dictated a message for him to deliver to Israel: "By the end of September, we will put cards on the table. There will be an earthquake in the negotiations, and the Israelis should prepare to empty their prisons."
He did not know what kind of earthquake Sinwar meant, but he said he sent the message to an Israeli intelligence official who acknowledged receiving it and to Mohammed Dahlan, a Palestinian confidant of the leader of the United Arab Emirates.
"What happened [on] the 7th of October is needless," Abu Zaida told NPR.
Days before the Oct. 7 attacks, the leader of the United Arab Emirates, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, called Netanyahu and told him that Hamas' leader in Gaza was planning a big assault against Israel, according to a person close to Dahlan. Dahlan was the Palestinian Authority's head of security in Gaza before Hamas seized control of the territory in 2007.
The Emirati leader told Netanyahu in a phone call that lasted more than 40 minutes that a "quake" would hit the region if no progress was achieved regarding a prisoner deal between Hamas and Israel, the person said.
The person spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity because of the diplomatic sensitivity of the call. The phone call was previously reported by Haaretz and The New York Times .
The UAE did not deny the report, saying only that it maintained dialogue with Israel.
People visit a memorial at a police station attacked by Hamas on Oct. 7, 2023, three years prior, in Sderot, southern Israel, on Oct. 4. Oded Balilty/AP hide caption
A senior Egyptian official told NPR that Egypt had specific intelligence about Hamas movements and that Egypt's head of intelligence at the time, Abbas Kamel, had traveled to Israel with two other senior officials and met with Israel's Mossad and Shin Bet intelligence chiefs.
The official said Kamel relayed a warning that Gaza was on the verge of an "explosion" because of Israel's blockade, the condition of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and concerns that Israel might move to annex the occupied West Bank.
The official was not authorized to speak publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity. The Atlantic reported that Kamel's visit to Israel was on Sept 26.
Nimrod Novik, a fellow at the Israel Policy Forum think tank and a former top adviser to late Israeli Prime Minister Shimon Peres, told NPR that he was informed before Oct. 7 by a person with firsthand knowledge that Egypt had delivered warnings to several senior Israeli officials that "Gaza is about to explode in your face."
Novik said one warning was an "urgent and dramatic message" from Egypt, delivered to a person close to Netanyahu some 10 days prior to Oct. 7.
"I'm certain that the issue of the early warnings on October 7 is going to continue to play with heightened emotions as we approach Election Day," said Novik. "This is going to be an indictment for history, not just for the elections."
Netanyahu has blamed Israeli security organizations for failing to stop the Oct. 7 attacks. He and his government have yet to establish a state commission of inquiry to investigate the failures around Oct. 7, despite public demand.
The new reports about warnings issued to Israel "actually turn the story on its head," pointing the finger right back at the prime minister, said Gayil Talshir, a political scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
"It violates the basic narrative that Netanyahu tries to tell Israelis," said Talshir.
NPR's Aya Batrawy contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: An early flu season means it might be time to think about a flu shot
articles.title_zh: An early flu season means it might be time to think about a flu shot
articles.content_orig:
An early start to the flu season means it might be time to consider a flu shot. Rebecca Blackwell/AP hide caption
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Fall has only just begun, but it's already time to start thinking about the quintessential winter bug: the flu .
The annual flu season usually starts in October or November. But this year, it looks like the flu started to pick up in early September.
"There are enough signs pointing in the same direction to make me think, 'OK, yes. This is the start of flu season,'" says Caitlin Rivers , an epidemiologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
The percentage of people testing positive for the flu in the West has been rising steadily since around the beginning of September, she says. And the number of people showing up in emergency departments because of the flu has also been rising for weeks, she adds.
"It's very uncommon to see flu activity rising this early. It's activity that we might normally see more like November or December," she says.
The timing of the flu season isn't the only thing that's odd. It's also unusual that flu activity seems to have started in Western states, such as California, Washington, Hawaii and Alaska.
"It typically starts in the South and then expands from there," Rivers says. "So two uncommon developments there."
Rivers stresses that the amount of flu activity is still very low in most parts of the country. But that's starting to change as the flu picks up nationwide.
It's unclear why flu activity would have started so early, and in such an unusual part of the country. But one clue might be a new variant that evolved a mutation, which appears to make it better at evading existing immunity, especially among teenagers.
"That's our best argument for what's going on right now in terms of this early flu season," says Dr. Alex Greninger , a virologist who heads infectious disease diagnostics at the University of Washington. Doctors there are seeing as much flu right now as they usually would around Christmas, and the mutated variant appears to be common, he says.
So Greninger, Rivers and others are urging people to think about getting their flu shot earlier than usual.
"It's crucial that people get an influenza vaccine," says Scott Hensley , a virologist at the University of Pennsylvania. "And this might be a year that people might want to get a vaccine early."
But the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention hasn't been promoting flu shots as it usually does. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who oversees the CDC, is a long-time vaccine skeptic.
"It is disappointing that CDC is quiet given that flu kills of hundreds of kids a year and can result in tens of thousands of hospitalizations and tens of thousands of deaths," says Dr. Demetre Daskalakis , who resigned last year as the director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to protest what he called political interference at the agency.
The CDC declined to make an official available to NPR for this story. In a statement, a CDC spokesperson said, "CDC is developing a communications strategy to provide clear, accessible information about influenza vaccination and other critical steps people can take to protect themselves during respiratory virus season. This includes information about the benefits and risks of vaccination to support informed decision-making."

articles.title_zh: AEW Grand Slam: France Dynamite Results – Will Ospreay Keeps AEW World Title from Okada, Mercedes Moné Retains AEW Women’s World Title vs. Queen Aminata, More
articles.content_orig:
AEW's debut in Paris was a special one, as Grand Slam: France Dynamite emanated from Adidas Arena on TBS and HBO Max! A major debut called for a huge card, and Paris responded with energy that could be felt from the opening bell and beyond the main event! As if the excitement wasn’t high enough, we’re just 11 days from AEW WrestleDream in Orlando!
In the main event, AEW World Champion Will Ospreay defeated AEW International Champion “The Rainmaker” Kazuchika Okada to retain his title in an unbelievable match, which marked the first time Ospreay beat Okada in a championship bout. As Ospreay celebrated in the ring with “Speedball” Mike Bailey, Samoa Joe appeared on the ramp to end the night, sending a message that he’s ready for Clockwork Carnage after qualifying by beating “Jungle” Jack Perry earlier in the night.
AEW Women’s World Champion Mercedes Moné got everything she could handle from Queen Aminata in front of a Parisian crowd that was fully behind Aminata’s quest to win her first AEW gold. Moné overcame Aminata in the end to get the win, but she could not celebrate for long because her WrestleDream opponent, Thekla, hit the ring to cut Moné in half with a spear!
The night began with ROH World Champion Bandido turning away AEW World Trios Champion Kofi while both men’s trios partners made their presence felt, specifically Swerve Strickland and “Hangman” Adam Page. Later, Swerve and The New Level challenged Page, Bandido and Brody King to face them in a 2-out-of-3 falls match for the AEW World Trios Championship at WrestleDream!
TNT Champion Darby Allin was left a bloody mess in his defense against former champion “The Protostar” Kyle Fletcher, but somehow Allin was able to leave Paris with a successful defense in a brutally violent encounter.  Plus, Mark Davis and Jake Doyle earned a huge win for the Don Callis Family in tag team action over Gabe Kidd and AEW Continental Champion Jon Moxley!
All that and more went down on our first night in Paris!
The night began with the ROH World Championship on the line! Kofi, one third of the AEW World Trios Champions, made his way to the ring to a raucous ovation inside the Adidas Arena, accompanied by another third of the champions, Austin Creed.
The champion came out next, and he wasn't alone either — Bandido was flanked by Brody King for this championship tilt.
The referee called for the Code of Honor, and not only did both men shake hands, but they embraced. A hyped-up crowd was fully behind this matchup, which only fed the energy of both Kofi and Bandido.
While both men brought a clear level of speed, there was an extended feeling-out process to start, with each grabbing a brief advantage before the action reset to a stalemate. After both went for dropkicks, Bandido popped right back to his feet, but Kofi came back with a second dropkick that sent Bandido to the floor. When Kofi tried to dive to the outside, Bandido simply stepped out of the way, and Kofi's head bounced off the top rope. Bandido tried to climb back to the apron, but Kofi caught him with another dropkick, knocking him to the floor again. Kofi then charged and flipped over the top rope onto the floor, crushing Bandido, and took control of the early going.
Kofi rolled Bandido back into the ring and climbed the ropes. As Bandido got to his feet, Kofi leaped off the top for a cross body — but Bandido caught him in mid-air and, in an incredible display of strength, lifted him into a delayed vertical suplex, holding him aloft one-armed as the crowd counted all the way to twenty before finally dropping him to the mat.
The sheer exhaustion of that suplex left both men down. It was then that Swerve Strickland, the third member of the AEW World Trios Champions, made his way out with Prince Nana to join Creed in supporting Kofi. Only steps behind him, however, was “Hangman” Adam Page, and when Swerve spotted him, Creed and Nana had to hold him back. Page simply walked past and joined King at ringside to support their partner.
Bandido played to the crowd before turning his attention back to Kofi, landing a pair of corner strikes followed by a diving gut check that doubled Kofi over in pain. Bandido fired off more strikes in an adjacent corner, but when he went for a third, Kofi slipped away and whipped him to the opposite corner. With Bandido seated against the turnbuckle, Kofi drove a running knee into the side of his face, followed by elevated stomps to the chest. Kofi then ran in from the opposite corner for a shotgun dropkick, connecting flush. He covered, but Bandido kicked out to keep his title reign alive.
A visibly frustrated Kofi took a moment to regroup before pulling Bandido up, hitting a headbutt and an uppercut to back him into the corner and hoist him up top for a superplex attempt. But when Kofi came up after him, Bandido turned it around with a gorilla press slam, dumping Kofi onto the top turnbuckle before following with a dropkick that put him on the mat! Bandido covered, but Kofi kicked out at two.
Bandido tried to whip Kofi across the ring, but Kofi reversed it with a kick to the stomach, then leaped for a leg drop to the back of Bandido's head. Kofi started building momentum, landing backhanded chops followed by a jumping side kick that put Bandido back down. Bandido avoided a follow-up jumping clothesline and whipped Kofi to the corner, but as he rushed in, Kofi flipped back with a pendulum kick through the ropes, then went up top for a frog splash cross body that got another near-fall.
Kofi bounced off the ropes for a jumping lariat, then fired up the Paris crowd before connecting with a Boom Drop. As Bandido stumbled to his feet, Kofi measured him for T.I.P., but Bandido ducked out of the way. Kofi spun him around in a rear waistlock and sent him to the corner. Bandido kicked his way out and leaped to the top rope for a reverse tornillo that got a two-count.
Bandido pushed Kofi into the ropes, but Kofi rebounded with a jumping spin kick to the head for another near-fall. The crowd roared as Bandido started to fight back, only for Kofi to cut him off with a kick to the gut. The two traded strikes off the ropes until Bandido popped Kofi up into a knee strike. As Bandido came off the ropes, Kofi leaped into the air and stomped him into the mat.
The crowd was fully invested as both men's partners continued to will them on from ringside. Bandido rose in the corner as Kofi waited in the opposite one; when Kofi charged in, Bandido met him with a kick combination and climbed to the second rope. As Bandido came off, Kofi caught him and rolled him through for an SOS into the second buckle! That’s a new and brutal variation on that move, matching Bandido's own escalating viciousness in this battle for championship gold.
As Creed and Swerve, along with the crowd, urged Kofi toward the top rope, he slowly made his way up. With Bandido doubled over below, Kofi leaped off and splashed him flat onto his back! That was an unorthodox execution, but even more devastating!  Bandido kicked out to preserve his reign!
Kofi dug deeper into his arsenal than ever before, fully aware of the caliber of champion standing across from him. He made his way back to the top rope, but with Creed's back turned to hype the crowd, nobody saw Bandido sneak up from behind to catch Kofi with a kick. Bandido joined him on the top rope, and with both men balanced precariously, Bandido grabbed Kofi and hit a Revolutionary Fly from the top! He covered, 1-2-Kofi got a hand on the bottom rope to stay alive! Bandido picked up Kofi for the X-Knee, but Kofi landed on his feet and hit an SOS for a near-fall!
An argument broke out between Hangman and Swerve at ringside, and the two got in a shoving match, with both men having to be separated from each other. In the ensuing commotion, Bandido pulled Kofi off the mat with the 21 Plex for the three-count. articles.title_orig: Trump says Iran could ‘take’ San Diego, Los Angeles; draws cross-party ire
articles.title_zh: Trump says Iran could ‘take’ San Diego, Los Angeles; draws cross-party ire
articles.content_orig:
Members of the Republican Party have joined Democrats in questioning remarks made by United States President Donald Trump about the California cities of Los Angeles and San Diego.
Much of the backlash came on Tuesday, a day after Trump told a midterm rally in Nebraska that Americans should be willing to make sacrifices to deny Iran a nuclear weapon — even though Tehran has long rejected accusations that it is seeking atomic bombs.
“It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe,” Trump said, seemingly in reference to the knock-on effects of the war, including rising fuel and fertiliser prices.
Then, he said: “They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon.”
The White House said Trump was arguing that if Iran were allowed to secure a nuclear weapon, it could strike US cities.
But Democrats and some Republicans accused the president of suggesting that some of the country’s cities were expendable.
Gavin Newsom, the Democratic governor of California and outspoken critic of Trump, said the president was “deranged”.
“This is not only madness. This is dangerous,” Newsom said in a video on the social media platform X, in which he called for Congress to rein in Trump’s behaviour.
Trump has downplayed the impact of the US-Israel war on Iran – now in its eighth month – despite polling that shows the conflict is widely unpopular in the country. He has also repeatedly promised the war would end soon, though no lasting ceasefire has been reached so far.
Newsom, a possible contender in the 2028 presidential race, has clashed repeatedly with Trump.
Last year, the two faced off over Trump’s decision to deploy federal troops to California, as part of an effort to support a crackdown on undocumented immigration in the Los Angeles area.
In December, a federal judge ruled that the deployment had been illegal and ordered its end. Newsom, who opposed the deployment, cited that conflict in his remarks about Trump’s Nebraska rally.
“The president of the United States – the same one who sent in the National Guard into Los Angeles, sent 700 active duty Marines to the second-largest city in the United States of America – just invited Iran to take out Los Angeles and San Diego,” Newsom said.
He added that Trump’s remarks should convince those who “didn’t think the November election mattered” to vote in the upcoming midterms.
Some from Trump’s party have also expressed shock at his remarks.
Jim Desmond, a Republican running for California’s 48th congressional district, was among those who distanced themselves from Trump’s statement.
“I vehemently disagree with President Trump’s comments. America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our Commander in Chief is to protect the American people and our homeland,” Desmond wrote on X.
“No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.”
US Representative Kevin Kiley, an independent who caucuses with Republicans and is running for re-election in northern California, also called Trump’s comments “unhelpful”.
But the White House has dismissed criticism of the remarks, calling it part of a “media freakout” that “is not rooted in reality”.
“He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped,” Steven Cheung, White House director of communications, wrote on social media.
“America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.”
California has the largest population and economy of any state in the US. Because of its population, it also has the most seats in the House – 52.
All 435 seats in the House are up for grabs in November’s midterms, along with a third of the Senate. Also on the ballot are key state and local races.
With Republicans’ control of Congress on the line, the results of the midterms are expected to weigh heavily on the final two years of Trump’s second term.

articles.title_orig: Collins and Jackson Clash in First Debate of Crucial Maine Senate Race
articles.title_zh: Collins and Jackson Clash in First Debate of Crucial Maine Senate Race
articles.content_orig:
Republican challenged by Democrat Troy Jackson in critical Senate race says she opposes Iran war and Canada tariffs
Susan Collins, the Republican senator for Maine , pointedly distanced herself from Donald Trump in a televised debate with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson on Tuesday, as she sought to present an image of independence in a state that has voted against Trump three times.
Proclaiming herself as not the US president’s “favorite senator”, Collins made the highly unusual boast for a Republican that she had voted with Joe Biden, a Democrat, more than 90% of the time when he was president. She also emphasized her differences with her fellow Republicans , saying she voted against her own party more than any other senator.
Collins’ defensiveness came amid a determined onslaught from Jackson, 58, a veteran former state legislator who was getting his first chance to present himself to a broad audience since replacing Graham Platner as the Democratic candidate in a contest that could be vital to the party’s hopes of winning the Senate.
Platner, a former harbor master, was forced to withdraw from the race in July after facing sexual assault allegations, which he denied, leaving Democrats racing against the clock to replace a candidate who had built up momentum campaigning on a populist progressive platform.
Jackson painted Collins as a Trump loyalist, saying she voted with the president 96% of the time. He also doggedly focused on her 2018 vote for the conservative supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, tying it to the court’s subsequent overturning of Roe v Wade, which had for half a century guaranteed the national right to abortion.
“Tonight is about who you stand with when it matters,” Jackson said in a pithy opening statement. “Eight years ago today, Maine women went to DC and begged Senator Collins not to confirm Brett Kavanaugh, but she did it anyways.
“He helped overturn Roe v Wade, and today she says she has no regrets. Would you trust her to pick the next supreme court justice?”
Collins, 73, who has been a senator since 1996, has frequently presented herself as a moderate who stands against more radical trends in her own party. The posture is in line with Maine’s profile as a more Democratic-leaning state, which Trump has not won in any of his three presidential campaigns and which has voted for Democrat presidential candidates in every election since 1992.
Nevertheless, Collins went to unusual lengths to differentiate herself from Trump on a range of issues, including the war with Iran, which she said she voted to end nine times, calling it “not well thought out”.
Collins reacted with something close to alarm when the moderator, Gregg Lagerquist, said Trump had suggested that the president might pay a campaign visit to Maine.
“I don’t think that President Trump is going to come to Maine,” she said. “He’s talking about going to a lot of different states. I’ve heard nothing from his office, and I’m not exactly his favorite senator.”
Collins stressed her differences with the president on specific issues pertinent to the Maine economy, including rural healthcare and tariffs against Canada, with which the state shares a border.
“I have been the most outspoken opponent of the tariffs on Canada,” she said. “Canada is not China. It’s our neighbor and our friends.”
Polls show the two candidates running neck and neck.
