articles.title_orig: China says industrial, supply chains with EU ‘mutually dependent,’ urges dialogue over trade ‘concerns’
articles.title_zh: China says industrial, supply chains with EU ‘mutually dependent,’ urges dialogue over trade ‘concerns’
articles.content_orig:
China has called bilateral trade ties with the 27-member EU “highly integrated and mutually dependent,” stressing a need for dialogue over trade “concerns.”
The statement came after France and Germany called Monday for new EU trade instruments, arguing that the bloc’s existing measures are no longer sufficient to address challenges facing its trade system.
“Between China and the EU, the industrial and supply chains are highly integrated and mutually dependent, and our economic and trade relations are mutually beneficial in nature,” China’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said in a written statement late Tuesday.
“It is hoped that the EU will work with China in the same direction and resolve each other’s concerns through dialogue and consultation, so that the two parties can jointly keep the global industrial and supply chains stable and unimpeded and promote the sound and steady development of China-EU economic and trade relations,” he said.
In a joint letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the EU was facing “unprecedented challenges,” and proposed to reduce European dependencies, resolve existing supply-chain concentration and prevent emerging concentration risks.
Their letter came ahead of a visit by EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic to Beijing, where he will be hosted by China’s Commerce Minister Wang Wentao.
Wang and Sefcovic will meet Thursday and Friday, their first meeting in three months after they last met in Brussels.
Sefcovic earlier said that Brussels was seeking progress particularly in automobiles, medical devices, and agri-food products and could resort to defensive trade instruments if negotiations failed.
The EU imported €559.4 billion ($634 billion) in goods from China in 2025 while exporting €199.6 billion, leaving a goods trade deficit of €359.8 billion.

articles.title_orig: World Shipping Council launch digital global Whale Chart with HUB Ocean
articles.title_zh: World Shipping Council launch digital global Whale Chart with HUB Ocean
articles.content_orig:
Kimberly Mathisen (CEO, HUB Ocean) & Joe Kramek (President & CEO, World Shipping Council) - download a high-resolution version of this image.
7 October 2026 – The World Shipping Council (WSC), in partnership with HUB Ocean, today launched a digital version of the WSC Whale Chart, making global information on measures to protect whales from ships even more accessible.
Since its initial launch in 2023, WSC’s Whale Chart was the first global mapping of all known mandatory and voluntary governmental measures designed to reduce harm to whales from vessels. These include speed restrictions, routing measures, areas to be avoided and measures addressing underwater radiated noise.
By partnering with HUB Ocean to produce the digital Whale Chart, these measures are now easier to explore, easier to keep up to date, and can plug directly into digital tools and operational systems.
“Mariners operate across many different jurisdictions, and the measures in place to protect whales vary from country to country and region to region. Bringing this information together digitally and making it available to mariners on the bridges of the ships they are navigating makes it easier to use in voyage planning and helps crews see where changing course or slowing down can make a real difference,” said Joe Kramek, President & CEO of the World Shipping Council.
“The Whale Chart has already become an important reference point for the shipping industry,” said Kimberly Mathisen, CEO of HUB Ocean. “Our hope is that by making this information easier to work with, it becomes part of more decisions, more voyages and ultimately more action to protect whales.”
The Whale Chart and all its underlying datasets are now available through HUB Ocean’s Ocean Data Platform, an open, cloud-based geospatial platform that turns ocean data into insight and action.
Bringing the Whale Chart into that ecosystem means it can be explored alongside other authoritative datasets such as marine protected areas and other ocean intelligence layers, supporting richer insights and decisions for mariners, ship operators, governments and researchers alike.
Alongside the new digital platform, WSC has released the fourth edition of the WSC Whale Chart handbook, providing a quick regional overview of whale protection measures. The digital Whale Chart complements this with more detailed, searchable and most current information for specific voyage areas.
Whales travel across national boundaries and through some of the world’s busiest shipping routes. Where shipping traffic and whale activity overlap, separating ships from whales is the most effective way to reduce the risk of collisions. Where separation is not possible, measures such as speed reductions can help reduce the risk and severity of ship strikes while also limiting underwater noise.
WSC will continue to update the WSC Whale Chart as measures change and new information becomes available.
The digital WSC Whale Chart on the Ocean Data Platform is available here and a preview is available on WSC’s Whales webpage .
About World Shipping Council
The World Shipping Council is the united voice of liner shipping, working with policymakers and industry groups to shape the future growth of a socially responsible, environmentally sustainable, safe, and secure shipping industry. We are a non-profit trade association with offices in Brussels, London, Singapore and Washington, D.C.
80% of everything we buy has come by ship. World Shipping Council members are the international container and vehicle carriers that make global trade possible by offering cost efficient and effective transport for everything from raw materials, food and machinery parts to consumer essentials like medication, clothes and electronics.
Read more at www.worldshipping.org
HUB Ocean is an independent non-profit foundation, dedicated to unlocking the power of data to protect and restore ocean health. The organization has built the performant geospatial and cloud-based Ocean Data Platform, giving scientists, experts, and organizations seamless access to fit-for-purpose ocean data from both public and private sources. Built for interoperability and speed, the platform is designed to connect a federated ocean data ecosystem and accelerate collective action for a sustainable ocean.

articles.title_orig: World stocks mostly fall back despite latest earnings-driven rally on Wall Street
articles.title_zh: World stocks mostly fall back despite latest earnings-driven rally on Wall Street
articles.content_orig:
Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.
A currency trader passes by screens showing the Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) and the foreign exchange rate between U.S. dollar and South Korean won at the foreign exchange dealing room of the Hana Bank headquarters in Seoul, South Korea, Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. (AP Photo/Ahn Young-joon)
World shares retreated Wednesday after U.S. stocks hit all-time highs, lifted by expectations of fat corporate earnings.
In early European trading, the CAC 40 in Paris lost 0.4% to 7,836.77, while Britain's FTSE 100 shed 0.1% to 10,532.87. In Germany, the DAX lost 0.4% to 25,338.97.
In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 lost 0.9% to 70,035.71, while the Kospi in South Korea dropped 2% to 6,803.90.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 0.6% to 24,130.50 and Taiwan's Taiex was nearly unchanged.
Markets in Shanghai were closed for a national holiday.
In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 erased early gains to edge 0.1% lower, closing at 8,727.70.
On Tuesday, U.S. stocks climbed to new heights despite an array of challenges.
The S&P 500 climbed 0.6% to a record of 7,818.93, topping its all-time high set in August . Despite worries over the Iran war , high inflation and pressures from the bond market , the index at the heart of many 401(k) accounts has soared 23% since hitting a trough in late March.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.5% to 51,521.28, while the Nasdaq composite tacked 0.4% onto its own all-time high set the day before, closing at 27,599.79.
“The rally reflected confidence that corporate earnings, particularly across technology and AI-related sectors, can withstand elevated energy costs and restrictive interest rates,” Ng Jing Wen of Mizuho Bank said in a commentary.
“The resilience suggests investors continue to prioritize earnings momentum over near-term inflation risks,” she said.
Record-high stock prices are helping investors feel better about their finances, or at least less bad, while Americans are generally feeling discouraged about keeping up with the fast-rising cost of living.
Many of the fears that sent the U.S. stock market to its bottom in March have indeed come true. Oil prices are high because of the war with Iran , which has made inflation worse. Yields have cranked higher in the bond market, which threatens to slow the economy by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money . And Americans broadly say they’re feeling more pessimistic about the economy and where it’s heading .
But one vital source of support has persisted: strong corporate earnings.
Lamb Weston, which sells frozen fries and other potato products, said on Tuesday that its profit and revenue during its latest quarter topped its projections, for example. The results also beat analysts’ expectations, and its stock rallied 7.5%.
Constellation Energy helped lead the way after announcing a long-term deal to provide Google with electricity.
All kinds of companies are expected to report robust profits for the July through September quarter. Delta Air Lines will report its third-quarter results on Friday, with several of the country’s biggest banks headlining next week.
Analysts expect companies in the S&P 500 to deliver overall growth of nearly 30% in earnings per share from a year earlier, according to data provider FactSet. If they’re correct, it would be the third straight quarter of growth better than 25%.
If companies fail to deliver such performances, stock prices could easily fall back from their records. Some critics also point to a possible bubble in stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry given how much they have soared in the frenzy around the technology.
AI stocks have been a huge force driving the U.S. market to records, including Nvidia’s 28.3% surge so far this year. That's roughly double the broad market’s gain.
Bond yields offered some slack on Tuesday after falling back from their highest levels in years or even decades.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which is the focal point of the U.S. bond market, eased to 5.28% from 5.31% late Monday. It fell after oil prices steadied somewhat.
But crude prices rebounded early Wednesday. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, was up 0.7% at $101.26. That's still below the nearly $110 it was at a few weeks ago.
U.S. benchmark crude rose 0.3% to $89.66 per barrel.
Also early Wednesday, the U.S. dollar fell to 158.13 Japanese yen from 158.10 yen. The euro slipped to $1.1197 from $1.1260.

articles.title_orig: Linux Foundation Launches OpenGrid to Build Open, Shared Infrastructure for the World's Electric Grid
articles.title_zh: Linux Foundation Launches OpenGrid to Build Open, Shared Infrastructure for the World's Electric Grid
articles.content_orig:
New open source initiative integrates and builds a data platform and tools to accelerate grid planning and energy infrastructure deployments worldwide
PRAGUE , Oct. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Open Source Summit Europe – The Linux Foundation , the nonprofit organization enabling mass innovation through open source, today announced the launch of OpenGrid, a new initiative building open source infrastructure to modernize power grid planning worldwide. Hosted by the Linux Foundation, OpenGrid creates a neutral, interoperable foundation that allows planners to work across the commercial and open source software they already use, helping reduce the time, cost and technical barriers involved in planning the infrastructure needed to meet rapidly growing electricity demand.
Grid planning has become a critical bottleneck as electricity demand grows, new data center and industrial loads come online and more generation and storage seek connection. More than 2,500 gigawatts of generation, storage and large-load projects are currently pending in grid connection queues worldwide, while annual grid investment needs to roughly double to more than $600 billion by 2030 . Meeting long-term energy needs will require adding or replacing 80 million kilometers of power lines by 2040, yet planning remains constrained by fragmented data, incompatible software and modeling capabilities that are inaccessible to many institutions and countries.
"Open source has repeatedly shown that shared architecture and interoperability accelerate innovation across entire industries," said Jim Zemlin, CEO of the Linux Foundation. "OpenGrid will bring the proven model of open collaboration to grid planning for faster and more reliable deployment. The Linux Foundation's neutral governance will ensure durability, longevity and usability of the technologies that support essential public-interest infrastructure."
OpenGrid is not developing a single replacement for existing grid planning software. Instead, it provides a shared data and interoperability layer that allows existing commercial and open source tools to work together. Its foundational efforts will include open standards and schemas, programmatic APIs and a centralized Data Hub for validated, model-ready datasets. Its first lighthouse application, the OpenGrid Translator, is in development for release in 2027 and will enable data and models to move between widely used commercial platforms and open source tools.
Access to modern planning capabilities is particularly uneven in fast-growing markets. At the same time, emerging economies are expected to account for nearly 80% of global electricity demand growth through 2030 . OpenGrid aims to give planning teams everywhere access to high-quality modeling capabilities, while enabling regulators, advocates and other stakeholders to inspect the models and data informing major infrastructure decisions.
"Reliable electricity supports healthier lives, stronger communities and economic opportunity, but delivering it requires credible plans. Today, too many plans rely on data others cannot verify and tools much of the world cannot afford," said Alice Yake, vice president of BE-GRIDS and chair of the OpenGrid Management Committee. "OpenGrid changes that: open data, open standards and access to planning tools that any utility, regulator or country can inspect and use."
Over time, the OpenGrid ecosystem plans to expand to include open solvers, no-code graphical interfaces, standardized planning workflows and integrations that use AI to support data preparation. By providing transparent, repeatable and accessible planning infrastructure, OpenGrid aims to help planners, infrastructure owners, regulators and communities work from a common technical foundation and make infrastructure decisions with greater confidence faster.
OpenGrid launches with support from Breakthrough Energy GRIDS, Global Grid Catalyst, Connected Grid Initiative and Google.org, with technical delivery partners including Open Energy Transition, Tapestry, TransitionZero and QXT Energy.
Organizations, researchers, regulators and community members interested in contributing to OpenGrid or learning more are encouraged to visit https://www.opengrid.org .
"Electricity systems are going through some pretty radical changes, with many new variable producers, storage and consumers connecting to the grid. OpenGrid supports the infrastructure we need to get quick consensus on how the energy transition should proceed, and to foster the innovation we need to drive it forward faster."
– Tom Brown, Professor of Digital Transformation in Energy Systems, TU Berlin and Managing Director, PyPSA Labs
"Planners shouldn't have to choose between the tools they already use and the open ones now emerging. Building enterprise-grade, open modeling software with Scenario Builder showed us how much time is lost moving data and models between formats. OpenGrid's shared standards and translators tackle that directly, and we're glad to help build them, so that planners anywhere can pick up a model, inspect it, use it and make decisions that cut the time it takes to build clean energy at scale."
– Matt Gray, Co-Founder and CEO, TransitionZero
"Accelerating scientific progress requires turning foundational research and open data into real-world solutions. Power grids are among humanity's most complex engineering systems, yet modeling them is too often limited by fragmented tools and closed data. OpenGrid will provide the shared digital foundation needed to make faster, more evidence-based decisions and ultimately strengthen our global grid infrastructure."
– Joseph Hassine, Scaled Impact Lead, Google.org
"OpenGrid is the catalyst that the power and energy industry needs to drive new software innovations that ultimately will produce better and faster decision making for the power grid. We keep hearing that these times are unprecedented and yet we have seen very few changes in the power software space. OpenGrid's ambitions to demonstrate that open source can be the driver for much needed innovation is something that QXT Energy is enthusiastic to support."
– José Daniel Lara, Co-Founder and CTO, QXT Energy
"The accelerating complexity of the modern power system demands better integration of economic and reliability planning tools, as well as coordinated planning across the transmission and distribution networks. OpenGrid is tackling this ambitious challenge by enabling these diverse tools, whether open source or commercial, to work together and by providing validated datasets. This has the potential to revolutionize grid planning across the globe."
– Debbie Lew, Executive Director, Energy Systems Integration Group (ESIG)
"At OpenET, we make water use data open and accessible, so I've seen firsthand how a shared baseline builds trust among diverse stakeholders. That experience convinces me that open data infrastructure is essential to sound resource management. By giving planners, regulators and communities a common ground truth they can all inspect and understand, OpenGrid will help them make the decisions the energy transition demands."
– Luis Villa, Board Chair, OpenET, Inc.
"Transparent and neutral governance ensures that all interested users have access to the tools in this initiative. It allows users to decide what is best for their purposes, and it keeps the door open for new tool development to foster innovation and avoid lock-in. Transparency in decision-making creates community buy-in. When parties come together on shared infrastructure, working toward common objectives and the methods and results can be vetted by many parties, this builds the trust and sense of fairness and legitimacy that will be necessary for OpenGrid to be successful."
– Karin Wadsack, Executive Director, Global Power System Transformation Consortium

articles.title_orig: Satellite images show attack jets, vehicles at new China-Laos base
articles.title_zh: Satellite images show attack jets, vehicles at new China-Laos base
articles.content_orig:
Tuesday, October 6, 2026 75° Today's Paper
By Greg Torode and Poppy McPherson / Reuters
Today • Last updated
                                            2:13 p.m.
VANTOR/HANDOUT VIA REUTERS
A satellite image shows what security analysts believe are Y-8 light attack fighters and support vehicles at a new China-Laos joint training facility in Ban Keun, Vientiane Province, Laos, on Sept. 30.
VANTOR/HANDOUT VIA REUTERS
A satellite image shows a new China-Laos joint training facility, with a runway that is being expanded, in Ban Keun, Vientiane Province, Laos, on Sept. 30.
HONG KONG/BANGKOK >> Light attack aircraft and military vehicles have arrived at the new China-Laos joint training facility announced on Sept. 29, according to satellite images reviewed by Reuters.
The images, taken by commercial satellite provider Vantor, show what security analysts believe are eight K-8 light attack jets and more than two dozen support vehicles on a runway that is still being built — China’s latest expansion of its overseas military presence.
Taken on September 30, the day after China’s defense ministry announced it had set up the facility at Ban Keun outside the capital Vientiane, the images also show extensive construction work around the runway.
The swift development of the new facility is being closely watched by regional military attaches and security scholars, some of whom say its construction potentially marks China’s first fully fledged overseas military base in Southeast Asia.
Despite more than 20 years of intense military modernisation, China is widely perceived to lack a strong network of overseas facilities beyond the South China Sea, port access in Ream, Cambodia and a logistics base in Djibouti.
Rachel Vandenbrink, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, said the selection of Ban Keun for a facility that the People’s Liberation Army could access “is likely more about a target of opportunity than filling an obvious operational need.”
Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
“Laos does have some geostrategic value as an accessible foothold in mainland Southeast Asia, given its shared border with China and infrastructure links, including (its) railway,” Vandenbrink said.
The Chinese defense ministry did not immediately respond to Reuters’ request for comment.
The Lao embassy in Bangkok and the Lao foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Singapore-based security analysts Collin Koh and Alexander Neill, as well as Vantor specialists, said the planes appeared to be Hongdu JL-8 aircraft, which both the Chinese and Lao air forces operate.
Also known as the K-8, the two-seater aircraft is extensively used for training as well as having light attack capabilities. It was jointly developed by China and Pakistan and is exported to other militaries.
Laos currently has four of the planes, according to the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies’ annual assessment of the world’s militaries. Koh, a scholar at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, described the Laotian planes as being of “questionable serviceability”.
As construction continues, diplomats and analysts are keeping watch for any sign of air defenses, ammunition and fuel storage as well as surveillance facilities — all of which could point to the base serving broader military functions beyond training.
Neill said while the airfield looked relatively short and innocuous at present, it could in future serve larger aircraft, including signals intelligence and electronic-surveillance planes to extend China’s reach into Southeast Asia.
“It looks like the airfield has been engineered to accommodate a runway extension allowing larger aircraft to operate,” said Neill, an adjunct fellow at Hawaii’s Pacific Forum think-tank.
In helping Laos build up Ban Keun, China is now occupying a site the US used covertly at the height of the Vietnam War.
During the US war against communist forces in Laos in the 1970s, Ban Keun was an airfield known as “Lima Site 44” used by Air America, an airline discreetly owned by the Central Intelligence Agency, according to records shared with Reuters by Ryan Wolfson-Ford, a Southeast Asia specialist at the Library of Congress.
The airline carried American-backed troops from the country’s Hmong highland minority as well as supplies into rough mountain airstrips known as “Lima Sites”.
As early as 1968, Ban Keun was used as a point from where Air America helicopters delivered Hmong troops to other combat zones, said Dr Joachim Leeker, an academic who has written about the history of the airline.

General Mills’ results were driven by the company’s work to invest in employees’ development, well-being and a culture of belonging.
MINNEAPOLIS – General Mills has been named one of the World’s Best Employers 2026 by Forbes. This prestigious award recognizes organizations setting the gold standard for workplace excellence and is presented by Forbes and Statista Inc., the world-leading statistics portal and industry ranking provider.
General Mills’ results were driven by the company’s work to invest in employees’ development, well-being and a culture where belonging is a daily reality, not simply a stated value.
“At General Mills, our people are at the heart of our success,” said Jacqueline Williams-Roll, Chief Human Resources Officer at General Mills. “We invest in their growth and development, take a whole-person approach to well-being, and work every day to build a culture where everyone feels they belong and can do their best work. Our ambition is to be the best place to grow a career, and we’re proud of our progress.”
The World’s Best Employers were selected based on an independent survey of more than 300,000 employees across 50 countries working for multinational companies with at least 1,000 workers. The final list recognizes the top 900 companies globally. The evaluation asked participants to rate their willingness to recommend their own employers to friends and family, and evaluated the company on criteria including benefits, talent development and career advancement, work-life balance and company reputation.
This recognition adds to General Mills’ growing list of employer-related accolades, including being named to 3BL’s 100 Best Corporate Citizens 2026 list and Newsweek’s America’s Most Responsible Companies 2026.
For more information on General Mills, visit GeneralMills.com or Careers.GeneralMills.com .

articles.title_orig: US stock market hits all-time high as investors continue to bet on AI
articles.title_zh: US stock market hits all-time high as investors continue to bet on AI
articles.content_orig:
The United States stock market has hit an all-time high as excitement around artificial intelligence continues to fuel a buying frenzy on Wall Street.
The S&P 500, the benchmark stock index, closed 0.58 percent higher on Tuesday, topping the previous peak reached in mid-August.
The Nasdaq Composite, which is more heavily weighted towards tech stocks, also hit a record high, finishing up 0.45 percent.
Tech stocks were among the top performers, with each of the “Magnificent Seven” apart from Meta closing higher.
Amazon led the pack with a 1.95 percent gain, followed by Microsoft and Tesla, which rose 0.78 percent and 0.51 percent, respectively.
Apple and Alphabet both rose 0.22 percent, while Nvidia gained 0.14 percent.
Meta, which has risen more than 20 percent since the launch last month of its new AI assistant, Muse, fell 0.41 percent.
Other big movers in tech included Marvell Technology, which rose 5.81 percent, and Cisco, which gained 4.54 percent.
Keith Lerner, chief investment officer and chief market strategist at Truist Advisory Services in Atlanta, Georgia, said the market rally should be seen as a “technology and AI surge”.
“Every bull market has a dominant theme, and technology and AI remain this market’s dominant theme,” Lerner told Al Jazeera.
“Technology and communication services were the only two S&P 500 sectors to rise last month, while the other nine declined.”
Wall Street has shrugged off a host of challenges facing the US economy amid hyperscalers’ multibillion-dollar investments in AI.
Despite the energy crunch caused by the US-Israel war on Iran and a sell-off of US government bonds partly driven by ballooning government debt, the market is well on track to record its fourth consecutive year of double-digit returns.
The S&P 500 has risen 14 percent so far in 2026, while the Nasdaq Composite is up 18.78 percent.
“Investors remain bullish on the prospects for AI,” Lochlan Halloway, a senior equity strategist at Morningstar Australia, told Al Jazeera.
“They are betting that the money pouring into data centres will earn a good return, and so far, that belief has outweighed rising interest rates, more expensive oil and a 10-year bond yield above 5 percent,” Halloway said.
“We are positive on AI too,” Halloway added. “But the range of outcomes is wide, and the market is concentrated in a handful of companies, so the outlook for US shares, and by extension global shares, relies on the AI story continuing to deliver.”
Lerner at Truist Advisory said the market rally had the potential to continue through the end of 2026 given historical trends and expectations for strong corporate earnings.
“We do not expect a straight line higher for markets,” Lerner said.
“Still, the fourth quarter of [US] midterm-election years has produced an average gain of 7 percent and has been positive 84 percent of the time since 1950.”
Lerner said that rising interest rates posed the biggest risk to the upward trend.
“Still, on balance, the weight of the evidence suggests this bull market still has more upside potential,” he said.
Despite the rally on Wall Street, Asian stock markets fell on Wednesday, with key indexes in Japan, South Korea, and Hong Kong racking up losses.
The Kospi in Seoul led the sell-off, falling 1.98 percent, while Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 dropped 0.92 percent.
In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Index was down 0.57 percent shortly before the market’s close.
Oil prices, which have been elevated since the start of the war on Iran, rose on Wednesday as traders weighed the fallout of fighting in Yemen between forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Iran-aligned Houthis.
Brent crude futures for December delivery stood at $101.16 a barrel as of 07:30 GMT, up 0.58 percent.

articles.title_orig: World leaders pay tribute to victims as Israel marks three years since 7 October attack by Hamas – live
articles.title_zh: World leaders pay tribute to victims as Israel marks three years since 7 October attack by Hamas – live
articles.content_orig:
1,200 died in attack that led to launch of devastating war in Gaza
‘All I want to do is cry’: trauma of 7 October survivors three years after the attacks
Here are some of the tributes by world leaders for the third anniversary of the 7 October attack (we reported earlier on Andy Burnham’s message here ):
German chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to fight antisemitism in Germany and continue to advocate for a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine . In his message, Merz said his country was witnessing rising antisemitism “that far too often goes unchallenged” and that his government “will do everything in its power” to combat it. “Germany stands firmly by Israel’s side. Our Israeli friends can count on our commitment to ensuring that such a crime never happens again,” he added.
French president Emmanuel Macron said his country shares the grief of Israel and the bereaved families. “We do not forget the names or the faces: those of Maya, Ohad, Valentin, and so many others,” he said. “Combating antisemitism and terrorism, everywhere and always, working for peace and the security of all: that is France’s commitment.”
Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese said his country stands with the Jewish community both at home and abroad as he reflected on the Bondi beach attack in December that killed 10 people. “For so many, no day since has been easy, but anniversaries fall with their own terrible weight,” he said in a statement. “And for many others, what compounds the pain is the approach of the first anniversary of the antisemitic terror attack at Bondi Beach. These few years have been hard beyond measure.”
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said the EU “stands with all those whose lives were forever changed by that day”. She added that the bloc “remains ready to help turn today’s fragile ceasefire into a durable peace, based on a two-state solution”.
Elsewhere in Israel, protesters against what they view as a lack of accountability for the security failure gathered outside parliament in Jerusalem, blaming prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu for refusing an independent inquiry into the attack.
Some protesters held signs reading: “The people will remember October 7 on October 27,” a reference to an Israeli general election 20 days away that is being viewed as a referendum on Netanyahu’s long tenure in power.
“We need the change and we need hope and we need to know that we have a government that cares about the public and doesn’t work also only for themselves,” said protester Shaked Arrad.
New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani has issued a statement marking the 7 October attack, saying “the suffering did not begin nor end that day” as he criticised the Israeli government for continuing attacks in Gaza despite a so-called ceasefire.
Mamdani said the anniversary was a “profoundly painful” day for New Yorkers and condemned the “horrific war crimes” committed by Hamas .
A staunch and vocal supporter of Palestinian rights, the bulk of Mamdani’s statement focused on Israel’s conduct in Gaza , where he denounced the war crimes committed “with impunity” by the Israeli government while he also criticising the US’s “complicity” in shipping arms to the country.
double quotation mark This day is profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers. It marks three years since the horrific war crimes of October 7. On that day, Hamas killed more than 1,100 Israelis and abducted 251 others. We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss.
The suffering did not begin nor end that day. It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians-including more than 21,000 children. Even since the so-called ceasefire, more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed. That suffering has intensified with every Israeli bomb dropped on ambulances waiting outside hospitals, every drone strike targeting a residential building or journalist, and every shipment of food aid turned away at a border crossing. Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them – all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes.
Three years later, we must refuse to accept a world in which occupation and apartheid continue, where war crimes are met with impunity, and our federal government continues its complicity with every arms shipment.
To honor the dead, we must fight for a world in which every person can live with freedom, safety, and dignity.”
US secretary of state Marco Rubio said his country “will never forget this act of barbarism against an ally” in his message to mark the anniversary of the 7 October attack in Israel .
double quotation mark Three years ago today, Hamas terrorists tortured, mutilated, and murdered 1,200 innocent civilians in Israel.
Among those slain were men, women, and children – including dozens of Americans.
We will never forget this act of barbarism against an ally and recommit ourselves to the defense of civilization.”
British Jewish organisations will gather in central London for a vigil honouring victims of the 7 October attacks in Israel on Wednesday, after a day of tributes from politicians and community leaders.
A 5pm vigil is expected to take place at Richmond Terrace, opposite Downing Street.
The Board of Deputies of British Jews said: “Three years ago, Hamas terrorists infiltrated Israel , murdering 1,200 men, women and children, injuring thousands and taking 251 people captive. May their memories for ever remain a blessing.”
Meanwhile, the Jewish Leadership Council said 7 October had been “the deadliest day for our people since the Holocaust.”
Commenting on the pro-Palestine march in London, the Board of Deputies of British Jews said it “would not be threatened or intimidated” after the protest reached the organisation’s headquarters in the city.
The group’s president, Phil Rosenberg , said:
double quotation mark On the anniversary of the worst massacre of Jews since the Holocaust, masked protesters demonstrated outside our office today, chanting about ‘intifada’ and harassing our neighbours.
We are grateful to the Metropolitan police for their swift response and making arrests on the spot.
We will not be threatened or intimidated by this small and extremist minority of British society.
We will continue undeterred to advocate for the Jewish people, here and around the world, and to stand up for peace and security for Israelis, Palestinians and the wider Middle East.”
In London, police have arrested five people at a student pro-Palestine demonstration on the anniversary of the 7 October attacks.
Despite calls for a ban or for the protest to be moved to a different date, about 100 people marched and chanted “free free Palestine” and “free the people, free the land” in central London, with a group holding a banner reading: “Holocaust survivor descendants against Gaza genocide”, the PA news agency reported.
Students from the University of London Coalition umbrella group demonstrated against what they said was complicity by the UK government, universities and businesses in Israel’s genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Counter protesters holding Israeli flags also gathered by Russell Square, shouting “scumbags” at the pro-Palestine protesters and chanting “terrorist supporters off our streets”.
The Metropolitan police said: “Earlier this morning, officers made arrests at a spontaneous protest outside the Board of Deputies in Camden.
“Five people were arrested for inciting racial hatred, involving allegedly shouting or chanting slogans calling for intifada. They remain in police custody. The protest in Camden has now ended.”
The pro-Palestine march has been labelled “shameful” by defence secretary Wes Streeting, while education secretary Lucy Powell urged students “to show compassion and protest on another day”.
The Board of Deputies of British Jews is expected to hold a vigil in Richmond Terr

articles.title_orig: Why AI is both the hope and the hazard for world leaders, according to IMF chief Georgieva
articles.title_zh: Why AI is both the hope and the hazard for world leaders, according to IMF chief Georgieva
articles.content_orig:
SINGAPORE — The technology that investors and governments are counting on to lift the global economy is also adding pressure that threatens growth, the head of the International Monetary Fund said, urging policymakers to stop delaying painful choices on debt.
Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva told the audience at a Wednesday event in Singapore that artificial intelligence is "rapidly becoming a key driver of countries' relative fortunes in the world economy."
But the triple forces of AI advancement, soaring energy costs and record public debt are challenging the already "underwhelming" growth this decade.
"Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here," Georgieva said.
Speaking ahead of a series of IMF and World Bank annual meetings that kick off next week, Georgieva framed the global economy as being tugged in two directions at once: a "negative energy supply shock" from the war in the Gulf, now in its eighth month, and a "positive demand shock" from the AI investment boom. The combined effect, she said, is "highly uneven across the world."
On the upside, global AI investment as a share of GDP will reach, and likely exceed, the amounts that went into building the railroads, electricity grid, or telecommunications network. AI hardware and related technology products already account for more than a tenth of world goods trade, she said.
The IMF estimates that AI could add up to half a percentage point to annual world growth if done right. "Going from 3% to 3.5% over a decade — that is like adding an economy the size of ASEAN to the world economy," Georgieva said.
But the benefits are likely highly concentrated. The boom largely bypasses economies less involved in the global AI supply chain, "increasing the risk of widening economic inequality across the globe," she said.
The boom also feeds the inflation worry that has dogged policymakers from the U.S. to Europe and Asia. "The AI building boom is inflationary," she said, as are energy and food shocks, tariffs and defense spending.
Oil prices have stayed above $100 per barrel as the Middle East conflict dragged on with few signs of a diplomatic off-ramp. Retail diesel prices also rose to record highs as refining capacity squeezed energy supplies.
That inflation pressure flows straight into bond markets, as bond yields in the U.S., Germany, and Japan have surged to their highest levels in decades . Ballooning long-term private bond issuance by AI-related borrowers also competes with governments for capital, although part of the rise may reflect expectations of faster growth, Georgieva said.
Global public debt is near its highest level since World War II and on track to soon exceed 100% of GDP, with advanced economies the "worst offenders," Georgieva said. For 17 years, governments had "a relatively easy ride" because interest rates stayed below growth rates. "Higher interest rates now put an end to that."
The interest-to-growth differential is now "much less favourable" and "set to climb higher," she said, which means the growth needed to reduce debt ratios without fiscal effort is now "out of reach in the near term."
The strain is already visible in Europe, where spreads over German bunds are widening not just for France and Italy but for Ireland, Portugal and others that had reduced debt and deficits after the euro-area crisis.
After a string of shocks that have ballooned public debt and most countries' fiscal deficits remained above pre-pandemic averages, "fiscal space is crying out for replenishment," Georgieva said.
Georgieva also pointed to a financial stability risk in the AI boom itself. Strong corporate earnings are driving share prices and wealth effects, she said, but "should earnings fall short, however, hyperscaler leverage and large and growing global holdings of U.S. equities could turn a disappointment into a far-reaching shock."
Citing Amara's Law, which holds that people overestimate a new technology in the short run and underestimate it in the long run, she said it is "somewhere in the transition between today's AI building boom and tomorrow's arrival of AI's benefits that we will traverse the period of maximum risk."
Georgieva said the first line of defense is regulation and supervision. "Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries' monetary policy," she said.

He also warned that the global landscape would remain unsettled if China and the United States failed to address their respective domestic issues.
Speaking at the Milken Institute Asia Summit 2026 in Singapore on Wednesday, Balakrishnan identified maintaining trust with both Washington and Beijing – whose relationship was in a “difficult phase” – as a key challenge.
The city state had to assure both superpowers that it would remain useful without serving as a proxy for either, he said.

articles.title_orig: IMF’s Kristalina Georgieva urges governments to rein in spending
articles.title_zh: IMF’s Kristalina Georgieva urges governments to rein in spending
articles.content_orig:
SINGAPORE — The technology that investors and governments are counting on to lift the global economy is also adding pressure that threatens growth, the head of the International Monetary Fund said, urging policymakers to stop delaying painful choices on debt.
Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva told the audience at a Wednesday event in Singapore that artificial intelligence is "rapidly becoming a key driver of countries' relative fortunes in the world economy."
But the triple forces of AI advancement, soaring energy costs and record public debt are challenging the already "underwhelming" growth this decade.
"Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here," Georgieva said.
Speaking ahead of a series of IMF and World Bank annual meetings that kick off next week, Georgieva framed the global economy as being tugged in two directions at once: a "negative energy supply shock" from the war in the Gulf, now in its eighth month, and a "positive demand shock" from the AI investment boom. The combined effect, she said, is "highly uneven across the world."
On the upside, global AI investment as a share of GDP will reach, and likely exceed, the amounts that went into building the railroads, electricity grid, or telecommunications network. AI hardware and related technology products already account for more than a tenth of world goods trade, she said.
The IMF estimates that AI could add up to half a percentage point to annual world growth if done right. "Going from 3% to 3.5% over a decade — that is like adding an economy the size of ASEAN to the world economy," Georgieva said.
But the benefits are likely highly concentrated. The boom largely bypasses economies less involved in the global AI supply chain, "increasing the risk of widening economic inequality across the globe," she said.
The boom also feeds the inflation worry that has dogged policymakers from the U.S. to Europe and Asia. "The AI building boom is inflationary," she said, as are energy and food shocks, tariffs and defense spending.
Oil prices have stayed above $100 per barrel as the Middle East conflict dragged on with few signs of a diplomatic off-ramp. Retail diesel prices also rose to record highs as refining capacity squeezed energy supplies.
That inflation pressure flows straight into bond markets, as bond yields in the U.S., Germany, and Japan have surged to their highest levels in decades . Ballooning long-term private bond issuance by AI-related borrowers also competes with governments for capital, although part of the rise may reflect expectations of faster growth, Georgieva said.
Global public debt is near its highest level since World War II and on track to soon exceed 100% of GDP, with advanced economies the "worst offenders," Georgieva said. For 17 years, governments had "a relatively easy ride" because interest rates stayed below growth rates. "Higher interest rates now put an end to that."
The interest-to-growth differential is now "much less favourable" and "set to climb higher," she said, which means the growth needed to reduce debt ratios without fiscal effort is now "out of reach in the near term."
The strain is already visible in Europe, where spreads over German bunds are widening not just for France and Italy but for Ireland, Portugal and others that had reduced debt and deficits after the euro-area crisis.
After a string of shocks that have ballooned public debt and most countries' fiscal deficits remained above pre-pandemic averages, "fiscal space is crying out for replenishment," Georgieva said.
Georgieva also pointed to a financial stability risk in the AI boom itself. Strong corporate earnings are driving share prices and wealth effects, she said, but "should earnings fall short, however, hyperscaler leverage and large and growing global holdings of U.S. equities could turn a disappointment into a far-reaching shock."
Citing Amara's Law, which holds that people overestimate a new technology in the short run and underestimate it in the long run, she said it is "somewhere in the transition between today's AI building boom and tomorrow's arrival of AI's benefits that we will traverse the period of maximum risk."
Georgieva said the first line of defense is regulation and supervision. "Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries' monetary policy," she said.

articles.title_orig: World Faces Risk Cocktail From AI, Oil and Debt, Says IMF Chief
articles.title_zh: World Faces Risk Cocktail From AI, Oil and Debt, Says IMF Chief
articles.content_orig:
(Bloomberg) -- Global governments must act urgently to address challenges from an unbalanced AI boom, a prolonged energy shock and record debt piles, the International Monetary Fund said as it prepares to host economy chiefs from around the world next week.
Apple to Launch Doorbell, Lock, Thermostat Developed With LG
Deeply Distressed US Loans Rise to Highest Level Since Pandemic, JPMorgan Says
SpaceX in Talks to Borrow $40 Billion to Buy Nvidia Chips
New Hazard for Treasuries Hides in Bond Futures' Fine Print
S&P 500 Climbs to Record High on Earnings Optimism: Markets Wrap
The rush to develop artificial intelligence is delivering a growth spurt that's so far confined to a handful of countries, Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said Wednesday in prepared remarks in Singapore ahead of the annual IMF-World Bank meetings in Bangkok next week.
Meantime the squeeze on key commodity supplies due to conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine is set to continue into 2027, and soaring bond yields have left governments that amassed too much debt under mounting budget pressure, Georgieva said — calling advanced economies the "worst offenders" on the latter count.
"The AI building boom is inflationary. The energy and food shocks are inflationary. Tariffs, defense spending, and high public debt can be inflationary," Georgieva said. She called for a "prudently hawkish bias" on the part of central banks, and said countries that have gotten used to running large budget deficits are in for "some very tough political choices."
The weeklong Bangkok gathering of top finance ministers and central bank governors takes place against a backdrop of turbulence in sovereign debt markets, as yields on US, European and Japanese bonds hit multi-decade highs. Total global debt has now surpassed $365 trillion, according to the Institute of International Finance.
"Policymakers had a relatively easy ride over the last 17 years as for all that time interest rates were stuck below GDP growth rates," Georgieva said. "Higher interest rates now put an end to that."
By contrast, the wave of AI investment — and expectations for the economic gains it will deliver — keeps propeling stocks to new highs, and has delivered record exports for Asia's powerhouse producers of chips and other equipment.
The bond selloff got underway after the US and Israel attacked Iran in February, choking off fuel supplies and raising costs worldwide. Georgieva said the energy shock has been "large but contained" so far. But she warned that "price pressures may build further as demand rises with the approach of the Northern hemisphere cold season and as countries replenish reserves."
The AI buildout is adding to energy demand, and it also risks widening economic inequalities, Georgieva said. "Growth in AI-related trade reflects the investment boom in economies embedded in its value chain," she said, but "it largely bypasses most others."

articles.title_orig: World Clean-up Day 2026: Community action for cleaner and more resilient communities - International Union for Conservation of Nature
articles.title_zh: World Clean-up Day 2026: Community action for cleaner and more resilient communities - International Union for Conservation of Nature
articles.source: International Union for Conservation of Nature
articles.content_orig:
On 19 September 2026, the ReSea Women Influencers, Gizela Lucilia and Onésia Mazelete, joined the ReSea team and community focal points in a clean-up campaign across Vilankulo, Mozambique bringing together community groups, local institutions, civil society organisations and students in a shared commitment to a cleaner environment.
World clean-up day in Vilankulo, Mozambique by ReSea women influencers.
World clean-up day in Vilankulo, Mozambique by ReSea women influencers.
World clean-up day in Vilankulo, Mozambique by ReSea women influencers.
The initiative focused on the Vilankulo Municipal Market and other locations within the municipality, combining practical cleanup activities with environmental awareness on responsible waste management, cleaner public spaces and the importance of community participation in reducing pollution.
This collective effort brought together representatives from the Municipality of Vilankulo, the Associação Juvenil Para o Desenvolvimento Comunitário (AJUPADEC), the Youth Action for Climate Action Mozambique (YACAC-Moz), the Higher School of Rural Development (ESUDER), ParCo, and pupils from local primary and secondary schools. The ReSea team was represented by Gizela Lucilia, Onésia Mazelete, Anselmo Nhanenge and Elcídio Cossa, alongside community focal points Ivanilde and Joalina.
For the ReSea Women Influencers, participation in World Cleanup Day is an important part of their commitment to environmental stewardship and community engagement. Through initiatives such as this, they continue to strengthen their role in environmental awareness, community mobilisation and the protection of coastal communities.
Activities such as World Cleanup Day also reinforce the broader objectives of ReSea, particularly community engagement, environmental stewardship and the protection of coastal communities and ecosystems from pollution.
Cleaner and more resilient communities depend on sustained local action. In Vilankulo, this means bringing communities, institutions and young people together to take shared responsibility for the spaces and ecosystems on which they depend.
The Regenerative Seascapes for People, Climate and Nature (ReSea) Project is a multi-million dollar initiative funded by Global Affairs Canada under the Partnering for Climate engagement. Co-implemented by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and Mission inclusion, the project aims to enhance the physical, social, and economic climate resilience of vulnerable coastal communities, particularly women and youth.

articles.title_orig: Russian Plague Scare: WHO Seeks Details About Reported Second Illness As Trump Plans Putin Call
articles.title_zh: Russian Plague Scare: WHO Seeks Details About Reported Second Illness As Trump Plans Putin Call
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he has a call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss the pneumonic plague , after the death of a female staffer at a Russian anti-plague lab that’s sparked public health fears worldwide.
Asked whether he had spoken with Putin about the matter, Trump told reporters on the White House South Lawn that he had a “call scheduled” and that it would take place “very soon.”
The Russian Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Trump’s remarks.
Trump had told reporters Monday that he was willing to help Russia, calling the pneumonic plague “a rough disease.”
“I hate to see them having it,” Trump said. “Anybody that has that kind of a problem, we’re always willing to help.”
A Russian health watchdog said last week that Darya Shipilova, 28, a staffer at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, had died from a “pneumonia of undetermined” origin.
The watchdog concluded that plague was not found among the staffer’s contacts, saying only that they found two cases of Covid and one of rhinovirus.
A State Department official told NBC News earlier Tuesday that the U.S. had been in contact with the Russian government regarding the incident since as early as Friday, following reports of Shipilova’s death.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that Russia should share more information with the world, but asked the public not to jump to conclusions.
“Maybe, you know, there’s nothing there. Maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know,” Rubio told reporters during a news conference in Iceland. “But I think it would be reckless at this moment, given the limited information we still have, to speculate about what this might or might not be or what this is or what this isn’t.”
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said Tuesday it was aware of and monitoring reports of the death, which it called “a suspected case of pneumonic plague in the Irkutsk region of Russia.”
“At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely,” the CDC wrote on X .
Raquel Coronell Uribe is a politics reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Frankfurt Book Fair 2026: Bertelsmann is the World’s Biggest Book Publisher
articles.title_zh: Frankfurt Book Fair 2026: Bertelsmann is the World’s Biggest Book Publisher
articles.content_orig:
The title of the world’s largest book publisher has changed hands once again, according to data compiled by consultant Rüdiger Wischenbart and the editors from Digital Publishing Report. In the recently released 2025 Global Publishing Ranking, Bertelsmann surpassed the 2024 leader, Thomson Reuters, which slipped to third place. Bertelsmann, the Germany-based owner of Penguin Random House, posted book publishing revenue of $6.98 billion last year, with $5.86 billion coming from PRH. Thomson Reuters’s book revenue rose from $6.24 billion to $6.62 billion, but that wasn’t enough to keep it atop the list.
In second place was RELX, with sales of $6.53 billion. Wolters Kluwer posted a 17% jump in sales to just over $5 billion, moving it into fourth place ahead of Pearson, whose sales increased 7.8% to $4.82 billion.
The scientific publisher Springer Nature (#7) had a solid 2025 with revenue topping $2 billion for the first time thanks to a 18% sales increase over 2024. Japan’s Hitotsubashi Group (#8) stayed in the top 10 thanks in large part to the success of manga publishers Shueisha and Shogakukan.
As noted by Wischenbart, the 10 largest publishers accounted for well over half of all revenue generated by the publishers on the list (56%, up from 55% in 2024). Publishers falling in the 11th to 20th spots accounted for another 20% of revenue.
According to Wischenbart’s analysis, STM and professional publishers accounted for 49% of all revenue of the publishers included in the ranking, while trade publishers generated 32% of sales and educational publishers 19%.
The largest U.S.-based publisher on the list is HarperCollins (#9), which had revenue of $2.15 billion in the fiscal year ended June 30, 2025. McGraw-Hill, another U.S. publisher, was in 10th place, with sales for the fiscal year ended Mar. 31, 2026, holding at $2.10 billion.
The latest ranking does not include Simon & Schuster, because the publisher has not disclosed its revenue since 2023, when it was acquired by the private equity firm KKR. The last reported figure was $1.04 billion, which would put S&S just outside the 20 largest publishers.
Jim Milliot is editor-at-large at Publishers Weekly .

articles.title_orig: Israelis mourn on the anniversary of the Oct. 7 attack as Palestinians live in devastated Gaza
articles.title_zh: Israelis mourn on the anniversary of the Oct. 7 attack as Palestinians live in devastated Gaza
articles.content_orig:
More than one in 10 people from Gaza’s pre-war population has been killed or wounded by Israeli fire since Israel launched its genocidal war against Palestinians in the territory in October 2023.
Nearly every family is now grieving for the dead or caring for the injured, while most residents have been forced to move repeatedly to escape fighting and evacuation orders.
With almost the entire population left homeless, the coastal territory has effectively become one of the world’s largest tent cities. Ramshackle canvas and nylon shelters blanket beaches, cover former agricultural lands and fill vacant lots.
Little is likely to change soon. A 2025 “ceasefire” deal halted large-scale offensives and the heaviest bombardment, but Israel still regularly strikes tents, cars and buildings in attacks that frequently kill women, children and other relatives.
People no longer have to flee from place to place, but few can rebuild because Israel continues to bar most construction materials from entering Gaza.
The “ceasefire” agreement’s plan for large-scale reconstruction has stalled, as Israel and Hamas have yet to reach an agreement on disarming the group and the withdrawal of Israeli forces.

articles.title_orig: U.S. News & World Report Partners with Candid to Bring Agentic AI Survey Innovation to Senior Living
articles.title_zh: U.S. News & World Report Partners with Candid to Bring Agentic AI Survey Innovation to Senior Living
articles.content_orig:
Strategic partnership modernizes how senior living operators capture real-time resident and family feedback.
WASHINGTON , Oct. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- U.S. News & World Report, the global authority in healthcare decision support, today announced a strategic partnership with and investment in Candid, an AI-powered engagement start-up serving senior living and post-acute care organizations, to modernize feedback collection and advance resident engagement and quality measurement standards across the senior living industry.
Through the partnership, U.S. News and Candid equip senior living communities to move beyond traditional static questionnaires through AI-powered, conversational engagement tools. The integration expands the tools available to operators to capture real-time insights from residents and their families, turning direct resident and family input into measurable quality improvements.
This collaboration comes at a pivotal time for the senior care sector. With 10,000 Americans reaching retirement age daily – known as "The Peak 65 Phenomenon" – the need for transparent, reliable data to guide family care decisions and evaluate community performance continues to grow. Building on U.S. News' 2026 Best Senior Living ratings , which evaluated communities based on feedback from more than 540,000 consumer surveys, U.S. News continues to lead efforts to standardize resident engagement measures and bring modern, data-driven capabilities to senior living operators and care providers.
"For five years, U.S. News' Best Senior Living ratings have provided families with trusted data and benchmarks as they evaluate their senior living options," said Sumita Singh, executive vice president and general manager of Health at U.S. News. "As millions of older adults enter retirement, improving how senior living communities capture resident and family feedback is a must. Our strategic partnership with Candid reflects our commitment to bringing frictionless technologies to senior living operators so they can gather real-time resident and family feedback across all modalities."
Candid's platform uses interactive voice and text conversations that allow residents, family members and employees to provide feedback in their own words. The platform combines quantitative metrics with qualitative sentiment analysis, identifying recurring themes, emerging operational concerns and trends.
Across current deployments – which span hundreds of senior living communities nationwide – Candid's conversational format averages an approximate 70 percent response rate, drastically outperforming traditional survey channels.
"Senior living organizations have historically had to choose between collecting structured data at scale and having meaningful conversations with residents, families, and employees," said Raphael Rubens, founder and CEO of Candid. "AI allows us to combine both, understand what is driving the feedback and turn those insights into action, ultimately improving the experience and quality of care for residents."
About U.S. News & World Report U.S. News & World Report is the global leader for journalism that empowers consumers, citizens, business leaders and policy officials to make confident decisions in all aspects of their lives and communities. A multifaceted media company, U.S. News provides unbiased rankings, independent reporting and analysis, and consumer advice to millions of people on USNews.com each month. A pillar in Washington for more than 90 years, U.S. News is the trusted home for in-depth and exclusive insights on education, health, politics, the economy, insurance, personal finance, travel, automobiles, real estate, careers and consumer products and services.
About Candid Candid Technology, Inc. ("Candid") is an AI powered engagement platform for senior living and post acute care. Its technology helps organizations collect resident, family, and employee feedback, improve online reputation, understand retention, and automate frontline applicant engagement and interviews. Candid has been deployed across hundreds of communities throughout the United States and is backed by leading investors. For more information, visit callcandid.com .

articles.title_orig: France’s student protests highlight a debt crisis that could spill over to the rest of Europe
articles.title_zh: France’s student protests highlight a debt crisis that could spill over to the rest of Europe
articles.content_orig:
France’s unprecedented wave of student protests has laid bare the country’s growing financial pressures, which will only become more difficult to tackle as Europe’s second-largest economy tries to rein in a ballooning budget deficit.
The country’s finances are in a precarious state. Public debt was more than $4 trillion in June, exceeding the size of the economy, according to the country’s statistics agency . The cost of servicing that debt has climbed by billions of dollars on last year, as bond yields spike .
At the same time, demands on the public purse are rising: Pension costs have climbed because of an aging population while the government looks to spend more on defense.
High school students, meanwhile, have called for a fix to staff shortages, overcrowded classrooms and crumbling school infrastructure.
Solutions to France’s financial troubles have led to social unrest in the past. Efforts to raise the retirement age sparked widespread protests in 2023 .
French school protests grow as workers join students
Last week, the French government proposed deep spending cuts and tax hikes aimed at narrowing the budget deficit, but bond buyers are concerned that fiscal measures may be watered down by lawmakers ahead of presidential elections next year, said Andrew Kenningham, chief European economist at consultancy Capital Economics.
The election could see President Emmanuel Macron ousted by either a far-right or far-left successor, raising questions over the country’s commitment to fiscal discipline. While Marine Le Pen’s right-wing National Rally recently proposed substantial spending cuts meant to stabilize the public finances, her party also remains committed to costly tax reductions, Kenningham said.
“Investors will also be concerned about greater fiscal populism after the elections,” he wrote in a note last week. “There is a big risk that spreads rise a lot further, either before or after next year’s elections.”
Worries about a potential debt crisis in France boiled over last week, leading to a selloff in French bonds and a sharp rise in yields.
The spread between French and German bond yields expanded to its widest level since 2012. That difference in yields means investors are demanding much higher returns to hold debt from France compared with Germany, which is deemed a safer alternative.
The French bond rout has sparked fears of spillovers to other high-yield European debt markets, with some analysts drawing parallels with the eurozone debt crisis of the early 2010s .
Global bond sell-off deepens, sending borrowing costs higher around the world
Given France’s size and systemic importance, “the potential for contagion into other countries and the Eurozone at large is very large and could potentially cause a serious crisis for the entire region,” Angel Talavera, chief European economist at Oxford Economics, an advisory firm, told CNN.
These worries in large part pushed the euro to its weakest level against the dollar since May 2025 on Monday. The currency, shared by 21 countries in the European Union, is worth around $1.12, having briefly dipped below that level.
The latest ructions in markets could weigh on a fragile economic recovery in Europe, bolstered by investment into artificial intelligence, stronger demand for European exports and higher defense spending in Germany.
Recent survey data showed that activity in manufacturing and services in the euro area increased at its fastest pace in nearly three-and-a-half years last month.
“(Economic) growth is staging a comeback and Europe has shown surprising resilience,” economists at Morgan Stanley wrote in a late September note.
Fall of yet another premier will make it hard for France to fix its finances. What’s behind its debt problem?
High bond yields are a clear risk to that growth, however.
If governments don’t cut spending , “interest rates will continue to go up,” Carsten Brzeski, head of macroeconomics at Dutch bank ING told CNN.
Higher bond yields push up the cost of borrowing throughout the economy, making home and car purchases more expensive and driving down investment. They also make it more expensive for governments to borrow money and force a certain degree of austerity to stop yields from rising further.
Yields on French, German and UK government bonds have broken multi-year records in recent weeks as concerns mount about the sustainability of public debt loads.
Europe’s public finances pose “serious risks to eurozone financial markets and to the economy,” Jack Allen-Reynolds, deputy chief eurozone economist at Capital Economics, told CNN.

articles.title_orig: Doja Cat’s ‘Tour Ma Vie World Tour’ tests her performer bona fides
articles.title_zh: Doja Cat’s ‘Tour Ma Vie World Tour’ tests her performer bona fides
articles.content_orig:
When an artist abandons the standard fanfare and extravagance of an arena tour, their true performance ability is put to the test. Doja Cat’s “Tour Ma Vie World Tour” demonstrated her showmanship needs no hefty entourage of backup dancers, elaborate sets or choreography.
The tour, which hit Chicago’s United Center on Oct. 3, traverses the R&B artist’s ’80s-infused 2025 album “Vie,” while incorporating older hits like “Need to Know” and “Say So.” Apart from a handful of male backup dancers and occasional pyrotechnics, her tour is largely an understated affair as she commands the audience’s attention almost entirely on her own.
Opening with a hearty brass interlude, Doja Cat began the evening with “Cards,” the first track on “Vie.” Her performance evoked sartorial themes of the ’80s, as she donned pink geometric yoga pants and a bright orange cheetah-patterned coat. Vibrant lighting punctuated the disco-heavy setlist as Doja Cat ventured further into the album, which combines dance-pop and disco.
Her newest album and its accompanying tour are quite a departure for Doja Cat, whose earlier discography is primarily contemporary R&B and rap.
While the show’s runtime focused heavily on “Vie,” Doja Cat gained substantial mileage from older hits like “Need to Know” from her 2021 album “Planet Her” and “Streets” from her 2019 album “Hot Pink,” a testament to her artistic depth.
The concert presents Doja Cat at her most comfortable, highlighting the signature unseriousness that makes her such a compelling performer. At one point, she playfully lit a cigarette before jumping back into song. Later on, she pied an audience member in the face during a tongue-in-cheek interactive skit.
Though there were scattered moments of grandeur, Doja Cat was at her best when she was alone onstage, commanding the audience without flashy costume changes or theatrical gimmicks.
The most memorable track from the evening was unequivocally “Paint The Town Red,” a hit from her 2023 album “Scarlet.” Unaccompanied by background vocals, Doja Cat exerted a larger-than-life stage presence throughout the track, eliciting deafening cheers from the audience.
True to form, Doja Cat concluded the concert on a high note, launching a pyrotechnics show to close out the night and putting her band centerstage for an epic guitar solo. Bouncing between fan favorites like “Tia Tamera” and new songs like “Stranger,” the artist underscored her thematic versatility as a performer.
Though her performance was notably unostentatious, Doja Cat’s “Tour Ma Vie World Tour” proves she is a born performer. With a refined yet metamorphic style, Doja Cat demonstrated she can be as dynamic as she is iconic.

articles.title_orig: EU negotiators head to China hoping to curb cheap imports of hybrid electric cars
articles.title_zh: EU negotiators head to China hoping to curb cheap imports of hybrid electric cars
articles.content_orig:
Mood in trade talks said to have changed as EU member states harden demands for protection against Chinese imports
EU trade negotiators are heading to China for two days of crunch talks aimed at sealing a breakthrough deal tackling Beijing’s record £1bn-a-day trade surplus by curbing its exports of cheap hybrid electric cars into Europe .
Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his team fly out on Wednesday and will be negotiating up to the wire in talks scheduled to start the following day and continue late into Friday.
Sources say they hope to achieve “tangible, meaningful and measurable” results before the meeting of EU leaders in Brussels on Thursday next week, where China is high on the agenda.
The main focus is on what has been described as a “proof of concept” pilot agreement involving one sector, which is expected to be cars, which could be scaled up for other sectors in the coming months.
Diplomatic efforts to avert a full-scale trade war started at the end of June, albeit with little hope that China could curb exports to the EU given its historic ability to pivot quickly any time trade barriers are put in its path. For example, after the EU imposed tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in October 2024 there was a boom in exports of hybrid cars , which were not subject to tariffs.
Last month, the EU asked China to voluntarily restrict hybrid exports to address soaring sales, warning that if they did not restrict them, safeguards – which could include quotas – could be enacted.
It is not known what China’s response was. But sources say the mood in talks has changed as EU member states have hardened demands for protection against Chinese imports that threaten their own industries.
On Monday, Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, agreed a “historic U-turn” on its policy on China by siding with the French president, Emmanuel Macron, in authorising effective permission for EU leaders to approve a new instrument to allow them to defend trade by cutting access to the single market at short notice.
In a joint paper with Emmanuel Macron, the two countries spoke of “a massive industrial shock … affecting sectors at the heart of the European industrial model and of systemic relevance [pharmaceuticals, aerospace, automotive, machine tools, chemicals, etc.]”.
The paper called for the use of all existing trade defence tools, but also for a new diversification instrument and “possible additional” new measures to allow the bloc to react when “third countries seek to undermine the restoration of a level playing field”.
Andrew Small, a former EU adviser on China, said Šefčovič’s talks will test the resolve of both Beijing and Brussels and will “determine whether China is willing to put sufficiently serious offers on the table”.
Small, who is the Asia director at the European Council on Foreign Relations in Berlin, warned: “China’s most effective tactic may be to draw Europe into a ‘process trap’ offering just enough to delay action, without addressing the forces driving European deindustrialisation.”
after newsletter promotion
Sources say the Franco-German proposals for a new instrument, dubbed a “kill switch”, were born out of frustration, particularly in Paris, that a so-called “trade bazooka” available to Brussels, officially known as the anti-coercion instrument, has never been used.
Paris pushed for the use of the ACI following Trump’s threat of tariffs last year but it never gained traction from others as it could take up to a year to implement.
Handlesblatt, the Germany business newspaper, described Monday’s change in policy as “nothing less than an economic turning point”, with chief political reporter Martin Greive concluding in a hard-hitting column that Merz was “putting an end to years of naiveté towards Beijing”.
“Merz has recognised in recent months that Germany is the epicentre of the China shock 2.0; that there might not be much left of German industry if Germany continues to stand by and watch as China gains enormous export advantages through trillions in subsidies, the unilateral siphoning off of knowhow, and a – to put it mildly – questionable monetary policy,” he wrote.
