articles.title_orig: Dow Jones Futures: S&P 500 Hits High As Astera, GE Vernova, Arista Lead Buys, But These Stocks Tumble
articles.title_zh: Dow Jones Futures: S&P 500 Hits High As Astera, GE Vernova, Arista Lead Buys, But These Stocks Tumble
articles.content_orig:
The United States stock market has hit an all-time high as excitement around artificial intelligence continues to fuel a buying frenzy on Wall Street.
The S&P 500, the benchmark stock index, closed 0.58 percent higher on Tuesday, topping the previous peak reached in mid-August.
The Nasdaq Composite, which is more heavily weighted towards tech stocks, also hit a record high, finishing up 0.45 percent.
Tech stocks were among the top performers, with each of the “Magnificent Seven” apart from Meta closing higher.
Amazon led the pack with a 1.95 percent gain, followed by Microsoft and Tesla, which rose 0.78 percent and 0.51 percent, respectively.
Apple and Alphabet both rose 0.22 percent, while Nvidia gained 0.14 percent.
Meta, which has risen more than 20 percent since the launch last month of its new AI assistant, Muse, fell 0.41 percent.
Other big movers in tech included Marvell Technology, which rose 5.81 percent, and Cisco, which gained 4.54 percent.
Keith Lerner, chief investment officer and chief market strategist at Truist Advisory Services in Atlanta, Georgia, said the market rally should be seen as a “technology and AI surge”.
“Every bull market has a dominant theme, and technology and AI remain this market’s dominant theme,” Lerner told Al Jazeera.
“Technology and communication services were the only two S&P 500 sectors to rise last month, while the other nine declined.”
Wall Street has shrugged off a host of challenges facing the US economy amid hyperscalers’ multibillion-dollar investments in AI.
Despite the energy crunch caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran and a sell-off of US government bonds partly driven by ballooning government debt, the market is well on track to record its fourth consecutive year of double-digit returns.
The S&P 500 has risen 14 percent so far in 2026, while the Nasdaq Composite is up 18.78 percent.
“Investors remain bullish on the prospects for AI,” Lochlan Halloway, a senior equity strategist at Morningstar Australia, told Al Jazeera.
“They are betting that the money pouring into data centres will earn a good return, and so far that belief has outweighed rising interest rates, more expensive oil and a 10-year bond yield above 5 percent,” Halloway said.
“We are positive on AI too,” Halloway added. “But the range of outcomes is wide, and the market is concentrated in a handful of companies, so the outlook for US shares, and by extension global shares, relies on the AI story continuing to deliver.”
Lerner at Truist Advisory said the market rally had the potential to continue through the end of 2026 given historical trends and expectations for strong corporate earnings.
“We do not expect a straight line higher for markets,” Lerner said.
“Still, the fourth quarter of midterm-election years has produced an average gain of 7 percent and has been positive 84 percent of the time since 1950.”
Lerner said that rising interest rates posed the biggest risk to the upward trend.
“Still, on balance, the weight of the evidence suggests this bull market still has more upside potential,” he said.
Asian stock markets fell on Wednesday, with key indexes in Japan, South Korea and Hong Kong slumping in morning trading.
The Nikkei 225 in Tokyo, Kospi in Seoul and Hang Seng Index in Hong Kong were down 0.79 percent, 1.36 percent and 0.71 percent, respectively, as of 02:30 GMT.
Oil prices, which have been elevated since the start of the war on Iran, rose on Wednesday as traders weighed the fallout of fighting between forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Iran-aligned Houthis.
Brent crude futures for December delivery stood at $101.45 a barrel as of 02:30 GMT, up 0.87 percent.

articles.title_orig: Nobel physics prize awarded for detection of cosmic neutrinos
articles.title_zh: Nobel physics prize awarded for detection of cosmic neutrinos
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain
            the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
            Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
            and JavaScript.
Francis Halzen received the Nobel Prize in Physics on 6 October for his contributions to neutrino physics. Credit: Althea Dotzour/University of Wisconsin–Madison
Belgian-born physicist Francis Halzen has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on detecting high-energy elusive particles called neutrinos that come from deep space.
The most unusual portrait of the Milky Way yet: mapping the Galaxy with neutrinos
The most unusual portrait of the Milky Way yet: mapping the Galaxy with neutrinos
His pioneering contribution is the founding of a giant detector, the IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the South Pole. Its results have helped to found the fields of neutrino and multimessenger astronomy, which enable physicists to unlock the mysteries of the Universe through observing highly energetic events from deep in the cosmos.
Halzen, who is based at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, takes home the prize of 12 million Swedish kronor (US$1.2 million), announced by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm on 6 October. It is the first time since 1992 that the the physics prize has been awarded to only one winner.
“It was a great surprise and I obviously didn’t expect it,” said Halzen, speaking to the Nobel press conference after the prize was announced. “This reflects on the really courageous people who joined me in this project when really no respectable conservative physicist would have joined me, but many talented people did and that’s why I’m here.”
Medicine Nobel awarded for brain ‘switch’ that controls neurons with light
Medicine Nobel awarded for brain ‘switch’ that controls neurons with light
Neutrinos are the second most common particle in the Universe, after photons. More than one billion neutrinos pass through a human hand every second, but high-energy neutrinos are extremely rare and hard to detect. IceCube was designed to study the particles after they fly out of some of the most energetic environments in the Universe, such as supernovae and γ-ray bursts. Because neutrinos pass straight through matter, they allow researchers to draw a straight line back to these events, providing them with a unique way of probing astrophysical phenomena.
Halzen is “a father figure for neutrino astronomy”, says Paschal Coyle, a neutrino physicist at Aix-Marseille University in France and the former spokesperson of KM3NeT, a similarly large observatory being built in the Mediterranean Sea.
The IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the South Pole was Nobel prizewinner’s Francis Halzen’s brainchild Credit: Ilya Bodo, IceCube/NSF
Despite being all around us, neutrinos are fiendishly difficult to detect because they are unaffected by magnetic fields and rarely ever interact with matter. In the 1980s, Halzen had the idea to use detectors attached to strings, lowered more than 1.5 kilometres into holes drilled into the clear ice of the Antarctic — which is free from many types of interference — to detect the rare and faint flashes of light when a fast-moving neutrino hits an atom.
As long as the volume of the set-up was big enough, Halzen theorized that it could catch neutrinos and their path would reveal the direction from which they come, allowing researchers to trace their origins in the cosmos (see ‘Neutrino observatory’).
The IceCube Neutrino Observatory — an array of 5,160 sensors — was completed in 2010 at a cost of US$271 million, mainly funded by the US National Science Foundation. It now involves a collaboration of about 450 researchers. “After one and a half decades of development, and another decade of construction, there was no guarantee we would ever see anything,” Halzen, principal investigator of IceCube, told APS News last year. “Many people thought we wouldn’t, but we did.”
Within two years, the detector had observed energetic neutrinos from beyond the Milky Way. In 2013, the IceCube collaboration published a result 1 showing that there was a population of neutrinos with energies so high that they could not have been produced anywhere in the Solar System. The finding helped to establish the new field of neutrino astronomy.
“The biggest risk we took is that nobody knew if the kilometre cube detector was actually large enough to detect neutrinos beyond our atmosphere from the Universe,” Halzen told the Nobel press conference. “But it only took two years to detect that.” .
“We found evidence for neutrinos coming from supermassive black holes in other galaxies, and they shine so strongly that when you look at a neutrino sky you don’t see the Milky Way.”
In 2013 and 2014, IceCube discovered three neutrinos with energies that blew all others out of the water. Nicknamed Bert, Ernie and Big Bird , they had energy levels measured in petaelectronvolts (a quadrillion electronvolts), thousands of times more energetic than those produced in Earth’s most advanced particle colliders. And three years later, the collaboration made a long-awaited discovery of a high-energy neutrino that they could for the first time trace back to a specific source — a distant galaxy, called TXS 0506+056, often referred to as ‘the Texas event’.
IceCube detectors are sunk deep into Antarctica’s ice — which is free from many types of interference — to catch neutrinos at high energies. Credit: Yuya Makino, IceCube/NSF
Follow-up observations suggested that the source was a blazar, a violent galaxy with a variable brightness that harbours a supermassive black hole at its core. Seven studies from a suite of telescopes viewing the blazar using various methods described the galaxy in 2018.
Halzen was born in Tienen, Belgium, in 1944 and studied at the nation’s University of Louvain in Louvain-la-Neuve. He trained as a particle physicist, working at CERN, Europe’s particle-physics laboratory near Geneva, Switzerland, before moving to Wisconsin in 1971.
As the principal investigator for IceCube from its original proposal in 1999, Halzen was the project’s “undisputed” driving force, says IceCube senior member Elisa Resconi, an astroparticle physicist at the Technical University of Munich in Germany. She says that Halzen deserves credit for having pushed for an experimental concept that many researchers initially saw as “the weirdest in the world”. The logistical challenges of building a large-scale facility not just in Antarctica, but at the South Pole, were enormous.
Francis Halzen, a pioneer in neutrino physics, is announced as the winner of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics. Credit: Christine OLSSON/TT NEWS AGENCY/AFP via Getty
“He has such a charisma that when he enters a room, everyone turns around,” Resconi says. He also takes special effort to cultivate talent — and can usually remember the names and academic histories of each member of the collaboration.

China’s Xiongan New Area is accelerating its hunt for technology firms as the city, designed partly to house state-owned institutions relocated from Beijing, moves to nurture its own industries, according to people familiar with its plans and local officials.
Officials were looking to attract tech companies that could reach valuations of 10 billion yuan (US$1.4 billion), hoping some would list on stock markets, including Hong Kong’s, in the next few years, sources said, adding that the key sectors would span artificial intelligence, satellite internet and robotics.

articles.title_orig: Are Chinese foreign agent busts on the rise? Federal officials make another arrest
articles.title_zh: Are Chinese foreign agent busts on the rise? Federal officials make another arrest
articles.content_orig:
by GEOFF HARRIS | The National News Desk
WASHINGTON (TNND)  — A woman accused of acting as an agent of China appeared in federal court in Los Angeles this week after prosecutors said she conducted surveillance last year near Seattle targeting the son of Taiwan’s president.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli said Wanying Zhang was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport.
According to an affidavit, Zhang acted at the direction and control of People’s Republic of China officials to conduct surveillance on family members of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official at their residence in the United States.
The case is the latest in a string of similar arrests pursued by federal officials. Research shows that under the current administration, there have been 60 PRC-related counterintelligence arrests, an 88% increase compared to prior periods.
Among other recent cases, Greg Lui, who was arrested earlier this month for allegedly orchestrating a $300 million illegal AI hardware smuggling ring to China. Plus, Eileen Wang, the former Arcadia, California, mayor, who pleaded guilty this past summer to a federal charge of acting as an unregistered foreign agent for the People’s Republic of China.
After Zhang’s arrest, FBI Director Kash Patel also posted a warning on social media. Writing, “Foreign adversaries take note: America is not your playground.”
When asked whether the number of such cases is likely to rise, Essayli said, “It probably will. And that’s a testament to this administration, the Trump administration and the attorney general, you know, prioritizing the resources of the department.”

articles.title_orig: Yemen’s Houthi Rebels Strike Two Airports in Saudi Arabia
articles.title_zh: Yemen’s Houthi Rebels Strike Two Airports in Saudi Arabia
articles.content_orig:
CAIRO — Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen on Wednesday claimed attacks on military facilities and airports in neighboring Saudi Arabia as the escalation deepened the latest front in the Iran war and threatened a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz .
The Houthis’ military spokesperson, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, said on social media that the rebels launched ballistic missiles and drones in the attacks targeting King Khalid International Airport in the capital, Riyadh, but did not provide evidence.
Flights to and from the airport were briefly disrupted, according to Flightradar24, a tracking platform.
Saree said Abha airport, a frequent target of Houthi drones and missiles, was targeted. The rebels also claimed to have hit an air base in the city of Khamis Mushait and two military bases, Najran and Asir. All are in southwestern Saudi Arabia and near the border with Yemen.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, said they intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile north of Riyadh.
Saudi Arabia and allied Yemeni forces in recent days have launched a major ground and air offensive against the Houthis in an attempt to retake territory that the rebels seized about a month ago along Yemen’s western Red Sea coast and on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait . Those positions gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping as they pursue a blockade of Saudi vessels.
On Monday, officials said forces of the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen recaptured several key areas around the strait.
The fighting has since then centered in and around the crucial town of Dhubab, some 30 miles south of the port city of Mokha, according to both the Houthis and the Yemeni government.
Clashes were also reported in the district of Waziayah in southwestern Taiz province, which links Yemen’s mountainous highlands to the Red Sea, and overlooks roads to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Houthi officials accuse Yemen of deadly market strike
The Houthis also said they launched a missile strike early Wednesday against Yemen’s port city of Aden, the seat of the internationally recognized government. An Associated Press journalist heard explosions around 2 a.m. (7 p.m. Tuesday ET).
The rebels hit a military camp close to the Aden airport with ballistic missiles, Saree said.
Security authorities in Aden said the Houthis targeted the airport with two missiles, with no casualties. The airport is close to the seat of government.
“The targeting of this vital civilian facility represents a direct threat to the safety of civilians, passengers, employees and flight crews,” the Aden police said in a statement.
The attack on the Aden airport threatened “a humanitarian disaster,” as one missile hit close to the runway just before the scheduled landing of a flight from Cairo, the Human Rights Ministry said.
Flight 603, operated by Yemen’s flagship airline, landed safely in Aden at 3:30 a.m., according to flight tracking platform FlightAware.
The ministry said the missile hit as other passengers were waiting to board their flight to the Saudi coastal city of Jeddah.
“The Houthis believe that they can maximize Saudi economic costs and compel Saudi Arabia to surrender to Houthi demands by striking civilian infrastructure, such as oil facilities and airports,” the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, wrote in an analysis .

articles.title_orig: Georgia governor candidates spar over the economy and Trump in lone debate
articles.title_zh: Georgia governor candidates spar over the economy and Trump in lone debate
articles.content_orig:
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms and Republican Rick Jackson clashed Tuesday night during their only scheduled debate of this fall’s race for governor in Georgia, taking aim at each other on economic issues, data centers and President Donald Trump.
Public polls show Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta and a former Biden administration official, and Jackson, a billionaire healthcare executive, locked in a close race four weeks out from Election Day, with early voting kicking off next week.
The hourlong, town-hall-style debate was largely civil, featuring live and taped questions from voters. Jackson frequently ripped his opponent over her record as mayor, while Bottoms attacked his praise of Trump.
“My opponent has said he wants to be Trump’s favorite governor. He wants to be Trump with a Southern tone. He said there’s not a single policy that he disagrees with Trump on,” Bottoms said in response to a question about the Trump administration’s cuts to federal funding.
“I will stand up to Donald Trump when necessary. I’m not running to be his favorite governor,” she continued.
Jackson responded, “I don’t owe anybody anything,” and said, “Nobody’s ever told me what to do.”
He then invoked Brian Kemp, Georgia’s popular, term-limited governor — the first of multiple times he did so.
“I will stand up to anybody, just like Brian Kemp has done. He works with both parties, both presidents, and he stands up when he disagrees,” Jackson said.
Trump endorsed Jackson’s rival, Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, during the Republican gubernatorial primary. But Jackson still attempted to claim the MAGA mantle and leaned heavily into comparing himself to the president. Since winning the nomination in June, he’s backed off that approach and sought to link himself more to Kemp, who had also backed Jones.
Jackson took several shots at Bottoms over her tenure as mayor, accusing her of being responsible for regional inflation in the Atlanta area that he claimed exceeded national inflation rates and pointing to higher crime rates in the city during the Covid-19 pandemic.
“This is the kind of policy that we cannot have in running Georgia, not having people feeling safe to go to work,” Jackson said. “Bad mayors don’t make good governors.”
While the candidates were asked about housing and education, the event focused predominantly on economic issues and affordability, with both candidates repeatedly pressed about how they’d bring down costs. Both focused heavily on tax relief.
Bottoms emphasized her proposals to cut or suspend state or local taxes on a raft of items, like auto insurance, groceries, hygiene products and diapers. Jackson reiterated his promise to cut state income taxes, property taxes and taxes on certain utilities.
Data centers and the controversial surveillance traffic cameras known as Flock cameras also took center stage.
On data centers, Bottoms repeated her desire to implement a pause on new construction. Jackson said he wouldn’t approve new construction as governor without first getting local community approval, establishing environmental standards and getting a commitment that local communities’ power bills would be reduced.
But the two sparred over the issue, as well, with Bottoms accusing Jackson of investing in data centers and Jackson accusing her of having approved building them as mayor.
Bottoms also said she wasn’t opposed to a moratorium on installing new Flock cameras, while Jackson said he was.
The issue of election security — which has hung over Georgia politics for six years — also came up.
Bottoms said she was “deeply concerned about Donald Trump’s rhetoric around our elections.”
Jackson, however, when he was asked whether he thought the U.S. Justice Department should be “overseeing and getting involved” in the state’s elections, deferred to Kemp again.
“I don’t think that’s necessary unless Gov. Kemp thinks it’s necessary,” he said.
Jackson has flooded the airwaves with ads, using tens of millions of dollars of his own money to outspend Bottoms 7-to-1 as of last week .
That disparity has worried many Democrats , who’ve seen this year as a prime opportunity to flip the governorship blue for the first time in 16 years.
Aiding Bottoms is the broader political environment in Georgia and nationally: Trump faces negative approval ratings and voter concerns about his administration’s handling of the economy.
I cover state legislatures, politics and policy — and how those topics coalesce into and intersect with national political trends. Given what state lawmakers have focused on in recent years, my coverage areas tend to veer into reproductive rights, voting rights and education policy. I was born and raised in Milwaukee, and I try to make my native state proud by covering as many of its fascinating political stories as I can.

articles.title_orig: US military will execute Fort Hood shooter by firing squad, a first in 60 years
articles.title_zh: US military will execute Fort Hood shooter by firing squad, a first in 60 years
articles.content_orig:
An undated handout image of Hasan that was released by authorities in 2012
The Pentagon has announced it will execute a former US Army major by firing squad, the first military execution in more than 60 years.
Nidal Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, injuring another 32.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced on social media on Monday that US defence secretary Pete Hegseth had made the recommendation and President Donald Trump approved it.
The execution is scheduled to take place at Fort Hood in Texas on 3 December, the secretary of the US Army said on Tuesday. It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two.
"Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," Parnell wrote on X.
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, killed 13 soldiers at the base in Texas in 2009 and later admitted in court he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes".
He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.
The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.
The attack took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.
Watch: Why is America running out of execution drugs? , external
Hasan is currently one of four inmates on the US military's death row.
A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law.
It also requires appellate review and a final judgment on its legality to move forward.
The US Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces deemed the military death penalty unconstitutional in 1983 but it was reinstated the following year by an executive order under then-President Ronald Reagan.
Military executions differ from those carried out at the state level.
The majority of executions in the US are carried out on the state level, with 27 states, the military and the federal government still having capital punishment as a legally available option.
Death by firing squad is rather uncommon. There was an execution by firing squad carried out last year in South Carolina, a first for the state and the first time the method was used in the US in 15 years.
Four other states allow the use of a firing squad, including Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma and Utah.
How widely used is the death penalty in the US?
Trump has been a proponent of the federal death penalty and re-instated it through an executive order on the first day of his administration in January 2025.
Under his predecessor, former President Joe Biden, the justice department had issued a moratorium on the federal use of the death penalty.
The executive order signed by Trump describes capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".

articles.title_orig: Calm Down, China and America Are Not Destined for War
articles.title_zh: Calm Down, China and America Are Not Destined for War
articles.content_orig:
For much of the past decade, debate about China and the United States has been shadowed by a familiar warning: when a rising power challenges an established one, war becomes more likely. The “Thucydides Trap,” popularized by the political scientist Graham Allison, has supplied a compelling framework for interpreting their rivalry. In public discussion, however, a warning about the dangers of power transitions too often hardens into a prediction that conflict is unavoidable.
That distinction matters. Allison himself does not regard war as inevitable. Yet the fatalistic version of his argument has become so pervasive that almost every trade dispute, technological restriction, or diplomatic confrontation can be presented as another step toward a collision. Such a reading leaves too little room for political judgment, negotiated compromises, or the possibility that leaders can recognize the costs of escalation and act accordingly.
My assessment, informed by exchanges with strategic scholars, business leaders, and participants in unofficial Chinese-American dialogues, is more guardedly hopeful. Despite their differences, leaders in Beijing and Washington retain powerful reasons to manage competition. Their diplomatic contacts suggest that both governments understand the dangers of allowing individual disputes to determine the entire relationship. Neither has to abandon its interests to recognize that an uncontrolled confrontation would threaten them.
China’s growing ability to shape that relationship is also changing its dynamics. Meanwhile, two features of American politics deserve closer attention: domestic division complicates the construction of a durable China strategy, and some economic disputes with Beijing resemble the quarrels Washington routinely has with its allies. Neither observation eliminates the risks of rivalry. Both challenge the assumption that every disagreement signals an approaching war.
The balance of power provides a useful starting point. Measured at market exchange rates, the American economy remains substantially larger than China’s. Purchasing power parity, which adjusts for differences in domestic prices, produces a different ranking, placing China first. These measures capture different aspects of economic strength. Neither, taken alone, can tell us how effectively a country will translate its resources into technological leadership, military capability, or diplomatic influence.
China’s industrial scale is harder to dispute. Its manufacturing value added reached approximately 34.7 trillion yuan in 2025, and, according to China’s National Bureau of Statistics, it has ranked first globally for 16 consecutive years. The breadth of that industrial base gives Beijing capabilities that the United States would struggle to reproduce quickly. Research and development spending reached roughly 3.9 trillion yuan in 2025, reflecting the resources China is committing to technological advancement.
The country has built substantial capacity in solar manufacturing, electric vehicles, and robotics, alongside a growing presence in artificial intelligence research and patenting. These strengths do not establish superiority in every technology. They do, however, make it increasingly difficult to imagine a strategy that permanently excludes China from the industries likely to shape future economic growth. Industrial capacity is a source of bargaining power as well as national income.
The United States retains formidable advantages of its own. The dollar’s international role, deep financial markets, leading research institutions, extensive alliances, and capacity to project military power all give Washington considerable influence. Those assets will not disappear simply because China continues to grow. The relationship is therefore better understood as an uneven distribution of strengths than as a straightforward reversal in which one country replaces the other across every measure of power.
In my view, this balance creates an opening for strategic stabilization. Washington has limited ability to halt China’s development, while Beijing has strong reasons to avoid a confrontation that would endanger its own economic gains. China’s ambitions need not require the dismantling of every American advantage. Both governments can defend their interests while accepting that an effort to impose comprehensive defeat on the other would carry enormous costs.
American domestic politics complicates this calculation. Analysts sometimes treat congressional hawkishness, campaign rhetoric, and executive policy as expressions of a single, coherent strategy. In practice, partisan polarization, disputes between Congress and the presidency, and tensions between federal and state priorities can pull policy in different directions. Elections can change the instruments of foreign policy even when the underlying concern about China persists.
That distinction is essential. There is considerable continuity in American suspicion of Beijing, but agreement about a rival does not automatically produce agreement about how to compete with it. Tariffs, industrial subsidies, export controls, alliance commitments, and diplomatic engagement impose different costs on different constituencies. A strategy that appears unified at the level of political rhetoric can become far less coherent when officials must allocate resources or sustain it across administrations.
Domestic pressures further constrain Washington’s choices. Social division, the erosion of manufacturing in some communities, and inequality absorb political attention and public resources. Taking a hard line on China can be an effective campaign message without resolving any of those problems. Analysts who assume that rhetoric translates smoothly into a sustained grand strategy risk overstating the consistency of American power and understating the difficulty of mobilizing it.
The nature of bilateral friction also deserves a more discriminating assessment. Disputes over trade, technology, and diplomacy are likely to remain ordinary features of Chinese-American relations. But economic disagreement does not, by itself, distinguish this relationship from all others. The United States regularly clashes with partners whose security and prosperity are closely bound to its own, sometimes with strikingly hostile public language.
Washington and European governments have argued over digital taxes, subsidies, steel tariffs, and market access. Canada and the United States have repeatedly disputed softwood lumber and border policy. Japan has faced American pressure over agricultural access and the costs of hosting U.S. forces. These quarrels can inflict serious economic damage while remaining within a broader relationship that both sides wish to preserve.
There are obvious limits to the comparison. Disagreements between allies do not carry the same strategic implications as disputes between nuclear-armed competitors. Nevertheless, their existence should caution against treating every commercial confrontation with China as evidence that war is drawing closer. The question is how governments manage conflicting interests and whether they have credible mechanisms for preventing a dispute in one area from overwhelming cooperation in another.
In the dialogues I have attended, I have encountered substantial support for that approach. Scholars and business leaders recognize that the noise of domestic politics does not erase the need for crisis management. Diplomatic, economic, and military communication matters precisely because competition is intensifying. Such channels cannot guarantee restraint, but their maintenance gives governments a means of clarifying intentions before a misunderstanding becomes a confrontation.
Meetings between national leaders can serve a similar purpose. Beyond their ceremonial functions, they allow governments to test assumptions, communicate limits, and establish expectations. Nuclear deterrence supplies an especially

articles.title_orig: Chinese woman snaps up nearly 200 parking spots to flip to neighbours for profit
articles.title_zh: Chinese woman snaps up nearly 200 parking spots to flip to neighbours for profit
articles.content_orig:
Residents argue that parking is a vital community asset that should not be monopolised by anyone seeking financial gain from resale
A woman in central China invested 14 million yuan (US$2 million) to acquire 196 parking spaces in a residential community, later selling them at a significant mark-up, which led to furious residents suing her.
The lawsuit centred around a residential block, the name of which was not disclosed, located in Changsha, Hunan province.
The property project was completed and put on the market in 2018. At the time, many were sceptical about the community’s prospects due to a lack of essential public facilities such as shops, schools, and public transport options. Consequently, there was little interest in both the flats and the parking spaces, according to Hunan TV.
Despite this pessimism, a woman surnamed Wu snapped up 196 parking spots in a single transaction, representing 40 per cent of the project’s total parking inventory, for a sum of 14 million yuan. The developer, facing severe cash constraints, agreed to her purchase.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX in Talks to Borrow $40 Billion to Buy Nvidia Chips
articles.title_zh: SpaceX in Talks to Borrow $40 Billion to Buy Nvidia Chips
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The company is reportedly looking for about $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt.
On SpaceX's August earnings call, CEO Elon Musk said the company had "decided to build exclusively on Nvidia" for its AI initiatives.
CFO Bret Johnsen previously hinted at full-year capital spending near $65 billion for SpaceX.
SpaceX shares fell 1% in after-hours trading on Tuesday after reports that the company is seeking $40 billion in financing to buy Nvidia chips, a fresh sign of how much capital the AI buildout is consuming.
The rocket manufacturing company's financing effort is expected to be led by Apollo Global Management, the Financial Times reported, citing people familiar with the matter. The company is looking for about $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt.

Pimco was among a small group of lenders in talks to fund the deal, the report said, adding that the transaction is expected to close in 2027. SpaceX and Nvidia did not confirm the report, the newspaper said.
The borrowing would tighten a tie Musk has already made public. On SpaceX's August earnings call, he said the company had "decided to build exclusively on Nvidia" for its AI initiatives because he considered the Vera Rubin platform the best AI architecture, and that SpaceX valued the partnership.
For Nvidia, a committed buyer of that size helps amid rising competition from rival chipmakers.
SpaceX's AI effort is now the bulk of the company, not a side project. After folding xAI into the group in February, it has been building the Colossus data-center clusters and renting that capacity to outside customers while also training its own Grok models.
The company's capital expenditures were $18.4 billion in the second quarter, and $15.8 billion of that went to AI infrastructure, about 86% of the total, against roughly $1.4 billion for Starlink and $1.2 billion for the space business. First-half spending was about $28.5 billion, while operations generated only about $3.5 billion of cash.
CFO Bret Johnsen told analysts on the August 4 earnings call that the next two quarters should look "very similar," which would put full-year capital spending near $65 billion if that pace holds. He said new compute capital is paying back in less than a year, and the company is aiming for a $100 billion annualized revenue run rate by year-end.

articles.title_orig: Fuel industry warns truck stops not to sell red dye diesel after Trump lifts restrictions
articles.title_zh: Fuel industry warns truck stops not to sell red dye diesel after Trump lifts restrictions
articles.content_orig:
Truck stops nationwide were warned to “proceed with caution” Tuesday by a major industry group after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to promote the use of “red dye” diesel fuel.
Red dye diesel is exempt from federal excise taxes because it is intended for farm equipment and other off-road uses.
The order, signed before farmers in Nebraska on Monday night, aims to bring down fuel prices by “temporarily” allowing highway use of red dye diesel fuel, according to a White House statement .
U.S. voters are deeply frustrated by the high price of gas, and the Trump administration is under intense pressure to bring down fuel costs before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Monday’s order instructs Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to “defer certain diesel fuel tax payment obligations and to provide penalty relief to the extent permitted by law.”
It does not waive the federal taxes, because only Congress can eliminate a tax.
Following Trump’s directive, the Energy Marketers of America warned gas stations to “proceed with caution.”
“Whether relief is available, whom it covers, and on what conditions depend on Treasury determinations and guidance not yet issued,” the group said. “Deferral is not forgiveness.”
Moreover, the order does not “resolve EPA or state restrictions” on the dyed variety of diesel fuel, the EMA said.
Other trucking and gas industry groups sounded a similar note of caution.
“The White House appears to be trying to encourage the supply chain to move toward selling dyed fuel in non-traditional ways,” the Society of Independent Gasoline Marketers of America and the National Association of Truck Stop Owners said in a note to their members.
“We do not expect most reputable diesel retailers and fuel marketers to do this,” they said. “First, the tax is still owed, so there’s limited upside.”
In addition, “the logistical challenges outweigh any visible upside: Residual dye lingers in tanks and fuel systems.”
For most fuel sellers, “the liability and customer risk outweigh any temporary, uncertain benefit.”
The White House did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
A group representing independent long-haul truckers also suggested Trump’s move would provide little benefit to its members.
“Allowing the wider use of red-dyed diesel will provide minimal relief. Market stability is essential to bring down costs for the long haul,” said Todd Spencer, president of the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association.
Since the war with Iran began, the price of diesel has surged from $3.76 per gallon to $6.32 as of Tuesday, a nearly 70% increase.
The Iran conflict is not the only conflict contributing to diesel’s skyrocketing price.
A recent escalation of the Ukraine-Russia war has included strikes by Ukrainian drones on Russian refineries.
Russia, traditionally one of the world’s large diesel exporters, has responded to the attacks by imposing a diesel export ban through at least the end of October.
Trump has urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russia’s diesel infrastructure .
“Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump told reporters in early September . “There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting the world.”
Oil prices also remain sharply elevated since the beginning of the year. Brent crude oil, which traded Tuesday night above $101 per barrel, is up more than 66% since the start of the year.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine Drone Attack Sets Fire On Oil Tanker With 23 Indian Crew Members
articles.title_zh: Ukraine Drone Attack Sets Fire On Oil Tanker With 23 Indian Crew Members
articles.content_orig:
Two injured crew members from one of the ships have been sent for treatment
A civilian cargo ship has sunk and its crew is missing after being attacked by drones in the Black Sea, Bulgarian officials say.
A second vessel - carrying grain - was also hit within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said. Its 18 crew were rescued.
Radev did not say who was behind the attacks, which come as Russia intensifies strikes in the Black Sea, particularly the eastern side, as part of its war against Ukraine.
Moscow has not commented on the latest incident, a day after it was accused by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of striking a civilian vessel carrying corn. EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the attacks were "unacceptable".
Air and sea drones were involved in the attacks at about 03:00 (23:00 GMT), some 70 miles (112 km) off the coastal town of Byala in eastern Bulgaria, Radev said.
The sunken ship was flying under the flag of Togo, he said. Named the Alfa Watan, it was a Turkish-owned general cargo ship and was reportedly heading for Sulina, Romania.
It is not clear what the Alfa Watan was carrying or how many people were on board.
A Bulgarian vessel was close by, but when they arrived all they saw was an overturned boat and rafts as well as life jackets. A search operation has been launched.
Radev said Bulgarian sailors had rescued the crew members from the second ship - including two who were injured in a fire on board. Eleven were Turkish and seven Indian nationals. That ship, the Able, was flying the flag of Palau and transporting grain.
Its last reported position was five nautical miles (9km) from the Alfa Watan.
Radev condemned the strikes as "a flagrant violation of maritime law".
He told reporters: "Such an attack within the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone is absolutely unacceptable."
He did not accuse Russia of carrying out the strikes, but referred to the war in Ukraine, saying: "As I have long maintained, if this war is not halted in time, it will continue to expand its geographical reach and increase risks, including the risk of a global conflict."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on X: "The situation in the Black Sea is increasingly concerning.
"Commercial ships â and innocent crews â are being targeted, with lives already lost at sea," she said. "While exact circumstances of these incidents are still being established, the developments are very concerning."
"Attacks on civilian shipping are unacceptable."
Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea is just over 29,000 sq km (11,197 sq miles), about 6% of the total size of the Black Sea.
A separate attack on Tuesday, near Odesa, saw a crew member killed and seven more injured. The ship was flying the flag of the Marshall Islands, according to Ukrainian media.
On Sunday, Russia's defence ministry said it would intensify its strikes across Ukraine in response to comments made by Zelensky earlier last week, in which he said Kyiv would ramp up its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

articles.title_orig: ‘Not exactly his favorite senator’: Susan Collins distances herself from Trump in Maine debate
articles.title_zh: ‘Not exactly his favorite senator’: Susan Collins distances herself from Trump in Maine debate
articles.content_orig:
Republican challenged by Democrat Troy Jackson in critical Senate race says she opposes Iran war and Canada tariffs
Susan Collins, the Republican senator for Maine , pointedly distanced herself from Donald Trump in a televised debate with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson on Tuesday, as she sought to present an image of independence in a state that has voted against Trump three times.
Proclaiming herself as not the US president’s “favorite senator”, Collins made the highly unusual boast for a Republican that she had voted with Joe Biden, a Democrat, more than 90% of the time when he was president. She also emphasized her differences with her fellow Republicans , saying she voted against her own party more than any other senator.
Collins’s defensiveness came amid a determined onslaught from Jackson, 58, a veteran former state legislator who was getting his first chance to present himself to a broad audience since replacing Graham Platner as the Democratic candidate in a contest that could be vital to the party’s hopes of winning the Senate.
Platner, a former harbor master, was forced to withdraw from the race in July after facing sexual assault allegations, which he denied, leaving Democrats racing against the clock to replace a candidate who had built up momentum campaigning on a populist progressive platform.
Jackson painted Collins as a Trump loyalist, saying she voted with the president 96% of the time. He also doggedly focused on her 2018 vote for the conservative supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, tying it to the court’s subsequent overturning of Roe v Wade, which had for half a century guaranteed the national right to abortion.
“Tonight is about who you stand with when it matters,” Jackson said in a pithy opening statement. “Eight years ago today, Maine women went to DC and begged Senator Collins not to confirm Brett Kavanaugh, but she did it anyways.
“He helped overturn Roe v Wade, and today she says she has no regrets. Would you trust her to pick the next supreme court justice?”
Collins, 73, who has been a senator since 1996, has frequently presented herself as a moderate who stands against more radical trends in her own party. The posture is in line with Maine’s profile as a more Democratic-leaning state, which Trump has not won in any of his three presidential campaigns and which has voted for Democratic presidential candidates in every election since 1992.
Nevertheless, Collins went to unusual lengths to differentiate herself from Trump on a range of issues, including the war with Iran, which she said she voted to end nine times, calling it “not well thought out”.
Collins reacted with something close to alarm when the moderator, Gregg Lagerquist, said Trump had suggested that the president might pay a campaign visit to Maine.
after newsletter promotion
“I don’t think that President Trump is going to come to Maine,” she said. “He’s talking about going to a lot of different states. I’ve heard nothing from his office, and I’m not exactly his favorite senator.”
Collins stressed her differences with the president on specific issues pertinent to the Maine economy, including rural healthcare and tariffs against Canada, with which the state shares a border.
“I have been the most outspoken opponent of the tariffs on Canada,” she said. “Canada is not China. It’s our neighbor and our friends.”
Polls show the two candidates running neck and neck.

articles.title_orig: Germany's former foreign intelligence chief arrested on suspicion of espionage and attempted treason
articles.title_zh: Germany's former foreign intelligence chief arrested on suspicion of espionage and attempted treason
articles.content_orig:
August Hanning served as president of federal intelligence service from 1998 to 2005
A former head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service has been arrested on suspicion of treason and spying on behalf of an overseas intelligence agency, in what prosecutors suspect could be the most egregious national security breach since the cold war.
August Hanning, 80, was head of the federal intelligence service (BND) – which operates outside Germany to gather information across the fields of political, economic and military intelligence – between 1998 and 2005.
He was arrested at his home in Nordwalde near Münster early on Tuesday. His former chief of staff, identified only as Manfred D, was arrested at the same time in Bavaria, on suspicion of “aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage”, according to a prosecutor’s statement. Media pictures showed Hanning, dressed in an open-necked white shirt, being taken from his redbrick house to a bullet-proof vehicle by masked officers.
Manfred D, who continued to work for Hanning’s successors at the BND after Hanning’s departure until the present day, is accused of using his role to gain access to classified information which he then handed to Hanning “in exchange for payment”, the prosecutors’ statement continued.
“The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the federal intelligence service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings,” the statement said.
Prosecutors believe that Hanning intended to resell the documents as part of a paid consulting role he had built up after leaving the BND, prosecutors added. To what extent and to whom he disseminated them remains part of an ongoing investigation.
He is accused of using the information to “draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service”, prosecutors said. It was unclear if this information had reached its intended recipient, they added.
Over several years, Hanning is also believed to have passed on potentially sensitive political information, in part based on information passed to him by Manfred D, to a close contact representing a separate foreign intelligence service.
Hanning and his legal team denied the allegations following his arrest. There was no immediate response from Manfred D. or his legal representatives.
Several properties connected to both men were searched simultaneously on Tuesday, including in Berlin.
Manfred D is due to appear before judges at the federal court of justice in Karlsruhe later on Tuesday, while Hanning is scheduled to appear on Wednesday.
The allegations prompted shock in German political and intelligence circles, where memories resurfaced of historic espionage scandals. Hanning is thought to be the most prominent person to be accused of treason in Germany since Günter Guillaume, one of Willy Brandt’s personal aides, was exposed as a long-term Stasi agent in 1974. The “Guillaume affair” brought an abrupt end to Nobel peace prize-winning Brandt’s career, as he swiftly resigned as chancellor of West Germany.
Marc Henrichmann, chair of the Bundestag’s intelligence oversight committee, said in a statement to AFP: “Whoever allies themselves with the enemies of our liberal democracy will be found out.” If proven to be true, Hanning’s alleged behaviour would represent “trampling his official duties underfoot”, he added.
Konstantin von Notz of the Greens, a prominent member of the same committee, urged the federal government to establish as soon as possible the “potential intelligence-related damage” that might have been done by Hanning’s alleged betrayal of Germany’s official secrets.
“This is a truly outrageous and deeply disturbing story,” he told Der Spiegel.
Suspicions over Hanning’s activities emerged as a result of an investigation into the kidnappings of the children from a prominent Hamburg business family, which is the focus of a major trial in the north German port city.
Investigators were led to Hanning over allegations, which he denies, that he helped Christina Block, the heiress of a steak restaurant dynasty, to organise the violent cross-border seizure in Denmark of her children from her estranged husband who has custody of two of their children. Block denies the charges.
After he left the BND, Hanning worked as a global consultant in the fields of security and business, based on his credentials as former intelligence chief. He is considered to have been well connected with government and business sectors in Russia and China, and also had contacts with top-ranking intelligence authorities in Israel.
Hanning was an officer stationed at the embassy-equivalent organisation for West Germany in communist East Berlin. After his role as president of the BND ended in 2005, he became the highest-ranking official in Germany’s security sector as the head of all security agencies under the federal interior minister Wolfgang Schäuble.

articles.title_orig: Houthis attack Aden airport as fighting intensifies in Yemen
articles.title_zh: Houthis attack Aden airport as fighting intensifies in Yemen
articles.content_orig:
Two Houthi missiles target Yemen’s Aden International Airport
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has accused the Houthis of firing ballistic missiles and drones at the main international airport under its control, as Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted another missile north of its capital, Riyadh.
In a statement on Wednesday, the Ministry of Transport said the Houthis targeted the runway and passenger terminal at the airport with at least two ballistic missiles and several drones.
“One of the missiles landed near the runway minutes before the Yemeni flight from Cairo was to land,” it said. “We cancelled the landing of the incoming flight from Cairo [in Egypt] and diverted its route to Jeddah [in Saudi Arabia] to protect the passengers.”
The ministry also said it evacuated the airport terminal and removed two planes from the tarmac during the attacks.
It added, “This incident could easily have turned a civilian flight into a horrific humanitarian disaster, claiming the lives of dozens of innocent people in an instant.”
Aden airport is the main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside Houthi control in the city that has been the seat of the government since the takeover of the capital, Sanaa, by the Iran-supported group in 2014.
The Houthis said in a statement they targeted “Saudi military supplies” arriving at the Badr camp near the airport with ballistic missiles. Saudi Arabia backs Yemen’s government.
Separately, the Saudi-led military coalition fighting in Yemen said it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile, launched by the Houthis, north of Riyadh.
In a social media post, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, said it was tracking the launch platform used in the attack via an intelligence system over Sanaa, and promised to destroy it.
The Houthis said in statements on Tuesday and overnight into Wednesday that they had targeted Saudi international airports in Riyadh and Abha.
The intensified fighting in Yemen comes amid mounting regional tensions set off by the US-Israel war on Iran. The Saudi-backed government forces launched a counteroffensive against the Houthis to retake the Red Sea port of Mocha and areas around the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
Fighting has concentrated in the southwestern province of Taiz.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa, described “all-out battles to take over the ground, the highlands and the mountains east of Bab al-Mandeb”.
“It’s a battle to take over the strategic western part of Taiz, and whoever controls the wider vicinity will overlook the region and have dominant military control,” he said.
“For the Yemeni government to take control of Mocha and the strategic bases and locations along the Red Sea coast, it first has to drive the Houthis off the mountains east of Mocha.”
Pakistan and Turkiye on Monday agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under their mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia and rapidly deploy forces to the Gulf kingdom to counter Houthi attacks.

articles.title_orig: Couple Charged With Conspiring to Abuse Numerous Surrogate Children
articles.title_zh: Couple Charged With Conspiring to Abuse Numerous Surrogate Children
articles.content_orig:
A California couple has been arrested on child abuse charges following an investigation into a surrogacy scheme involving at least 21 children ranging in age from a few months to 13 years, authorities said Tuesday.
Silvia Zhang and her husband, Guojun Xuan face several counts of child abuse and conspiracy to commit child abuse, accessory after the fact, and dissuading a witness, Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said.
“This case is unprecedented. It is horrific. And the physical abuse, beating and punishment that these very young children received, is despicable,” Hochman said during a news conference Tuesday morning.
Prosecutors are seeking a $100 million bail for the couple because of the serious nature of the charges and due to their flight risk potential, Hochman said. They will be arraigned at the Pasadena courthouse later Tuesday.
Fifteen children were removed from the couple’s opulent home in Arcadia last year after an allegation of abuse, and another six living elsewhere were also located. They ranged in age from 2 months to 13 years, with most between 1 and 3. Police believe Zhang gave birth to one or two of the children while the rest were born by surrogate.
Hochman said the couple set up a surrogacy agency that they operated from their home and used that agency to hire surrogates throughout the US.
“The house could only be described as a house of horrors for these incredible young children,” Hochman said.
Zhang and Xuan were first arrested in May 2025 after a hospital reported that their 2-month-old infant had a traumatic head injury, the result of a nanny at the home violently shaking the baby, according to Arcadia police.
Arcadia police did not file charges at the time, in order to finish a full investigation, they said.
21 children removed from California home amid abuse investigation and claims of surrogate mothers being misled
Hochman said the couple set up three rooms they called learning centers, where the children spent several hours a day sitting at desks under the supervision of nannies.
Through an extensive surveillance system including motion-activated cameras, the couple watched as their nannies subjected the children to daily beatings and physical abuse, he said.
The nannies were told “not to leave any physical marks on the children,” Hochman said.
Before police arrived to investigate in May 2025, Zhang and Xuan told the children to deny they had been beaten.
Police examined surveillance footage that showed the nannies beating the children. They issued an arrest warrant for the nanny seen hurting a 2-month-old infant, Chunmei Li, but she could not be found.
“There will be a reckoning” for the defendants, one of whom faces more than 17 years in prison if convicted, Hochman said.
When asked about the couple’s motivation, Hochman said that was part of the ongoing investigation, as is the parentage of each of the children.
Mitchell Krems, Xuan’s attorney, previously told ABC7 that Xuan’s goal was to raise children who become productive adults.
“The reason he has all these children is because he wants them to contribute to society. He is not a man who is self-indulgent,” Krems said. “Some who are wealthy might spend on jewelry or cars, but he is actually spending his resources to help his children become educated so that they can be the philosophers, the physicians, the researchers and the inventors that help society.”
Krems did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment on Tuesday’s arrests.
Surrogacy is an agreement between parties to have a woman become pregnant, typically through an embryo transfer, and deliver a baby for another parent.
The practice has no federal regulation, leaving it up to states to set the rules if they choose to allow it.
California is considered a “surrogacy-friendly state” because it has clear laws governing the process. Both sides are required to have lawyers, and there must be a written, notarized contract before an embryo transfer takes place.
Investigators have said they were looking into whether the couple had misled surrogates around the country. At least eight women had come forward to say they were aggressively pursued by the couple to serve as surrogates.
The women, many of whom were first-time surrogates, say they were given misleading or incomplete information about the couple’s family situation and intentions.
At least one, Kayla Elliott, is now trying to get custody of a baby she birthed for the couple.

RAPID CITY, S.D. (KOTA) - Rapid City freshmen are getting hands-on lessons in the consequences of risky decisions through the annual Freshman Impact: Caught in the Moment program.
The full-day program is being held Tuesday, Oct. 6, at Central High School, and Wednesday, Oct. 7, at the South Dakota National Guard Armory for Stevens High School students. Nearly 1,000 freshmen are expected to take part.
At Central, students tried navigating a driving course while wearing Fatal Vision goggles that simulate impairment.
“It was like, you know, those kaleidoscopes where you look into them. It’s all spinny triangles,” said student Henry Zimmerman.
The program includes stations on seat belt use, CPR, substance use and online safety. A new station features a state snowplow, teaching students about the truck’s blind spots and the dangers they can pose on the road.
In the afternoon, students see a mock crash response involving first responders, followed by a mock funeral and sentencing hearing.
“We’re trying to do a little bit of mind changing where they make better choices,” said Rick McPherson, director of Freshman Impact.
Organizers say emergency vehicles, equipment, lights and sirens at the schools and armory are part of the planned prevention exercise. Visitors must sign in at the welcome desk.

articles.title_orig: Nobel winner Halzen says years of October 'misery' finally over
articles.title_zh: Nobel winner Halzen says years of October 'misery' finally over
articles.content_orig:
Halzen is the principal investigator of the NSF IceCube Neutrino Observatory, the world’s largest telescope.
Will Cushman, wcushman@wisc.edu, (563) 543-2318
Today, Francis Halzen , a University of Wisconsin–Madison professor of physics, was named the recipient of the Nobel Prize in physics at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, Sweden.
The prize was conferred for Halzen’s contributions to our understanding of the astrophysical particles known as neutrinos, produced by the universe’s most energetic events.
Watch the livestream of the press conference with Professor Halzen and leaders from UW–Madison.
“This is a celebration of a very unusual project,” says Halzen. “It is difficult to imagine that we could have pulled this off anywhere but at UW–Madison with its unique research infrastructure. The success of this project involved some luck, and I was fortunate to be at UW, where unconventional ideas can thrive and where I had the support of a remarkable community, from talented engineers at the Physical Sciences Laboratory to long-time colleagues on the faculty and supportive administrators. It is hard to imagine this project happening anywhere else.”
Halzen is the principal investigator of the NSF IceCube Neutrino Observatory , the world’s largest — and perhaps strangest — telescope. The U.S. National Science Foundation-funded observatory is operated by an international collaboration of scientists led by the Wisconsin IceCube Particle Astrophysics Center based at UW–Madison.
Embedded in a cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice, IceCube uses thousands of light sensors to survey the universe for neutrinos, nearly massless particles that rarely interact with other matter. Neutrinos provide information about the workings of black holes, galaxies and other objects in the cosmos.
“IceCube is like no other telescope in the world,” says UW–Madison interim Chancellor Eric M. Wilcots. “And there is no other scientist quite like Francis Halzen, whose idea to create a neutrino detector under almost a mile of ice has led to a remarkable multinational and multi-institutional scientific collaboration and a fundamental shift in how we think about the universe.”
Unlike the neutral neutrino, cosmic rays are charged particles whose paths cannot be traced directly back to their sources. But the powerful cosmic accelerators that produce them, like supermassive black holes, will also produce neutrinos. These so-called “ghost particles” travel nearly undisturbed from their accelerators, giving scientists an almost direct pointer to their source.
Along with observations by other telescopes, the neutrino first detected by IceCube provided the first-ever evidence of a source of high-energy cosmic rays, whose origins have been notoriously difficult to pinpoint since their discovery over 100 years ago by 1936 physics Nobel laureate Victor Hess.
In 2013, IceCube announced the first detection of high-energy neutrinos from outside the solar system. The finding opened a new era of “multi-messenger astrophysics” in which not only light but particles like neutrinos and gravitational waves can provide us with information about distant cosmological events, like supermassive black holes located at the heart of galaxies. The discovery won the 2013 Physics World Breakthrough of the Year Award.
Four years later, in September 2017, IceCube detected a high-energy neutrino from a supermassive black hole at the center of a distant galaxy in the direction of the constellation Orion. More recently, IceCube provided the first evidence of high-energy neutrino emission from an active galaxy 47 million light-years away, in 2022, and from the Milky Way, in 2023. These detections demonstrated that all three of these sources produce cosmic rays. Most recently, IceCube was successfully upgraded, marking the observatory’s first significant expansion since its completion 15 years ago.
With this award, Halzen becomes the sixth physicist connected to UW–Madison to earn the Nobel Prize. It’s the 23rd Nobel Prize tied to UW–Madison overall , in a legacy that spans medicine, chemistry, economics, engineering and physics. The last active UW–Madison faculty member to win a Nobel Prize was Howard Temin in 1975 , honored for his discovery of reverse transcriptase — a breakthrough that reshaped molecular biology and deepened understanding of diseases like Hepatitis B and HIV.
Tags: faculty awards , IceCube , Nobel Prize , physics , research
UW–Madison has been named the top volunteer-producing university since 2017.
“Best Value Schools” ranking also jumps 23 spots, placing UW–Madison 24th in the nation.
WSUM rules the airwaves thanks to creative freedom and hard work.
The project ensures that UW–Madison’s efforts at IceCube remain at the forefront of neutrino astronomy for years to come.

articles.title_orig: FlyDubai Attacker Was Part of Pilot Hiring Spree at Fast-Growing Airline
articles.title_zh: FlyDubai Attacker Was Part of Pilot Hiring Spree at Fast-Growing Airline
articles.content_orig:
TEL AVIV — The pilot accused of trying to bring down an Israel-bound flight had been planning a 9/11-style attack by crashing into the country’s main airport in Tel Aviv, a Middle Eastern official has told NBC News.
The pilot, identified by NBC News as Hamman al-Hamammi , told investigators Monday that he wanted to evade Israel’s defenses and crash into the Ben Gurion Airport or another building, said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the person was not authorized to speak publicly.
Multiple sources from three agencies briefed on the investigation and a diplomat in the Middle East identified al-Hammami, an Omani citizen. Authorities have not officially released the identity.
He is currently being questioned by investigators in the United Arab Emirates after he was transferred from Saudi Arabia. The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was diverted to an airport in Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely, after last week’s dramatic midair incident.
Emirati authorities said Saturday that the pilot attacked his fellow pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar , with a crash ax and tried to take control of the aircraft’s flight controls.
The jet, which was carrying 174 passengers, most of them Israeli, then plummeted 14,000 feet in just 29 seconds, according to data from the aviation tracking service Flightradar24, causing panic onboard.
Machchhar, an Indian national and a veteran pilot of 17 years, said in a call Friday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that his fellow pilot told him he was going to pray, something he didn’t consider unusual as observant Muslims pray five times a day.
A few minutes later, he said he felt a strong blow to the head. “Because of his initial blows, my vision was almost like nothing, and I was completely blurred out,” he added. “The next feeling that I had was that the aircraft was sharply going down.”
A video of the call was released by Netanyahu’s office.
Initially, Machchhar said, he thought there was “catastrophic damage to the aircraft,” but once the blows kept coming, he “realized that it’s not the aircraft, it’s the other guy who was in the cockpit with me.”
In a separate call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, also Friday, Machchhar said he managed to open the cockpit’s door on the second attempt, despite the blows raining down.
“I gave everything that I had and just went for the door and opened the door. And thankfully, people were waiting to pounce back,” he said.
Focus has shifted onto the missed security signals ahead of the flight.
Citing sources familiar with the matter, The Wall Street Journal reported Saturday that al-Hammami had “previously been banned from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted radical ideological views.”
It is unclear how a citizen of Oman, an Arab country with no diplomatic relations with Israel, was allowed to fly the plane carrying Israelis to Tel Aviv.
According to Israeli law, airlines must provide information about passengers and crew members, including their names and nationalities, up to 48 hours before a flight.
Israeli investigators are leaning toward the assessment that the pilot was acting as a lone wolf, according to an Israeli official and a source familiar with the matter, although they said there is still more to learn about what led to his radicalization.
In the meantime, Netanyahu has called on the head of the National Security Council to appoint an examiner to review “all security aspects” of Israel’s civil aviation in the aftermath of the incident.
Elsewhere, Vice President JD Vance underlined the concerns about potential security failures.
“That person should not have been flying an airline, and so we’re certainly looking at our procedures within the United States to make sure that people who are obviously flight risks are not getting behind the wheel of an airplane,” he told a reporter at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, on Monday.
Keir Simmons is chief international correspondent for NBC News, based in Dubai.

Tropical Depression Nine has formed off the coast of Mexico in the Gulf of America, and forecasts show it will be the Atlantic's first hurricane this season, making a dangerous landfall threat to the U.S.
The system is currently getting better organized, and the National Hurricane Center (NHC) said it is forecast to be a tropical storm on Wednesday and a hurricane on Thursday.

Now the question turns to what the Southeastern Conference, along with the University of Alabama, will do about the impending weather event. Officials from both schools involved, and the SEC, have been monitoring the situation over the past two days.

If this storm continues to strengthen, I would imagine these entities will be doing more than just monitoring. Every school, and conference, has contingency plans for events like this, especially in areas prone for hurricanes.

articles.title_orig: Jaguar targets young Americans with Type 01 EV – but it’s too long for UK parking spaces
articles.title_zh: Jaguar targets young Americans with Type 01 EV – but it’s too long for UK parking spaces
articles.content_orig:
Latest model is launching in New York to target rich US buyers – and is more than 5.2 metres long and 2 metres wide
It has no rear window, will not fit into a UK parking space and – starting at £130,000 – ($172,000) is aimed squarely at rich tech industry buyers driving the wide open roads of America.
Jaguar’s electric car, the Type 01, was launched in New York on Tuesday night and marks the culmination of a two-year rebrand that has been one of the most scrutinised in automotive history.
Bosses hope the vehicle will appeal to a younger, richer audience than the manufacturer’s previous “shrinking and ageing” customer base of “men in their 50s”, said Rawdon Glover, 58, Jaguar’s managing director.
With an ultra-long bonnet, low roof and muscular design, the Type 01 is a sharp departure from its predecessor, the F-Type. It is also double the F-Type’s starting price of about £62,000.
Buyers are likely to be rich, “urban” and “very design literate, very technology literate”, Glover said. “The person making this purchase will be choosing the car because it’s a bold choice.”
A senior JLR executive close to the Type 01 project put it more bluntly: “It’s the type of car that you park up and everybody stops and says: ‘Fucking hell, what have you just turned up in?’”
The launch comes at a critical juncture for parent company Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), which has grappled with falling sales as cheaper Chinese rivals eat into its UK market share. It is still recovering from a massive cyber-attack last year that cost the economy an estimated £1.9bn.
JLR recently announced 4,000 job cuts in an attempt to save £1.7bn over two years, citing “intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty”. The Guardian understands Jaguar employees working on the Type 01 programme were offered voluntary redundancy along with the rest of JLR’s non-manufacturing workforce.
The car will go on sale in early 2027, with the first deliveries anticipated in the second half of the year.
“It’s really important that we put Jaguar back on a more solid financial footing,” Glover said. Asked if doubling prices would be effective, he said it was better than “to toil away as we have done for the last two decades in the volume premium space”.
Range Rover also unveiled its first fully electric model in September with a starting price of £154,070 compared with £107,530 for its combustion engine predecessor.
Waning demand in China, a key market for luxury cars, has also hit Jaguar hard. Glover revealed that the Type 01 will not launch in the country for “a couple of years. We’ve decided just to hold off on that.”
However, he added that China would eventually be “an important part of the equation … it’s very difficult for any car manufacturer to exclude the single largest car market in the world”.
after newsletter promotion
PB Balaji, the JLR chief executive, has said the parent company will pivot towards North America and target more sales to millionaires and billionaires to turn its fortunes around.
Glover admitted that while the Type 01’s launch was in New York, it “absolutely” could have been in Silicon Valley instead, reflecting the type of buyer Jaguar is targeting. He recently took a prototype to the offices of Nvidia, the California-based AI company, whose boss, Jensen Huang, had a ride and “loved it”.
The car has no rear window, instead mounting a rear-facing camera where a traditional mirror would be. The car produces more than 1,000 horsepower and Jaguar says it will travel up to 400 miles on a single charge.
It follows a controversial rebrand that started with an ad in late 2024 featuring stern-faced models without a car in sight. The ad prompted a backlash online and was followed by the Type 00 concept car that was unveiled in “Miami pink”, which Donald Trump described it as “woke” while Nigel Farage said Jaguar deserved to go bust.
Glover admitted the backlash “wasn’t always easy” but added: “The reality is we will need to attract a new audience.”
It is just as well: at 2 metres (6ft 5in) wide the Type 01 will hog the British country lanes frequented by Jaguar’s old customer base, while at more than 5.2 metres in length it will not fit in a standard 4.8 metre UK parking space.
“There are long cars out there on the market,” Glover argued, adding that a Land Rover Defender with a wheel on the back is longer than the Type 01, which he claimed had the “turning circle of a Fiat 500” with its all-wheel steering. “It is incredibly manoeuvrable.”
The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said: “Jaguar’s new EV is a crucial step in JLR’s plans to invest over £15bn in the UK, and another big vote of confidence in our world-class automotive industry. “This cutting-edge new model being designed, engineered and built in Britain will support thousands of jobs across the West Midlands and North West, and builds on over £1bn of UK automotive investment secured just last month – marking another step forward in our mission to reindustrialise Britain.”
